How a MAGA influencer with ties to Russia became Trump’s Arctic adviser
As Thomas Dans holds forth in the U.S. and abroad, it’s not always clear where the administration’s agenda ends and his own begins.
For more than 40 years, the U.S. Arctic Research Commission has advised Congress and the president on what to study in the frigid and dynamic far north, from the environment to military security. It’s typically done so without making waves, led by people well-versed in science and public policy.
That was until December, when President Donald Trump appointed a Texas venture capitalist and MAGA influencer with no formal background in science as the commission’s chair. Since then, Thomas Dans has traveled the globe generating headlines. Serving as the administration’s main voice on the Arctic, he’s advanced some of the president’s wildest ambitions, like a takeover of Greenland, and rankled NATO allies in the process.
Yet as Dans holds forth in the U.S. and abroad, it’s not always clear where the administration’s agenda ends and his own begins.
He has repeatedly said, for example, that the U.S. needs more icebreakers, ships that Trump has long viewed as critical to dominating the Arctic. In doing so, Dans has championed one shipbuilder in particular — Damen Shipyards, a Dutch company with which he had a business relationship.
“They’re the largest builder of icebreakers and ice-class vessels in the world,” Dans said at an event in Anchorage, Alaska, in April. At the time, his consultancy was working to help Damen land an icebreaker contract with the federal government.
As he’s spoken to audiences of government officials, diplomats, academics and journalists, Dans — who wears his Arctic commission lapel pin and exudes a professorial air — has also waded into foreign policy.
In the media and at public events, he’s backed Trump’s push to take over Greenland. And he’s advocated enthusiastically for closer U.S. relations with Russia — even as a bipartisan group of lawmakers calls for tougher sanctions on the country and more aid to Ukraine. Dans and Damen have long done business in Russia, and Dans has regularly shared social media posts that reflect a pro-Kremlin viewpoint.
“We want a peaceful Arctic, we want a peaceful world,” he said at an event a few days after he announced plans to travel to Moscow. “Russia and the United States gotta get along for that to happen.”
Opining so broadly on foreign policy is “far beyond” the Arctic Research Commission’s scientific mandate, said Fran Ulmer, who served as commission chair for more than nine years before being replaced by Trump in 2020. “And certainly outside the bounds of what the U.S. Arctic Research Commission has done in the past.”
Dans, whose consultancy Almiranta Strategies “advises investors and businesses working in the Arctic,” according to his profile on the Arctic commission’s website, is far from the first in the Trump administration to mingle public and personal interests. The finances of many senior officials and the industries they regulatehave drawn scrutiny as Trump has disarmed government safeguards against conflicts.
“It’s become standard for people to pursue their personal financial interest,” said Robert Weissman, co-president of the nonprofit watchdog Public Citizen.
Under the law, Dans’ position gives him access to government information from other federal agencies — an arrangement that could benefit his private interests. Such potential conflicts are typically governed by federal ethics rules. But the nature of Dans’ role affords him more leeway than other appointees. Commission members are not considered government employees and thus not required to file an ethics form disclosing conflicts.
Indeed, a White House official told ProPublica that Dans’ consulting work did not constitute a conflict of interest for that very reason.
“Tom Dans is doing a great job leading the Arctic Research Commission, and his shipbuilding expertise has helped him succeed in this role,” said White House spokesperson Anna Kelly. “The President appreciates all he is doing to advance American interests in the Arctic.”
The White House official said Dans is one of two commission members the law designates as representatives of “the interests of industry.”
Even so, Dans’ lack of research experience stands out. The other industry rep is a Ph.D. and former director of the United States Geological Survey.
Dans declined multiple requests to be interviewed for this story and did not respond to written questions from ProPublica, but he told The New York Timesthis year that his post did not preclude him from working in private business.
The Arctic commission has arguably never been more important. The region is warming at unprecedented rates, accelerating sea-level rise and causing severe weather in the U.S. and elsewhere. The melting ice also has geopolitical consequences. Russia and China are conducting joint military exercises in the far north. New shipping lanes have opened there. And mineral deposits are becoming potentially more accessible.
At a public appearance in July, Dans cited the commission’s four priorities: military and national security, energy security, economic development in the Arctic and “what we’ll call ‘community security.’” He did not define the term.
From Russia, With Love
Dans has long been taken with Russia, the country that has by far the most Arctic coastline.
His fondness dates back at least to seventh grade, when he says he was recruited to learn Russian in his Maryland public school. He later visited Moscow as an exchange student, then returned to work in finance in the mid-1990s.
He worked at a private equity fund financed by the U.S. Agency for International Development, which aimed to grow the private sector after the Soviet Union’s breakup. 924e2bb08fb3.text: The Epstein files fight that consumed the House last year is threatening to engulf Republicans all over again. Why it matters: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) is now just one Republican away from having the support he needs to force another politically painful Epstein vote — and he and his allies are hunting for the final GOP signature. Retiring Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) signed Massie's new discharge petition Monday, joining Massie and Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.). Massie and Mace told Axios they're actively targeting retiring Republicans and members in vulnerable districts for the fourth GOP signature that will get them the magic number to force a vote on the Epstein Files Transparency Act II. Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.), one of four Republicans who bucked President Trump and GOP leadership to sign Massie's first Epstein petition last year, told Axios she's considering signing again and has been having conversations with Massie. The big picture: The push is reviving one of the most disruptive fights of Trump's second term for House Republicans. Last year's Epstein discharge petition became a months-long headache for Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) and the White House before ultimately securing 218 signatures and forcing the issue onto the House floor. The bill passed with almost unanimous support in the House. The Epstein Files Transparency Act II would enforce and expand the release of remaining files at DOJ. "The Department of Justice continues to unlawfully withhold over 3 million Epstein files that should be released to the public. In addition, the DOJ is unlawfully maintaining heavy redactions on the files it is releasing," Massie wrote in a s tatement last month . Reality check: Even if Massie locks down the Republican support he needs this week, the House is set to leave Washington Thursday until after the November midterms, meaning any potential floor showdown would come post-election. Democrats also still need to provide the remaining signatures needed to reach the 218 required to discharge the bill, though Democratic leadership is encouraging members to sign on. Massie said he views that as just a logistical problem: "I haven't found any Democrat who's against it." Behind the scenes: Massie and Mace are focusing their recruitment efforts on Republicans who may have less to lose from crossing Trump. "I've got one hero slot left," Massie told Axios. Massie said he's talking to members in districts "where they're polling 10 points down," arguing they can either stay off the petition and risk losing anyway or sign it and make the issue part of their reelection pitch. Mace told Axios she is also "talking to Republicans who are leaving, and some Republican districts that we need to focus in on now." The intrigue: Boebert could provide the fourth Republican signature, but Massie says he doesn't expect the Republicans who took the political risk last year to do it again. "Anybody who did the first one is not obligated to put their head in the guillotine again," Massie said when asked about Boebert. "I think it's somebody else's turn." "Ralph Norman did it. He's a new one, and I think there are other new ones out there that we can get," he added. Between the lines: Massie is again accusing Johnson of manipulating the House calendar to deny him the time needed to force a vote. Johnson recently canceled two of the House's three remaining September work weeks. "He got a call from somebody that's above his pay grade that said, 'Take those two days off the calendar. Don't you dare give Massie the runway to get that plane off the ground,'" Massie alleged. But Johnson then formally moved to cancel session weeks, as Massie had predicted.

NGA official takes top AI job at Cyber Command
Ronzelle Green succeeds Reid Novotny, who pushed the combatant command to embrace the technology.
U.S. Cyber Command, the Pentagon’s combatant command responsible for planning and conducting military cyberspace operations, has a new artificial intelligence lead, a spokesperson confirmed on Tuesday.
“U.S. Cyber Command welcomes Rear Adm. Ronzelle Green as the Command’s new Chief Artificial Intelligence Officer and thanks Brig. Gen. Reid Novotny for his leadership and service,” a representative for the combatant command told Nextgov/FCW.
Green, who has worked at the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency for roughly three years — most recently as its director of geospatial intelligence innovation and research — is Cyber Command’s second-ever AI head. Novotny was the first official tapped for the position last November and served in a dual role as CAIO and as cyber force generation lead for the Pentagon.
The Record first reported the news of Green’s new role.
In a LinkedIn post last year announcing his new position, Novotny said “part of my role is embracing AI because like anything new, it is not the technology but yet the culture that is difficult to change.”
Novotny further outlined his approach to adopting AI during an April conversation with Axios, saying that he was solely focused on providing Cyber Command’s personnel with the best AI capabilities, regardless of their origin.
"To survive anywhere, just in case our operators want an open-source, made-in-China model or something very boutique, we have to create the infrastructure and that ability to be agile — no politics,” he said at the time.
In addition to his prior work at NGA, Green also brings more than 30 years of IT experience in the private sector and within intelligence community agencies to his new role as Cyber Command’s CAIO. He previously served as the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency’s chief information officer from 2020 until 2022, and has held roles within the Pentagon and National Counterterrorism Center throughout his career. Green is also a senior officer with the U.S. Coast Guard Reserve.
Cyber Command is led by Gen. Joshua Rudd, who also serves as head of the National Security Agency in a dual-hatted leadership role. NSA and Cyber Command, however, have taken somewhat differing approaches in their adoption of and focus on AI.
Under Rudd’s watch, NSA is in the process of a major reorganization that would establish five mission centers focused on AI, China, cybersecurity, combat support and global intelligence. The planned creation of the AI-focused center comes after NSA officials have voiced support in recent months for the use of more AI tools to bolster the agency's cyber and intelligence analysis operations.

- Published
OpenAI boss Sam Altman thinks people should have more faith in his company and others like it to do the right thing when it comes to artificial intelligence (AI) development amid rising public concerns about all the risks.
"The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it's the right thing and we feel the magnitude of this," Altman said on Tuesday during a conference in San Francisco.
However, Altman noted that people were justified in their fears around AI, as the capability of the tools has progressed rapidly.
"It doesn't take as much imagination as it used to for [us] to imagine how this could go wrong," he said. "I think the world is right to be afraid of this."
Altman's comments came during an appearance at an annual conference hosted by Salesforce.
It was the first time he had spoken publicly since a post went viral last week from an artificial intelligence researcher who quit the AI firm Anthropic. The researcher claimed AI could kill all humans by the end of the decade if left unchecked.
A handful of other AI executives and experts responded by saying they agreed with the assessment, though they didn't explain how they came to their conclusions or how exactly AI could accomplish such a thing.
The fervor over the claims has led to more scrutiny of AI development in recent days, and in response, Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei called for the pace of all AI development to slow, external and urged governments to regulate the industry.
The post was applauded by Altman, as well as co-founder of Google's DeepMind Demis Hassabis, and Elon Musk, owner of social media site X and AI assistant Grok.
But, some industry figures have also argued the fears were overblown and were being jumped on to generate hype for the industry.
During the conference, Altman addressed a crowd of hundreds of business people, telling them they should use AI tools to aid in their work, but also needed them in order to protect their businesses from potentially AI-enabled cyber attacks.
With no real AI regulation on the horizon in the US, Altman said Tuesday that he felt AI companies like his own were capable of essentially regulating themselves.
"We will get it right, I'm very confident in our company's and industry's ability to do this safely," Altman said, adding that he was sure that they would "keep alignment and safety way ahead of capabilities" and if they couldn't, they would "slow down or stop".
Jensen Huang, head of Nvidia, also said at the same conference that the AI firms should decide if new versions of the technology should be released and not be managed by outside forces.
"We don't need new laws or regulations," Huang said, adding that there should not be a "false choice" between the speed of innovation and the safety of AI products.
Nvidia is the biggest company in the world by valuation, with its profits having boomed as a result of rampant demand for the AI computing chips it makes.
"Safety is paramount. However, safety is an engineering problem," Huang said.
He added that if at any time a leader of an AI company lacks confidence in their product they should choose to not release it.
"That's a very obvious thing to do," Huang said. "Run as fast as you can, but if at any time you feel the institution is not in control, take a pause."
The idea of AI executives being left to entirely regulate themselves has struck some in the industry as a bad idea.
Jack Clark, an Anthropic executive and co-founder, told the BBC on Monday that leaving AI to be a "totally unregulated industry" was "rolling dice with immense risks".
Patrick Hillman, the chief operating officer of Logical Intelligence, which is chaired by Yann LeCun, a sage of the AI industry, noted Tuesday how little faith people have in tech companies to do anything truly in the public interest, external.
"The only institution that Americans might trust less than Washington these days is Silicon Valley. I have worked and lived in both and I assure you both have earned this scepticism," Hillman said.
"If you believe what you are building is dangerous, show us what you are prepared to stop doing," he added.
Leaders of OpenAI and Anthropic have said they have recently started working towards some sort of industry-wide agreement on safety.
Amodei, during a cameo at the conference on Tuesday, said Anthropic is now in "a dialogue with the rest of the industry" about committing to better safety standards and checks on AI tools and development.
He also said that one of the biggest surprises of the AI boom was not how the technology itself has advanced, but its broader impact.
"We didn't appreciate that it would lead to companies growing so fast, and how quickly they would become central to things," Amodei said.
OpenAI executive Chris Lehane said last week that the company was also working with other AI labs, external "to advance frontier AI standards, building a voluntary effort now, with or without government support." Those labs include Anthropic and Google Deepmind.
"With stakes this high, we cannot let the perfect become the enemy of the good," Lehane wrote.

Heathrow's third runway cannot be approved without changes to current climate policies, the government's advisers have said.
The Climate Change Committee (CCC) , externalsaid expansion can still go ahead but only if the aviation industry funds cleaner fuels and pays for machines that suck carbon dioxide out of the air.
Making the industry pay could push up the cost of flying with a return trip to Alicante costing around Â£150 more by 2050, and a return to New York up Â£400 in today's prices, it said.
Once built, the expanded airport would produce more carbon dioxide than any other single sector of the economy by 2050. Heathrow said expansion and climate goals were "not a choice" and it would deliver both.
"Our advice today is clear - Heathrow expansion is not currently compatible with the UK's Net Zero target," said Nigel Topping, the CCC chair.
"Government needs to ensure that the aviation industry takes responsibility for the emissions it creates and bears the costs of decarbonisation. Those conditions do not exist today."
The CCC report cannot block a new runway but it wants the government to pass legislation pushing responsibility for the long-term clean-up of aviation onto the industry.
The government would "carefully consider" the advice alongside other responses to its consultation according to the Department for Transport (DfT).
The government has an ongoing consultation which aims to judge any expansion against four tests - economy, climate, air quality and noise.
It does not approve a runway - that will come in a Commons vote expected later this year.
The Â£33bn project would raise Heathrow's capacity to 150 million passengers a year - up from 85 million.
A DfT spokesperson said any expansion would need to align with the country's climate targets, but added it "could deliver around Â£40bn to the economy and support up to 60,000 local jobs".
Technologies to cut emissions not at scale
The CCC has said carbon-removal machines must be deployed to cut more than a third of the emissions by 2050.
But almost none of that technology currently exists at scale, and the committee says credible plans exist for just 1% of these engineered removals needed by the late 2030s.
The committee argued making the industry rather than the government bear the costs of clean up was the fairest way of cutting carbon.
It believes the extra investment needed would likely be passed on to passengers but would be modest if spread over time.
Phased across 25 years, the cost of a flight to Alicante would rise by a few pounds a year - "less than a cup of coffee each way", Topping said.
However, the airline industry rejected the committee's approach.
Tim Alderslade, chief executive of Airlines UK, said carriers backed the government's target of net zero by 2050 but added that the transition "has to be affordable".
He warned that the CCC plan would put holidays "out of reach for millions" and turn the clock back to "a time when flying was the preserve of the rich".
Alderslade said the answer was airspace reform and scaling up sustainable fuels - such as those made from waste oil and plant matter.
On carbon removals, he added this was more challenging to deploy, and the aviation sector "cannot and should not shoulder the burden of scaling up this industry alone", and needed government support.
Some researchers believe the committee's advice does not act as a barrier to Heathrow's expansion and will fail to achieve the reduction in planet-warming gases required.
Dr Lois Pennington of the Tyndall Centre for Climate Change Research told the BBC that because cleaner fuel and carbon removal were unlikely to arrive at the scale needed, the only reliable way to stay within the UK's carbon limits was to stop the expansion of flying - or even to reduce it.
"We need to make sure that we are not flying more than we are now," she said.
Although the government has said it would consider the CCC's advice, ministers have left little doubt it intends to proceed with the expansion.
Last week in response to opposition questions, Chancellor John Healey said of the expansion: "After years of delay, years of indecision, years of often vexatious challenge, we have given the go-ahead to this project quite simply because the economic case stacks up and will help bring growth."
A formal vote in the House of Commons will still be needed to approve the planning framework for Heathrow's expansion, and that is expected later this year.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham opposed a third runway before entering Downing Street, arguing it would divert investment away from the north and "trap it in London and the South East".
The Mayor of London, Lord Sadiq Khan, has also raised concerns about its climate and noise impact.
The plan is also strongly opposed by many residents and councils under the flight path, with around 750 homes facing demolition to make way for the new runway amid long-standing concerns over noise and air pollution.

Alex Saab, a former Venezuelan official and aide to ex-Venezuelan President NicolÃ¡s Maduro, has pleaded guilty to money laundering charges in the US.
The US case against Saab has been closely watched as Maduro and his wife, former First Lady Cilia Flores, face trial next year in New York on weapon and drug charges, which they deny.
As part of the plea deal, Saab, 54, must forfeit $195m (Â£145m), and agree to co-operate fully with US prosecutors. He could face up to 20 years in prison.
Maduro and Flores were seized by the US military in a dramatic raid in Caracas in January. Saab's plea deal has raised speculation that he could testify against Maduro at trial.
Saab agreed to the deal on Tuesday in a court in Miami, Florida, having previously committed to fight the charges.
He was extradited to the US in May by Venezuela's acting President Delcy Rodriguez, who took over from Maduro.
Saab, a former Columbian businessman, was accused of embezzling money from a welfare plan for hungry Venezuelans, and transferring some of the proceeds to US bank accounts.
Venezuela has faced chronic shortages of food and medicine as a result of years of political and economic crisis.
"Criminals like Alex Saab who stole from the people of Venezuela and worked to exploit and misuse American financial institutions to fund illicit activities will be held accountable by this FBI," said FBI Director Kash Patel.
The plea deal does not specifically mention the case against Maduro in New York.
But it says that Saab "will not protect any person or identity through false information or omission".
This is the second US criminal case against Saab.
In 2020, he was extradited to face money laundering charges for allegedly siphoning $350m out of Venezuela.
But former US President Joe Biden granted him clemency in 2023 as part of a prisoner swap.

58f465c242eb.text: Ed Sheeran's world tour spiraled into chaos this week after one opener was removed, every remaining opening act quit and stadiums threatened to pull the plug on the tour. Why it matters: The turmoil reveals the power dynamics behind major concert tours, showing how even a global star like Sheeran can be forced to take a back seat on decisions about his own shows. Driving the news: All four of Sheeran's remaining supporting acts announced Tuesday that they were dropping out. Irish musicians Aaron Rowe and Beoga , as well as Danish band Lukas Graham , said Tuesday they were leaving the tour. Rowe was set to replace Macklemore as the opener for the U.S. shows, AP reports. Finneas, who was due to tour with Sheeran in South America later this year, also announced he was exiting the concert series, saying on Instagram that "artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed." Catch up quick: The moves came one day after rapper Macklemore, who was scheduled for most of the remaining tour dates, was dropped after using his sets to voice support for Palestinians and condemn the war in Gaza during shows on Sept. 4-5 at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. Macklemore told the MetLife crowd on Sept. 4 that he wanted to do the tour so he could "say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: 'Free Palestine.'" His performance included images of war-torn Gaza playing on the video board. The tour's promoters, Messina Touring Group, told Rolling Stone Monday that concert venues threatened to cancel shows unless Macklemore was dropped from the tour after his pro-Palestinian comments. Zoom in: Macklemore said the decision came after he spoke with Sheeran, alleging that the headliner faced pressure from stadium owners including Robert Kraft, owner of the New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium. According to Macklemore, Sheeran is typically "apolitical" and the recent round of backlash "challenged" him "in a way it never had before." The other side: Sheeran shared on Instagram Tuesday that the decision to remove Macklemore from the tour came not from him, but from the promoters. "I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living." Sheeran also wrote on Instagram that he didn't want his Loop Tour drawn into a public discussion around the war in Gaza. "I am appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine," Sheeran wrote on IG. "The suffering and pain caused on both sides is a human tragedy. There are too many wars across the world causing immeasurable pain, none of which should be tolerated." He added: "I have my personal views on the devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care. Nor does it mean I don't support causes in my own personal way." Zoom out: The turmoil over Sheeran's concert tour raises broader questions about political speech at concerts. As Rolling Stone notes, several stadiums that opposed Macklemore's appearance are publicly owned. One such venue is Raymond James Stadium in Tampa, Florida, which faced calls to cancel Ye's shows earlier this year due to his past antisemitic comments. The bottom line: Sheeran has tried to keep politics off his stage. The fight over Gaza has now made that neutrality difficult to maintain.

A 19th century magazine borrowed from a library in New Hampshire 132 years ago has finally been returned.
Concord Public Library said the overdue September 1894 issue of The Century Illustrated Monthly Magazine was returned last week after the library announced a freeze on fines.
The magazine was 48,220 days overdue and would have incurred a $12,055 (Â£8,950) fine.
The patron who returned the magazine, John, said it had been "hanging around" his house for decades, but he had no idea how it ended up in his home.
He decided to return the magazine after reading about the library's fine freeze in the local newspaper.
"We've witnessed many happy faces since announcing our fine freeze," Concord Public Library wrote on Facebook. , external
"Of course, we expected long overdue books to be returned, but certainly not something from the late 19th century!"
Concord Public Library declared a year-long amnesty on overdue fines from 1 September 2026, with plans to evaluate the effects of a "fine-free library".
"Understandably, it won't be placed back in circulation, but perhaps it deserves a spot in the Concord Room," the post on social media said, referring to a section of the library dedicated to local history.
"Thankfully, he won't have to pay the $12,055 fine for being 48,220 days overdue."

The US has announced visa restrictions targeting people it accuses of discriminating against South Africa's white minority, in the latest escalation of tensions between the two countries.
The Trump administration has criticised South Africa over several issues, including policies aimed at addressing racial inequality that it says discriminate against Afrikaners, descendants mainly of Dutch and French settlers.
South Africa has repeatedly denied the claim.
"The South African government has not adequately addressed the previously laid âout concerns," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement announcing the restrictions on Tuesday.
He said the visa restrictions would target those who promote "race-based discrimination, incite violence, or enable land confiscation without compensation in South Africa."
Rubio did not immediately name any individuals targeted by the restrictions.
Relations between the two countries have been on a downward spiral since President Donald Trump returned to office early last year, with the US leader cutting aid, expelling the South African ambassador and offering "refuge" to white South Africans fleeing "persecution."
But the South African government has repeatedly rejected allegations that it is persecuting white people or confiscating their land.
South Africa's latest crime statistics do not indicate that more white people have fallen victim to violent crime than other racial groups.
Trump offered refugee status to Afrikaners last year after South African President Cyril Ramaphosa signed a law allowing the government to seize land without compensation in rare instances.
The legislation allows the state to expropriate property in the public interest and provides for circumstances in which compensation may be set at zero. But it also requires authorities, in most cases, to first try to reach an agreement with property owners, and disputes can be taken to court.
Land ownership remains a highly sensitive issue in South Africa more than three decades after the end of apartheid, under which the black majority was dispossessed of land and denied many basic rights.
The government says land reform is necessary to address those historic inequalities and insists the new law does not permit arbitrary seizures.
Most private farmland is owned by white South Africans, who make up just over 7% of the population.
In a separate social media post on Tuesday, Rubio accused South Africa's government of pursuing "racial grievance against the Afrikaner minority" and said those responsible for what he described as injustices "have no place in the United States".
He said the South African government had failed to adequately address US concerns about what Washington describes as "government-sponsored discrimination" against Afrikaners and other minorities.
"The United States will not allow such behaviour to go unchecked," he added.
He said the actions targeted by the policy undermined "peace, economic stability and the rule of law."
The South African government is yet to respond to the US restrictions.
The US embassy in Pretoria said Washington believed dialogue with South Africa had run its course and accused the African country of failing to demonstrate a commitment to strong bilateral relations.
It warned that the new visa restrictions were the beginning of tougher measures, adding: "This visa restriction policy is only the first step in a series of escalatory measures that will show America's firm resolve in this matter."
South Africa made efforts to soothe tensions with US, with Ramaphosa going to the White House last May with a large delegation that included white members of his coalition government and also famous white South African golfers.
But Trump ambushed the Oval Office meeting with claims that white South African farmers were being killed and "persecuted" - producing unsubstantiated evidence that has been widely discredited.
Further efforts by South Africa to mend the relationship have failed, with Africa's largest economy being hit in August with 30% tariffs on goods being exported to the US - the highest rate in sub-Saharan Africa.
The latest visa restrictions are being imposed under a provision of US immigration law that allows the secretary of state to bar foreign nationals whose entry is considered potentially damaging to US foreign policy interests.

Runaway horse captured by police on motorbikes
A runaway horse was chased by police on motorbikes in Santa Fe, New Mexico, when it escaped before a parade on 13 September.
The unharmed horse was eventually cornered by police, before being lassoed.
Police officers followed and cornered the horse on motorbikes, before it was wrangled by a lasso-carrying cowboy.
The horse was given a drink of water before being walked back to the start of the Desfile de la Gente parade, Santa Fe Police Department said in a post on Facebook.

Five moon bears that spent decades living in cages in South Korea have arrived at their new home in Suffolk.
Jimmy's Farm & Wildlife Park near Ipswich and its charity, Space for the Wild, transported the animals 5,500 miles (8,850km) to their new forever home at the park.
The bears, which arrived on Thursday, had been kept at one of South Korea's last bear bile farms â sites which have now been banned in the country.
Jimmy Doherty, founder of the wildlife park, said the bears would now live a "profoundly better life".
"I will never forget meeting the bears for the first time," he said.
"It was truly hell on earth. You cannot unsee these things.
"It made us all the more determined and focused on our mission - to get these bears safe, protected and living a profoundly better life.
"The work, dedication and public support of so many have made this a reality. I couldn't be more grateful to all involved."
The rescued bears - Bara, Rumi, Saebit, Yonggi and Huimang - are enjoying a new reserve at the park created specifically for them.
It includes space for them to climb, swim and rest among trees and grass.
The park launched a campaign to fund the rescue and has raised more than Â£90,000 out of a target of Â£200,000.
South Korea banned the breeding and possession of the bears last year, along with the extraction of bile from their gallbladders.
The bile was used in medicines while the bears themselves were often kept in poor conditions.

Three people have died and two others taken to hospital after a news helicopter crashed in suburban Los Angeles, fire authorities in the city have said.
NBC Los Angeles confirmed the helicopter was its NewsChopper4, which also operated for Telemundo 52, and was in the area on Tuesday reporting on a deadly bus crash.
The station's hosts said both people on the helicopter, who were "valued friends and colleagues" had died, naming them as Eliana Moreno and George Marciniw.
They said the third victim was on the ground at the time of the crash, but did not name them.
The aircraft went down just before 19:00 local time (01:00 BST) between two commercial buildings in the Chatsworth neighbourhood, a Los Angeles Fire Department (LAFD) spokesperson told the BBC.
Fire from the crash spread to four vehicles and two storage containers, and more than 70 firefighters were deployed to the scene, the LAFD added.
During emotional live coverage on NBC4, veteran news anchor Colleen Williams confirmed it was the local news station's helicopter that crashed.
"We knew it was a news chopper. We knew we'd lost contact with our people out there, and we've just received confirmation," Williams said.
Earlier, LAFD Captain Branden Silverman told the local affiliate of the BBC's US partner CBS: "We do have one confirmed patient that seemed to be outside of the helicopter when it crashed.
"That person was declared deceased on scene," Silverman said.
Several news helicopters were in the area at the time of the incident reporting on a bus crash.
Earlier in the day, two people were killed and six others were injured after an SUV crashed into a city bus in Chatsworth, BBC's US partner CBS reported.
LAPD's Central Division posted on X that it extended "thoughts and prayers to the family, friends and colleagues of KNBC 4, Los Angeles".
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass wrote on X she was "absolutely devastated by the loss of life in Chatsworth tonight".
"My heart is with the families and loved ones of those we lost in the tragic bus collision and helicopter crash," she added.
California Governor Gavin Newsom wrote on X that "our hearts are with the victims and families of tonight's devastating Metro bus and helicopter crashes in Chatsworth, and with the entire NBC4 family".
"Thank you to the first responders working tirelessly tonight."
The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) will lead the investigation into the incident.

79527d1b5cb6.text: Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) filed a complaint against the top Republican and Democrat on the House Ethics Committee on Tuesday, accusing the lawmakers who investigated him of breaking their own rules. Why it matters: Edwards is escalating his fight against the committee just two weeks after the House voted 413-2 to censure him over its findings that he violated House rules related to sexual harassment and a hostile workplace. Edwards' complaint asks the Office of Congressional Conduct to investigate Ethics Chair Michael Guest (R-Miss.) and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier (D-Calif.) over their handling of his case. The Ethics Committee has previously disputed Edwards' account of the process. When it released its report last month, Guest and DeSaulnier said Edwards had agreed to waive certain procedural steps after reviewing a draft of the report several days earlier. The committee's findings follow Axios' reporting that Edwards singled out two young female staffers in their 20s for special attention that multiple sources described as inappropriate. Driving the news: "There was nothing ethical about this process," Edwards said in announcing the complaint. He alleges the committee circumvented its own rules by adopting its final report and recommending his censure before receiving his formal response. Edwards has maintained that his conduct did not violate House rules, though he did apologize to his wife, family, and the two women he allegedly harassed. The committee declined to comment. Catch up quick: The Ethics report's findings corroborated several anecdotes previously reported by Axios, including handwritten correspondence, personal gifts, drinking outings, and casino trips, and cited them as supporting evidence for its findings. He told one staffer that she had "written a complex chapter in my heart" shortly before she was set to leave his office in a three-page handwritten letter previously reported by Axios. Edwards gave the two young female staffers numerous gifts, including jewelry worth over $1,000, as well as "designer purses, guns , shoes, flowers, a laptop and cell phone, KitchenAid mixer, robotic vacuum, vacations, tickets to performances, and one-on-one dinners," the Ethics panel found. What they're saying: "He has no remorse, and now he's trying to turn the tables and say somehow ethics did something wrong," Rep. Teresa Leger- Fernandez (D-NM), the chair of the Democratic Women's Caucus, told Axios. "It just shows you how hard to touch the man is," she added of Edwards. DeSaulnier told Axios he had not yet read Edwards' complaint but was confident the committee followed the proper process.

At least 12 people have been killed, including children, and dozens are missing after a war-damaged building collapsed in the Gaza Strip, according to local rescue teams.
Video footage shows the search for bodies and survivors continuing in the rubble of the multi-storey building in the Tal al-Hawa area of Gaza City, its floors sandwiched together.
Locals said 10 families had been living in the apartments despite warnings that they were unsafe.
Members of the Hamas-run Civil Defence rescue service said they had initially been working with "empty hands" due to tight Israeli restrictions on equipment allowed into Gaza. However, they have since been able to borrow some heavy machinery.
On Tuesday, Israeli air strikes in Gaza killed at least five Palestinians, including two children and a Hamas commander, according to health officials and Hamas sources.
The Israeli military said it killed a Hamas commander in southern Gaza and another fighter in the north. In both cases, a child was also reportedly killed.
Separately, the British charity Medical Aid for Palestinians said that a patient was killed by an Israeli drone at a health centre it supports in Jabalia in northern Gaza.

From next year, people who attempt to climb Mount Fuji during off-peak seasons and then require rescue by helicopter will have to pay for the service, authorities governing the northern part of the peak say.
The fee is among a series of measures Japan's Yamanashi prefecture is introducing to deter reckless and poorly prepared climbers.
A similar fee of 8,000 yen ($51; Â£38) per five minutes is already in place in nearby Saitama prefecture for other mountainous areas and will be used as a reference.
Yamanashi authorities will also require those looking to scale Fuji during the off-season, which runs from early September to July the following year, to submit detailed climbing plans.
"We ask the general public to refrain from climbing during the off-season. We hope that these measures will cause people to rethink what climbing Mount Fuji during the winter is like," Yamanashi Governor Kotaro Nagasaki said on Monday.
Officials in Yamanashi and neighbouring Shizuoka prefecture, which governs the southern part of Fuji, have seen a rise in off-season and unplanned climbs, some of which have left climbers stranded.
Shizuoka authorities say they will impose penalties on people who fail to register their off-season climbing attempts and strengthen efforts to keep climbers out of restricted areas.
They did not announce a helicopter rescue fee.
Mount Fuji's official climbing season runs from July to early September, with about 200,000 hikers attempting the summit each year.
Climbing outside of those months is highly discouraged although permitted up to the fifth of ten stations.
However, most mountain huts and toilet facilities are closed off season. The weather and trail conditions also tend to be more severe.

"Wouldn't it be lovely if Canada was the 28th state of the European Union rather than the 51st state of the United States?" asked Finland's President Alexander Stubb this summer.
The question was rather tongue-in-cheek. US President Donald Trump, who is currently locked in an escalating tariff tussle with Ottawa, has, on a number of occasions, declared his ambition to make Canada the 51st American state - causing deep offence amongst many Canadians.
Finland is one of the EU's 27 member states and a close ally of Canada as a fellow Arctic nation. Teasing tones aside, President Stubb put his finger squarely on the pulse of deepening EU-Canadian relations. "Canada is more Europe-minded than most Europeans!" is a smiling retort you often hear in Brussels at the moment.
On Sunday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters Canada was seeking a "unique alliance" with the EU.
The catalyst for this very public, ardent new love-in is Donald Trump. Just the other day, the US president posted a map of North America on his Truth Social site, including Canada and Greenland - a territory that's part of EU country Denmark - all overlaid with the US flag.
Trade negotiations between the US and Canada broke down late last month. European countries, which have been hit by their own Trump tariffs, have privately watched the spat play out with a mixture of interest and, for many, admiration.
While the EU, led by the European Commission, simply accepted new blanket Trump tariffs without fighting back, Carney has prominently stood up to the US president, swiftly imposing counter-tariffs on the United States.
When it comes to courting the EU, Canada appears to some to be even keener than one of the bloc's closest neighbours.
"Canada right now seems more interested than the UK to get as close to Brussels as possible, as a non member state" says Mark Lowen, director of the European Council of Foreign Relations think tank. "It's remarkable."
Canada, but not the UK, successfully joined the European Union's Security Action for Europe (SAFE) defence fund earlier this year. The UK remained on the sidelines following a row over costs and political tensions. A summit designed to reset and improve EU-UK relations has just been delayed - again - over cross-Channel differences.
By contrast this week, Carney is invited as a special guest to the European Commission President's annual State of the Union address in Strasbourg, France on Wednesday. Carney will hold a speech in the European Parliament there on Thursday, a day after President von der Leyen outlines the EU's political and policy priorities.
Officials on both sides insist this is more than just "blah blah politics", as one EU diplomat put it to me. He was speaking on condition of anonymity so as to be able to discuss the subject freely. Carney and von der Leyen are both expected to mention plans to forge closer ties. "As close as you can get without (Canada) actually becoming an EU member," the diplomat told me.
'Trump effect' prompts efforts to diversify - but are they achievable?
In the corridors of Brussels, there's whispered talk of constructing a "special association agreement" with Canada.
The unofficial aim for both sides, I'm told, is to reduce reliance on Washington in several key areas:
- Digital and tech developments, in which the US and China dominate
- Energy: Canada is rich in liquified natural gas (LNG) the EU needs since it cut back its energy dependency on Russia
- Raw materials and critical minerals: Canada has them in abundance
- Trade and defence procurement: Canada has been on a "buy European" spree of late, purchasing German attack submarines, for example, and airborne early-warning planes from Sweden's Saab. Its view appears to be: why reward the US by buying American equipment after being slapped with trade tariffs amounting to 50% in some sectors?
A Nanos opinion poll from April suggests more than four in five Canadians favour strengthening ties with the EU.
Close to three in five support Canada actually joining the bloc, though Article 49 of the EU Constitution would appear to make that impossible. Without wanting to seem facetious, the European Union is not (yet) the Eurovision Song Contest, in which indisputably non-European Israel and Australia have - controversially - been allowed to compete.
Back to trade: ties between Canada and the EU are far from novel. The EU is already Canada's second-largest trading partner - albeit far behind the US, which buys about 70% of Canadian exports.
The far-reaching Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) trade deal was agreed just under a decade ago and has been provisionally implemented, eliminating 99% of tariffs on Canadian goods exports.
Privately, European officials admit this renewed high-level courtship between Ottawa and Brussels has everything to do with the actions of Trump's second term in office.
The US president is by now infamous amongst US allies for what they view as his unpredictability and his penchant to use trade or security ties as leverage.
There's a growing sense in Europe - which has, since World War Two, looked to the US as its closest ally abroad - and in Canada, whose economy has been intertwined with the US for decades, that neither can any longer fully rely on Washington. They believe it's time to diversify.
"The Canadian government is committed to trade diversification, doubling non-US trades in the next 10 years, and doing more with the European Union will be very key to achieving that target," Mark Camilleri, president of the Canada EU Trade and Investment Association (CEUTIA) told the BBC.
An even tighter Canadian-EU alliance, covering far more sectors than trade alone, would continue a recent trend of both parties to form new association agreements around the world. In Canada's case, this includes a sectoral deal with China, which raised international eyebrows earlier this year.
EU insiders put all of this down to the "Trump effect".

8bd0ff1b1777.text: The nerdy, traditionally apolitical world of federal data is increasingly getting swept up in the Trump administration's push to control every level of government. Across the federal government, agencies are changing how they collect and publicize information. More and more, politics and ideology are part of the equation. Why it matters: Reliable, unbiased data informs nearly everything the federal government does — from distributing benefits and enforcing workplace discrimination laws to responding to public health threats. Driving the news: The administration's moves in recent weeks span an array of agencies and types of data. 🩺 Measles. Reuters reported that Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. asked the CDC director to remove a reference to two deaths in Pennsylvania from its online tally of measles cases. The move came after the CDC had already accepted Pennsylvania officials' explanation that the deaths were linked to measles. Kennedy and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro had spent days sparring on social media, each accusing the other of politicizing the deaths. Kennedy is a longtime vaccine skeptic. 🏡 Census Bureau. Last month, the Commerce Department did away with language barring political interference that had been part of the department's scientific integrity policy , NPR reported . The department oversees the Census Bureau and several other agencies. The move came after the bureau issued an unauthored report — promptly touted by President Trump — that found that 24,000 noncitizens voted in the 2020 election. The team behind the report, however, included officials with ties to the Trump-linked America First Institute . ⚠️ Anti-discrimination. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission is planning to stop collecting data that's helped the agency investigate claims of workplace discrimination, The Guardian reported . For 60 years, the agency has examined the demographic makeup of company workforces to enforce anti-discrimination laws. The EEOC is now planning to do away with the so-called EEO-1 reports, which require companies to provide data on their workforces broken down by race, ethnicity, sex and job title. The move comes amid a broader Trump administration crackdown on DEI — diversity, equity and inclusion — initiatives. At a July hearing, Andrea Lucas, an EEOC commissioner appointed by Trump, said the data collection was burdensome for employers and encouraged discrimination against white workers, per the Guardian. What they're saying: "The level of politicization in this administration is beyond anything I've seen," says Denice Ross, former U.S. chief data scientist and currently director of the Data Policy Institute at the Federation of American Scientists. "I've been doing this work for 25 years." Zoom out: Fears about the handling of data that doesn't comport with Trump's worldview have been around for years . Last year, Trump fired the head of the Bureau of Labor Statistics hours after the agency released disappointing jobs numbers. "Today's Jobs Numbers were RIGGED in order to make the Republicans, and ME, look bad," Trump wrote. The Department of Homeland Security has stopped regularly publishing comprehensive immigration enforcement statistics, including data that allowed outsiders to assess the administration's deportation efforts. The official who oversaw DHS's independent statistics office resigned in July, The Atlantic reported . According to a tracker run by former federal government data scientists, 38 datasets have been eliminated since Trump returned to office. Hundreds of other datasets have been altered or disrupted. The other side: "The Trump administration is committed to providing the American people with timely, accurate, and relevant data that's helpful to inform meaningful research, discourse, and decision-making," White House spokesman Kush Desai said. "Ensuring public health and other critical data actually reflect reality while refusing to waste taxpayer resources on ideological pet projects are all important parts of that mission." The bottom line: "We really take data for granted," Ross said. "It's invisible infrastructure, like a bridge or cell service. We don't notice until it's gone."

Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Steve Bannon. The pollâs results, Bores argued, show that âif you show good work on AI, youâre winning over voters, even though AI isnât their top issue.â
Boresâ new organization, Who Decides, aims to help the broader Democratic coalition unite around a âshared baselineâ for AI protections. The organization will help traditionally Democratic groups like labor and civil society craft AI policy messages, Bores said.

1b36061db868.text: Data: U.S. Census Bureau, Current Population Survey, 1968 to 2026 Annual Social and Economic Supplements ; Note: Census identifies breaks in the series in 2013 and 2017 due to methodological changes; Chart: Russell Contreras/Axios U.S. household income hit a record in 2025, but the lowest earners barely shared in the gains, new Census data show. Why it matters: On paper, Americans look richer than ever. But broader measures of financial security show millions still getting squeezed by medical costs , uneven income gains and a thinning public safety net. The 2025 Census report largely captures the economy before the major safety-net reductions in President Trump's " Big Beautiful Bill" took hold. That makes this year's record income and near-record-low official poverty numbers an important benchmark for measuring what happens next. By the numbers: Real median household income rose 2.6% to $87,460 in 2025, the highest inflation-adjusted level since Census records began in 1967. Median post-tax household income climbed 3.1% to $76,060. The official poverty rate fell for a third straight year, dropping slightly to 10.2%, or about 34.5 million people. Child poverty fell to a record-low 13.4%, while poverty among Hispanics dropped to an unprecedented 13.9%. State of play: The economy delivered historic topline numbers without spreading the gains evenly. Income among the wealthiest 10% of Americans rose 1.7%, while income among the bottom 10% showed no significant change — indicating that the low-income households largely missed out on the gains. Households at the 90th percentile earned about $261,300, more than 13 times the roughly $20,010 earned at the 10th percentile. The top fifth of households captured 52.4% of all household income. The bottom fifth reported earning just 3%. Zoom in: Latinos offer one of the clearest examples of the split-screen economy in 2025. Hispanic poverty fell to its lowest level since Census began tracking it in 1973. But the median household income among Hispanics, $73,260, showed no significant change from 2024. Meanwhile, 21.8% of Hispanic adults ages 19 to 64 were uninsured in 2025, down a bit from the previous year — but still the highest uninsured rate among the major racial and ethnic groups shown by Census Yes, but: Big racial income gaps remain even as some groups posted gains. Asian American households had the highest median income at $126,300 in 2025, compared with $91,930 for white households and $59,980 for Black American households. Black Americans' household income rose 4.8% from 2024 and whites' household income rose 3%, while Asian Americans' household income showed no significant change. Zoom out: A broader measure of hardship paints a less rosy picture. The Supplemental Poverty Measure , which factors in taxes, government benefits, housing, work and medical expenses, held statistically steady at 13.1% — nearly 3 percentage points above the government's official poverty rate. Medical expenses put an estimated 7.7 million more people below the supplemental poverty line in 2025, the Census Bureau said. Between the lines: Health insurance coverage held steady overall in 2025. The uninsured rate remained statistically unchanged at 7.9%, or 26.7 million people. Medicaid coverage fell 0.5 percentage points nationally, from 17.6% to 17.1% of the population — representing about 1.4 million fewer people with Medicaid coverage in 2025 than in the previous year Among adults ages 19 to 64, 17.3% had public health coverage — including Medicaid, Medicare and VA/CHAMPVA coverage — down 0.5 percentage points from 2024. Census says the decline was driven by a 0.6-point drop in Medicaid coverage among working-age adults. What we're watching: The 2025 numbers may represent the last snapshot before major federal safety-net cuts begin showing up in the Census data, Robert Greenstein, a visiting fellow at the Brookings Institution, tells Axios.

fd593749b349.text:
States bet big on rural health startups, with a Silicon Valley twist
When Josh Fleig, Louisiana’s chief innovation officer, learned his state had set aside $20 million a year, for five years, to invest in startup rural health companies, his reaction was not surprising: “Wow!”
In rural America, where people are often reported to be sicker with poor access to healthcare, the cash influx is a relief. In the economic development space where Fleig operates, it’s an opportunity.
“Look, that’s a lot of money for what we do,” said Fleig, whose state-funded economic development office invests in corporate launches, ranging from software startups to shipbuilders.
Louisiana and a handful of other states set aside money from their share of the $50 billion federal Rural Health Transformation Program to quickly invest in new technologies, mirroring private industry moves. Lawmakers added the rural health program to offset more than $900 billion in reduced Medicaid spending expected over 10 years from Republicans’ sweeping 2025 tax and spending law.
But rather than filling the budget hole, the rural program’s assignment is to find new approaches for revitalizing rural communities where doctors are in short supply and hospitals have been downsizing and closing for decades. The federal government doled out the first-year rural health program awards to states this year, with pots ranging from $147 million in New Jersey to $281 million in Texas.
Modernizing technology infrastructure is a key pillar of the federal rural health program, and the catalyst money epitomizes the administration’s strategy to move fast and experiment with untested technology — much like the “move fast and break things” mantra during the heyday of Silicon Valley.
Instead of breaking things, though, the goal is to “move fast, fast-fail, innovate quickly, and move to sustainability,” said Aaron Bujnowski, a managing director with the healthcare industry group at the consultancy Alvarez & Marsal. “This is a transformation that is still meant to serve the people.”
Rigorous Rules and Tight Deadlines
Beyond Louisiana, Timothy Foster, a spokesperson for the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, confirmed that Delaware, Georgia, Massachusetts, Nebraska, South Carolina, Virginia, and West Virginia are also creating rural health tech catalyst funds.
Every year, states must compete for rural funding in the five-year federal program. Federal regulators will take money away from states that do not meet the goals promised in their applications, including whether they designated money to companies for tech innovations.
CMS, which is overseeing the program, released a seven-step guidance document for states to follow when creating the tech catalyst operations. No more than 10% of each state’s award can be spent on a rural tech catalyst fund.
States’ initial annual progress reports for the rural fund were due at the end of August. CMS has declined to publicly post those reports; it plans to publish an annual report on state progress. States must show that first-year funds will be obligated — but not necessarily spent — by Oct. 30, according to the CMS guidance document.
Daniel X. O’Neil, a technology consultant who advocates for open data and open government, created a state tracker and parsed the original state applications to find dozens that mention catalyst awards and technology funds.
O’Neil said he is “looking forward to the clawbacks and the craziness of October because, you know, that’s serious stuff.”
For the rural health catalyst funds, CMS requires states to submit the list of finalists “at least 15 business days” before announcing winners, along with “sufficient information” for the agency to “assess each proposed project,” according to the guidance document.
The document outlines intellectual property and federal rights but does not provide guidance or standards for patient rights or protections. CMS spokesperson Foster stated in an email that the technology investments must comply with federal “privacy, security, interoperability, and patient safety” requirements.
Protecting Patients
Maya Sandalow, director of the health program at the Bipartisan Policy Center and one of the leading analysts watching the rural fund, said the catalyst funds are “public dollars” and has called for more transparency in the overall rural health program. The center is a nonprofit think tank in Washington, D.C.
Accurate and timely reporting must be done to ensure “the necessary guardrails are in place” to protect patients, she said, adding that the innovation needs to be “tested in a way that’s safe for the patients that they are going to be used on.”
To apply, startups must be less than 10 years old and have raised less than $50 million in early funding. Companies that win a portion of state catalyst funds must meet predetermined milestones before being paid — and federal officials will make “targeted reviews as needed,” according to the guidance document.
Louisiana officials announced the state’s tech catalyst fund with an event in rural Natchitoches, known as the filming location of the 1989 film Steel Magnolias. The fund quickly drew more than 200 companies competing for between $250,000 and $3 million in seed money.
Tiny startup Greens Health was invited to the event. The 2-year-old company analyzes Medicare claims to identify patients with chronic diseases, such as diabetes, and works with local home health nurses and senior facilities to improve care.

Outcome of Suit Against Department of Labor Could Boost Skimpy Employer Health Plans
A long-running lawsuit challenging what it means to be an employee and therefore have access to work-based health plans is being closely watched by health policy analysts. Its outcome could spur the availability of lower-cost but potentially skimpier health coverage that skirts some consumer protections.
Court papers indicate a settlement in the case against the Department of Labor may be in the works, although the parameters of any such deal are unknown.
It would come amid premium surges on Affordable Care Act marketplaces that have led millions to drop coverage this year. The Trump administration has also been sharply focused on expanding access to alternative coverage, such as short-term plans that avoid ACA rules on preexisting conditions and benefit requirements.
“Depending on what happens with the settlement, this could be an even bigger expansion,” said Katie Keith, director of the Center for Health Policy and the Law at the Georgetown University Law Center. “People are worried that it is the opening salvo into promoting junk plans that don’t meet the ACA requirements.”
The plaintiff, Data Marketing Partnership, filed its case against the Department of Labor in 2019, during the first Trump administration. It wants official recognition as an employer so it can continue to allow its limited partners to buy into a type of job-based health insurance that doesn’t have to comply with state insurance rules or offer coverage as robust as required under the ACA.
But to grasp the claim, one also has to understand how the coverage works.
A consumer shopping for health insurance may come across information online or from a marketer about this concept, sometimes called “limited partnership” coverage. The pitch? Buy insurance offered through Data Marketing Partnership and handled by LP Management Services. To qualify, the consumer must download an app that tracks their internet searches. The company could then sell that data.
Some potential consumers may be turned off by the thought of their internet searches being tracked, but others may find it appealing because it allows them to become a limited partner eligible to buy into the company’s employee health insurance plans. But can these partners be considered employees?
The court’s answer has potential implications for regulators and consumers. Some health policy and market experts warn that a green light could lead to a proliferation of aggressively marketed and potentially questionable insurance with limited recourse for consumers because the plans would be exempt from state oversight.
“If this took off, you logically could see the rise of a whole bunch of what, functionally, would be unregulated insurance companies,” said Ali Khawar, who was the principal deputy assistant secretary of the Department of Labor’s Employee Benefits Security Administration during Joe Biden’s presidency and now runs his own consulting outfit.
No one knows if the department is going to change its long-running stance defending the case. But any settlement could add more uncertainty to insurance markets.
Already insurers are requesting double-digit increases in ACA premiums again next year, partly because declining enrollment often means that the healthiest policyholders are leaving. That trend could accelerate in coming years as more people are drawn into alternatives such as limited-partnership policies.
States Act as Federal Case Plays Out
The Department of Labor defended the case throughout the first Trump administration and the Biden era, issuing a sharply worded advisory opinion in early 2020 stating that people who simply download software to “capture data as they browse the Internet” are not “employees or bona fide partners.”
A district court judge in Texas, who had previously ruled the ACA unconstitutional in a decision ultimately rejected by the Supreme Court, called the advisory opinion “arbitrary and capricious” in a 2020 ruling in favor of the data marketer. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit largely upheld the lower court’s decision but ordered it to reconsider whether someone who downloads software is either a “working owner” or a “bona fide partner.”
The employer-employee relationship is at the heart of the case because of a 1974 federal law designed to help large, self-insured employers offer retirement and health benefits to workers without having to meet varying rules from multiple states.
That law — the Employee Retirement Income Security Act — allows such plans to avoid most rules set by the states, which generally regulate most other types of insurance and assist consumers who report problems with their policies. As self-insured employer plans, the policies also don’t have to comply with some ACA rules, such as the requirement to cover 10 broad categories of “essential health benefits.”
“If the case goes the wrong way, it could impact consumers or hamstring the states,” said Marie Grant, Maryland’s insurance commissioner.
Arguments over what constitutes an employer plan are not new, and other organizations have tried offering such coverage. Some states have taken action against purveyors of limited-partner policies.
Maryland in 2024 fined a company, The Vitamin Patch, for offering limited-partnership insurance after investigating complaints and determining it was not licensed to sell coverage in the state.
Washington in 2021 ordered another company to stop offering its plans in the state and fined it $25,000.
Maine and Connecticut in 2024 warned consumers about this type of coverage.
“These plans do not provide comprehensive medical coverage and can leave consumers with large, unpaid medical bills,” according to Connecticut’s notice.
Maine’s announcement noted that entities offering these types of health insurance included The Vitamin Patch as well as Affiliated Workers Alliance, Consumer Data Partners, Employers Business Alliance, Socios Buenos, and

In the East Tampa neighborhood where Dee Morales bought her house, residents have been asking for a supermarket for 10 years. They still don’t have one. So Morales did the math out loud: In the decade the neighborhood has spent waiting, a community garden could have grown thousands of pounds of food.
Morales runs 813 Hood Garden, a network of growing spaces across East Tampa, Sulphur Springs and Ybor City. Two of these gardens are in neighborhoods the federal government classifies as “food deserts,” places that are both low-income and far from a grocery store.
She started 813 Hood Garden during the pandemic, after discovering the only way to get her oldest son to eat vegetables was to let him grow them himself. Adults who visited, she found, had never seen a pepper on the plant.
In Hillsborough County, more than 15 percent of residents are food insecure, according to Feeding America’s 2026 Map the Meal Gap, based on 2024 data. Across Florida, there was an increase in food insecurity from about 10 percent of the population in 2020 to 15.4 percent in 2024. Food insecurity has climbed nationally since the COVID-19 pandemic as food prices surged, according to the USDA.
Yet as need grows, the government’s willingness to measure food insecurity is shrinking. Last fall, the U.S. Department of Agriculture canceled its long-running annual survey of household food security—the most authoritative national count—calling it redundant and politicized. Increasingly, the task of mapping where hunger exists is falling to nonprofits and researchers building models of their own.
Geographer Jaryd Hinch built a model that scores every neighborhood in Hillsborough and Pinellas counties for community-garden “suitability,” weighting poverty and income most heavily—above factors like transit access and available land—in what he calls an “equity-first” design meant to steer gardens toward the residents facing the steepest barriers to fresh food. The study began as a graduate course project, was not funded or requested by any agency and was written by Hinch, a doctoral candidate at the University of South Florida whose research centers on aviation sustainability.
Published this year in the peer-reviewed journal Southeastern Geographer, it maps where a garden could, in theory, do the most good, then overlays the gardens Tampa Bay already has. The match is loose. About 58 percent of existing gardens fall in the neighborhoods his model flags as “highest priority,” better than the 40 percent random placement would predict, yet still far from alignment. Maps show some of the highest-need neighborhoods have no garden, while some of the county’s most established gardens flourish in comfortable suburbs—one of the most successful sits in Carrollwood, a middle-class area that is nobody’s idea of a food desert.
Hinch’s paper frames that gap as a planning problem: The region lacks “spatially informed decision-making tools,” he wrote. But the people closest to the work describe a different problem entirely.
“The tool doesn’t matter,” said Monica Petrella, the food-systems coordinator at the University of Florida’s Hillsborough County extension office and, in effect, the audience Hinch’s model was built for. She won’t consult a suitability map, she said, until a project already has about 30 committed volunteers and $10,000 for beds, soil and water. In her day-to-day life, she isn’t looking at any map to decide where a garden goes—she’s trying to help the gardens that exist find enough volunteers to survive.
That inverts the study’s premise. The binding constraint on community gardens, Petrella said, isn’t information about where need is highest. It’s people and money. And those, she noted, tend to pool where affluence already is: Gardens demand so much volunteer labor that they thrive in neighborhoods where residents have leisure time, disposable income and the knowledge to file for nonprofit status and chase sponsors.
According to the Coalition of Community Gardens, of the 12 gardens that started in the region between 2009 and 2011, six had failed by 2015—a 50 percent failure rate. After the coalition formed to network and support them, none failed over the next six years.
This story is funded by readers like you.

Donate Now
Petrella is blunt in her belief that gardens won’t close the hunger gap. Food insecurity, she said, is a function of economics: Grocery chains skip low-income neighborhoods they deem unprofitable, residents without cars are left with convenience stores and no amount of backyard tomatoes changes that arithmetic.
The produce itself rarely reaches the people who need it most, she said; most gardens run on individual plots, where growers take home what they raise, leaving little surplus to give away. The connection between a community garden and a hungry household, she said, is “a scenic route.” Gardens are “a cherry on top,” she said. They’re valuable for the community they build, but not a fix.
Morales agrees a garden is “part of something bigger.”
“It’s our responsibility as the people to advocate for what we want,” she said. Community gardening, in her telling, is a short-term answer while neighborhoods keep fighting for the grocery stores, transit and wages that would actually move the needle.
Notably, Morales didn’t fault the model—she called it a promising resource, as long as it captures “the actual need of the people,” something a survey, not a spreadsheet, would catch. Her frustration runs elsewhere.
“The issue isn’t that we need more community gardens,” she said. “We need support for the gardens that exist.” Organizers like her aren’t paid for their time; she works a job and pours the rest into the garden as a passion project. Jim Justice is getting the itch. And it could set up a battle of GOP titans.
The West Virginia GOP senator is considering a run for his old job as governor in 2028, which would potentially set up a race between him and incumbent Gov. Patrick Morrisey. Justice told Semafor heâs âsure thinking about itâ before quickly interjecting that he loves âwhat Iâm doing hereâ in the Senate.
He also jabbed at Morrisey but insisted he wants the governor to be successful: âGov. Morrisey has a more difficult time bonding with people and everything, but beyond that, I want him to do great, I really do. Iâm not in a food fight at all.â
âI do love the people of West Virginia, and I spent eight years trying to build it back. Got it really going,â Justice continued. âI just want goodness for West Virginia, but I want goodness for the whole nation too. Weâll make a decision.â
Know More
West Virginia is a small state thatâs also the home of bare-knuckled politics and big personalities. Republicans recruited Justice, a former Democrat, to run against former Sen. Joe Manchin, I-W.Va., in 2024, though Manchin ultimately decided against seeking reelection. Manchin narrowly defeated Morrisey in 2018, but Morrisey mounted a political comeback in 2024 by emerging from a crowded GOP primary and winning the governorâs mansion.
A Morrisey ally told Semafor that Justice has myriad vulnerabilities and hasnât had to win a tough GOP primary against someone like the incumbent governor (though Justice did easily defeat former Rep. Alex Mooney, R-W.Va., in 2024). The ally added that the conservative Club for Growth is already committed to opposing Justice, put Morriseyâs war chest at nearly $5 million across several political entities, and noted that Justice is in debt and is now sharing control of his familyâs Greenbrier resort.
But Justice said people in West Virginia are encouraging him to run: âYouâre going to hear people come to you and say, âBoy, weâd love to have you back as governor.â You know, thatâs natural and everything. I donât pay a whole lot of attention.â
Manchin also flirted repeatedly with running for his old job as governor, which he used to call the âbest job in the world.â Manchin never ran after serving in the Senate, but Senate Republicans believe Justice is more likely to run than not, according to several GOP sources. Regarding the 2028 governor race, Manchin said on Tuesday: âCanât we get through this election before worrying about the next election?â

Democratsâ decision to bump up New Mexico to their fourth primary spot in 2028, right after the now-familiar trio of South Carolina, Nevada, and New Hampshire, bestows growing prominence and sway on congressional delegations from all four states. Populous Michigan and Virginia, fifth and sixth on the primary calendar, will be right behind them.
Democrats in the previous cast of early states are going to find new opportunities to wield their clout with a field that could easily number in the dozens. And lawmakers from states newer to the early-primary lineup are already preparing to elevate what matters to their constituents, as they get wooed by presidential aspirants.
âI want them to come to New Mexico and look at the issues that we face,â said FernÃ¡ndez, D-N.M. âI want to see the candidates inspire the kind of communities that will make a difference in both the primary election and the general election.â
With competitive midterm races happening in nearly all of the early states, potential Democratic presidential candidates are already on the trail with purple-district incumbents and candidates. Other lawmakers from early-primary states are fielding calls from 2028 contenders looking to appear with them.
