âWe have a lot of really unique issues that are not something that you learn about through osmosis in other parts of the country,â Heinrich said.
New Mexico will get âpresidential candidates to care about water, public lands, national laboratories,â he added â âthings that many of them just donât have that much familiarity with.â
LujÃ¡n also said his state has great food, but cautioned candidates about a regional tripwire: feeling compelled to choose between the stateâs famous green and red chiles.
âIt depends what theyâre eating. Anyone that gives you an answer? They donât know the state,â he said. âYou canât pick one.â
Know More
Democratic incumbents in tight races are hoping to reap electoral benefits from 2028 candidates who are coming through their districts. The visits tend to energize the base ahead of the midterms and may also broaden congressional candidatesâ appeal.
âI always look at the quality of events. Are they putting me in front of voters who I really havenât connected with before? Thatâs sort of my No. 1 goal,â said Rep. Susie Lee, D-Nev., who represents a purple district.
She called herself a âButtigieg fanâ this time and said she would endorse in the 2028 cycle, though she was waiting to learn more about other candidatesâ positions.

Room for Disagreement
Not every Democrat is sold on the new calendar. Those in New Hampshire say their state law supersedes the partyâs revised order, which puts South Carolina ahead of them.

1883a06fccf0.text: Data: NFHS ; Map: Brad Jennings/Axios Girls flag football has become the fastest-growing high school sport, as tens of thousands take up a game that barely had a varsity footprint a few years ago. Why it matters: Few girls high school sports have moved from niche to mainstream so quickly, broadening athletic opportunities in the process. By the numbers: More than 102,000 girls played high school flag football in 2025-26, a 551% increase in the past four years, according to the National Federation of State High School Associations . Catch up quick: In 2024, just 12 states sanctioned high school girls flag football, viewed as a safer, more accessible version of America's most popular spectator sport. Today, 23 states plus Washington, D.C., sanction it as an official varsity sport , and 3,990 schools reported participants in 2025-26. The NFL is backing its growth, too. It has invested millions to launch and expand high school programs , and featured the sport in its Super Bowl commercials . Beyond high schools, flag football will debut at the 2028 Olympics, and at least 40 NCAA schools already offer it as a collegiate varsity sport. Reality check: It's not yet clear whether flag football is mostly creating new high school athletes or pulling girls from established sports. A recent Newsday analysis on Long Island found flag participation rising sharply while girls lacrosse, softball and track participation fell. What we're watching: Girls varsity wrestling is undergoing its own boom. All 50 states now report girls wrestling participation, and 40 state athletic associations hold girls wrestling championships, up from just five about a decade ago.

According to Donald Trump, concerns about the dangers of artificial intelligence technology â that "robots will be marching into our cities and getting rid of us all" â are a hoax.
It's the kind of language the US president typically reserves for the objects of his most intense derision â theories about human-driven climate change, investigations into Russian election-meddling, and the drives to impeach and remove him from office during his first presidential term.
Styling himself as the "hoax buster", in a series of social media posts on Monday he issued a full-throated endorsement of what he called "the greatest economic development engine in history" and scorned those who doubted the benefits of the technology.
The ranks of doubters have been growing in recent weeks, however, amidst anxiety over the disruptive nature of AI - if not worries about potentially civilisation-threatening danger - among some industry insiders and politicians, including from within Trump's own Republican Party.
None of that has deterred Trump, however, whose latest social media fusillade was only his latest effort to turn back growing AI scepticism through sheer force of will.
Whether the president views the AI fight as pivotal to his economic legacy, a key battleground in a global struggle for power, or another example of his enemies conspiring against him, he has, by fully joining the fight, elevated the issue to the forefront of American politics. That is even at the risk of crossing longtime allies.
"We think this could be a great technology, but we're not going to give these guys a carte blanche," former Trump adviser Steve Bannon said at a "pro-human" conference on the dangers of AI on Tuesday. "There's been no debate."
Just before Bannon spoke, democratic socialist Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont told the same crowd that Washington policymakers had not addressed the "potentially catastrophic consequence" of unregulated AI.
"Congress under both Democratic and Republican control has been asleep at the wheel," he said. "And now we have a president whose ignorance regarding this issue is truly embarrassing."
According to Trump, however, what's needed isn't debate or new policies, it's trust in his authority and judgement.
"The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades," he wrote. "We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies."
A desire for centralised presidential authority is a familiar theme for Trump in his second term in office. If he decides something is good, he should have the authority to allow it; if he deems it bad, he ought to be able to end it by unilateral presidential order.
It's similar to his outlook on immigration and trade. He believes that he, as president, should have the sole power to decide who can enter and remain in the country, and when and where to impose tariffs.
Unlike tariffs and immigration, which have been issues of interest for Trump for decades, the rise in artificial intelligence technology is a recent development.
But if this is no long-time, deep-seated interest on the part of the president, what could explain his willingness to press ahead?
The 'hottest' economy and the driving force of AI
Trump regularly likes to tout America as the "hottest" country in the world. Many economists indicate that investment in AI technology â including infrastructure and equipment â has been the driving force in the US economy for several years.
According to a recent report by the forecasting firm ING, tech investment accounted for more than a third of all US economic expansion in the second quarter of 2026.
The stock market is booming, and much of that rise in corporate value (and, by extension, surging retirement portfolios of many Americans) can be attributed to the massive spending on computer chips, data centres and the other infrastructure behind AI.
Anything that threatens this growth, which Trump considers to be a hallmark of his presidency and a key to his political legacy, quickly draws his suspicion.
Trump also sees the AI expansion as a large-scale industrial competition between the world's two largest economies, the US and China. In the zero-sum game of global power, if China is ahead, then America is behind.
"We're leading China in AI," Trump said on Saturday, "and frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI wins."
The president often touts a familiar conservative view that his opponents on the left are against the free market and economic liberties, and rely on alarmism to justify greater government intervention and control.
Of course, Trump â who touts partial US ownership of US Steel and the semiconductor manufacturer Intel, and has no qualms about picking winners and losers in the American economy â is hardly a traditional small-government conservative.
Tech bosses vary in views - and their access to Trump
Trump's close ties to prominent tech moguls and AI entrepreneurs from the start of his second term may also help explain his AI evangelism. Tech entrepreneur David Sacks, a co-chair of the president's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology and his informal AI tsar, has been a longtime supporter. Sacks's publicly aired scepticism of AI regulation mirrors recent comments made by the president.
"I think this is becoming a panic," he said this weekend in an interview with CBS News. "We're in an election season, and there is an incentive for political actors to try and amplify the fear."
Elon Musk, despite a rocky relationship, has shaped the direction of this administration. Mark Zuckerberg of Facebook, Amazon's Jeff Bezos, OpenAI's Sam Altman and former Apple head Tim Cook all had prominent seats at Trump's inauguration.
These men, along with Anthropic head Dario Amodei, hold a range of views on the necessity of greater AI regulation, and have differing levels of access to, and influence on, Trump.

Saudi Arabia intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone south of the Islamic holy city of Mecca on Tuesday evening, according to the spokesman of the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen.
Turki al-Maliki said the targeting of Mecca, which is the home of Islam's most sacred shrine and the focal point of the Hajj pilgrimage, was a "disgraceful act".
The 57-nation Organisation of Islamic Cooperation said attacks on Mecca and Medina province, where Islam's second holiest shrine is located, constituted an "unacceptable and intolerable transgression".
But the Houthis, an Iran-backed armed group that controls much of western Yemen, denied targeting Mecca and accused Saudi Arabia of "fabrications and lies".
"There is no threat whatsoever from Yemen to the holy sites. Our operations target their oil facilities and military bases, and are far removed from the holy places," military spokesman Yahya Sarea said.
Sarea added that the Houthis had launched drones and missiles at Saudi Arabia in retaliation for more than 450 Saudi air strikes on their territory over the past week.
He also said they had shot down a Saudi fighter jet over Marib province.
There was no immediate response from the Saudi-led coalition, but Maj Gen Maliki did say that its forces would "not hesitate to take the necessary and deterrent measures against the terrorist Houthi militia and its hostile and terrorist behaviour".
On Tuesday, Saudi authorities issued a series of brief security alerts for incoming projectiles in a number of western areas, including Mecca and Jeddah, the kingdom's second largest city.
Meanwhile, the US embassy in Saudi Arabia issued a "reconsider travel" advisory, warning that Houthi attacks had targeted cities, infrastructure, airports, military bases, diplomatic facilities and energy facilities.
The Houthis have recently seized control of large swathes of Yemen's Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed pro-government forces.
Last week, they captured the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the southern gateway to a key shipping route that links Asia and Europe via the Red Sea and the Suez canal.
The Houthis said they posed no threat to international shipping but reiterated that they would target vessels from Saudi Arabia, which has relied on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
At the same time, Saudi Arabia's key East-West Pipeline, which was being used to transfer crude oil from the Gulf to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, had to be closed after it was badly damaged in a strike that the kingdom blamed on Iran-backed militias in Iraq.
Some experts have said it could take more than a month to repair the pipeline, but US Energy Secretary Chris Wright predicted on Tuesday that oil should be flowing through it within days.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the country's de facto ruler, has personally pressed US President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News, the BBC's US media partner.
Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, offering instead to assist with intelligence and targeting support, the sources said.
A senior Trump administration official told the BBC: "We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen government regarding regional stability."
The United Nations Security Council held an emergency meeting on Tuesday, during which both Yemen's government and Saudi Arabia called for more decisive action against the Houthis, who they accused of choking the Bab al-Mandab Strait as a way of applying economic pressure.
Council members agreed that freedom of navigation in the Red Sea must be maintained to prevent disruption to global supply chains.
More than 90,000 people have been displaced in Yemen by the fighting between the Houthis and pro-government forces, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
"Families are being forced to flee for the second or third time in this conflict, with almost nothing left," Amy Pope, the IOM's director general, warned last week.
The World Health Organization (WHO) said on Sunday that at least 500 people had been reported killed since the start of August, including 297 over the previous week.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
The fighting has reportedly left more than 150,000 people dead and triggered one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, with more than 22 million people in need of some form of aid, according to the UN.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

The president of the European Commission has backed proposals for Canada to become the EU's first "associate member".
Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament on Wednesday she wanted to work on "opening the door" for Canada, which would involve closer ties on various key sectors.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney last week spoke of seeking a "unique alliance" with the EU. The country currently faces tense relations with the US, compounded by an ongoing dispute over trade.
Without mentioning US President Donald Trump by name, von der Leyen said offering Canada some sort of EU membership was "not a partnership against anyone else, but for our common strength".
She added: "Partnerships are a strategic choice for Europe. But they also respond to the fracture in the international rules-based system".
Carney was in attendance at the annual key note speech in Strasbourg, and is due to address the parliament on Thursday.
Trade talks between Canada and the US collapsed last month, sparking a series of new tariff measures.
Von der Leyen told the EU's State of the Union address that the bloc and Canada "see the world with the same eyes", including on topics ranging from AI, to climate change and geopolitics.
"And we have stood together: on Ukraine, on defence, on raw materials and on supply chains. But above all... Europe and Canada believe in democracy."
She listed manufacturing, technology, AI, defence, energy, critical minerals and economic security as key areas for cooperation under the partnership.
The EU and Canada already have a free-trade agreement eliminating duties on 99% of goods exports called the Comprehensive Economic Trade Agreement (CETA).
"We will move from CETA to an Alliance for the Future to create a common prosperity and economic security space," said von der Leyen.
The move comes as EU members have also been hit trade tariffs under Trump's administration and as the bloc faces what its chief described as "an openly hostile world".
Setting out the EU's political and policy priorities for year ahead, von der Leyen also proposed the formation of a European Security Council, which would include the UK and Ukraine, amid an ongoing threat to the continent from Russia.
"For a long time, we have discussed a leaders' format focused on the security of our continent, with partners like Canada, Norway, Ukraine, the United Kingdom and others involved," she said in the wide-ranging address.
"This is even more urgent now, given the nature and scale of the risks at play. This is why we will set out our ideas to make a European Security Council a reality."
Alongside global threats, von der Leyen also said many European families were worried about the cost of living, and the "dizzying speed of change" of technology and its impacts on jobs and society.
Other proposals included inviting the world's largest AI labs for talks on how to support industry efforts to pace the frontier, as well as slashing bureaucracy for businesses in the EU.
A new emergency tool to help countries better deal with mass migration movements following the deadly influx of migrants to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in July would also be outlined.
Plans to curb social media use among children, including banning platforms for under 13s, were also put forward. Under the proposal, children aged 13 to 15 would only be able to set up social media accounts which are supervised by parents.

- Published
White-tailed eagle chicks have successfully fledged from wild nests in England for the fourth consecutive year.
Two out of five pairs of eagles released by a reintroduction project successfully bred and raised young with one chick fledging from a nest in Dorset and two more in Sussex.
The project, run by Forestry England and the Roy Dennis Wildlife Foundation, aims to return the species to England. Nine birds have been born in the wild since it began in 2019.
"This year's breeding success is another important milestone in the return of this lost species to England; it shows what can be achieved by very skilled wildlife managers," Roy Dennis OBE from the foundation said.
The foundation has called the breeding attempts "remarkable", adding that one of the male adult birds has only one leg after losing it five years ago.
Human persecution had caused the bird's extinction, with the last pair breeding in southern England in 1780.
"Restoring a species takes many years and requires the support of a wide range of communities and organisations, in particular landowners and farmers," Dennis added.
Steve Egerton-Read, white-tailed eagle project officer for Forestry England, said: "We are delighted that these three chicks made it through and will be closely watching their progress as they begin to explore the landscape."
To date, 56 young white-tailed eagles have been released including, for the first time this year, additional releases of six birds at Exmoor National Park, in partnership with Exmoor National Park Authority.

Wooden container huts meant for thousands of athletes have become the subject of heated criticism ahead of the opening of Japan's Asian Games on Saturday.
Jung Jae-yong, vice-president of the Korea Basketball Association, told AFP news agency the accommodation was the "worst it has ever been".
"Athletes who are over two metres (6ft 7in) tall cannot even stretch their legs out on the beds. It's unreasonable."
The Games, held in the city of Nagoya and wider Aichi prefecture, have faced weeks of concern about a potential shortage of beds. More than 17,000 athletes and officials are attending - exceeding the initial 15,000 expected.
The containers, which will be housing around 2,000 of the guests and are designed to be reused as disaster evacuation facilities, have been beset by complaints.
A member of the South Korea basketball team posted a video of a leaking pipe and soaked floor in his room, with the caption: "Please help me."
Athletes were also briefly evacuated from the containers as record rainfall lashed Nagoya last week and caused widespread flooding. Water leakage was reported in some of the competition venues too.
Jung, the basketball official, told AFP that concerns over accommodation were shared by representatives from the other countries at the Games.
Indian authorities have built replicas of the huts to get their athletes used to living in them.
Accommodation manager Yuta Matsuo told Reuters the hosts were "fully aware of the dissatisfaction and concerns voiced by the athlete delegations".
They were "taking concrete steps to improve the environment for the athletes", he said.
Unlike the Olympic Games, where there is usually a designated athletes' village, organisers have opted to use temporary accommodation for competitors.
Beyond the container huts, between 4,000 and 5,000 participants will be staying on an Italian cruise ship which docked in Nagoya on Tuesday. The rest of the attendees will stay in hotels.
Initially, 15,000 athletes and officials had been expected to attend the Games.
But in mid-August the Olympic Council of Asia said the number would be closer to 17,000 after teqball - which combines elements of football and table tennis - and padel were included.
Hideaki Omura, president of the organising committee and Governor of Aichi Prefecture, previously said authorities had set aside a budget for 15,000 people and had "neither the manpower nor the budget to make the necessary arrangements" for the additional athletes.
"There is simply nowhere for them to stay. If they still wish to come, they will have to make their own arrangements."
But last month, organisers and the Olympic Council of Asia said all "17,000-plus" athletes and officials who had registered before the deadline in July have been provided with "Games-appropriate accommodation".
"The final preparations are all on track and progressing smoothly ahead of what promises to be the most spectacular Asian Games held for generations," their statement read.
Philippine Olympic Committee president Abraham Tolentino told AFP that while all the country's athletes have secured a bed, some officials and coaches were staying in "different hotels and Airbnb".
Though basketball and football matches have already started, the Asian Games officially begin on Saturday and will end on 4 October.

cdb1df3ccd14.text: Members of Congress and governors are under increasing pressure to regulate AI , but more than two dozen of them who spoke with Axios said they don't use the technology or have rarely done so. Why it matters: That striking admission — particularly among older, influential lawmakers — comes amid calls for an AI slowdown and warnings within the industry that it could end humanity if left unchecked. Critics argue that it's impossible for politicians to grasp how rapidly the technology is changing — and the threats or scientific breakthroughs it might unleash — if they don't use it or even dismiss it. One House Democrat called it "f*cking absurd," arguing, "Anyone who's overseeing this has to be someone who's a regular user." "That's a real problem," said Rob Flaherty, a 35-year-old Democratic digital strategist who co-founded a group to push his party to move faster in confronting AI. "Understanding what it can do is essential to figuring out what we ought to do about it." "As we begin to legislate on issues related to AI, it helps to have experience using it," said Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.), who's 47. Zoom in: Several lawmakers, including those steeped in seniority and in charge of key committees, told Axios they simply haven't tried AI. "Heavens no," said Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.), 75, chair of the Armed Services Committee, when asked if he uses AI. "Personally? I don't think I've ever used it," said Rep. Frank Pallone (D-N.J.), 74, the ranking member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee. "No," Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-Hawai'i), 78, said when asked if she uses AI, but that "doesn't mean I won't." She added, "I don't think we in Congress have gotten quite our handle on what we should do and how much AI we should be regulating." "I do not personally use it," said Sen. James Risch (R-Idaho), 83, the Senate Foreign Relations Committee chair. On a personal level, "no," said Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.), 83. The House Appropriations Committee ranking member added that she needs a "primer on AI, and now with the scare that we have out there, it's much more important to be engaged." A GOP senator, speaking anonymously to offer candid remarks about their colleagues, told Axios that the number who use AI is "not very high." That's helped lead to a knee-jerk negative reaction toward AI among several lawmakers, the senator added, as polls show growing numbers of voters turning against it. Some elected officials said they don't utilize AI much personally, though some on their teams employ the technology. Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D), who's 48, said he uses AI "on the Google, when you can get a little bit of that search summarized for you. But otherwise no. I do not use it in research. We do not use it in our writing." He said that he supports robust regulation and though some in his state government use AI, final decisions must be made by humans. Other politicians were unsure if they've ever used AI — or said they've only done so by accident. "I don't think I do," said Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), 70, when asked if he utilizes it. "If I Google something, it kicks off an AI thing, but that's about as far as I go." "I don't know. I can't remember," said Rep. Maxine Waters (D-Calif.), 88. Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), 73, said she doesn't seek out AI on her own, but that "it pops up on my phone occasionally." "Not intentionally," said Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.), 68. "The only AI use that I'm kind of familiar with is an AI tool attempting to summarize email chains, and they often get it wrong." What they're saying: Some lawmakers such as Kaine argued that they don't need to use AI to write legislation about it. He said he has read a lot about it and trusts his judgment more than AI. After we spoke with him, Pallone shared a statement through a spokesperson that said: "You don't need to do drugs like heroin to know they should be regulated. Members of Congress don't need to spend their time talking to AI chatbots all day to know we need to rein in this dangerous technology." Friction point: But some members of Congress were irked or surprised that colleagues don't use a technology they're seeking to regulate. "Are you serious?" Sen. John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.), 74, said in response to our question. "I use it for everything! I can't believe there's a senator that doesn't use AI." Yes, but: There are members of Congress who are frequent AI users, including some in Hickenlooper's age range. Rep. Bobby Scott (D-Va.), 79, the ranking member of the House Education and Workforce Committee, told Axios he uses AI "every day." Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.), 76, went back to school to get a master's degree in machine learning and said he prefers Claude. Catch up quick: Some of the most powerful elected officials in the country have told other media outlets in the recent past that they don't use AI. In late 2025, House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), 54, said in an interview that he didn't think he'd ever used AI. About the same time, Karoline Leavitt, then press secretary to President Trump, 80, said that she didn't think Trump personally uses AI, though his social media account regularly posts AI-made content.

Olu Jacobs, one of Nigeria's best known actors, whose career spanned several decades across theatre, television and film, has died at the age of 84.
His wife, veteran actress Joke Silva, announced his death and asked for privacy while the family mourns.
Silva announced his passing in a statement describing the celebrated actor as "The Lion of Lufodo" and saying his life was "well lived and fought".
Some of his notable films include My Kingdom, Covert Operation and One Fine Day.
He was regarded as one of the father figures of Nollywood, as Nigeria's film industry in known, commanding widespread respect and admiration across the country.
"We call on all bloggers and social media influencers to respect our family's privacy at this time," Silva said in a statement.
Born on 11 July 1942, Jacobs was trained at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London before embarking on a career that included appearances in British television productions and international films.
He later became one of the defining figures of Nigeria's film industry, appearing in numerous Nigerian productions and earning recognition for his commanding screen presence and versatility.
His career spanned more than five decades, during which he received several major honours, including the African Movie Academy Award for Best Actor in a Leading Role and lifetime achievement honours.
In 2011, Jacobs was conferred with the national honour of Member of the Order of the Federal Republic (MFR) in recognition of his contribution to the Nigerian film industry.
Jacobs and Silva jointly established the Lufodo Group and Lufodo Academy of Performing Arts, contributing not only to film and television but also to developing and training performing artists in Nigeria.
In recent years, Jacobs had largely stayed away from the public spotlight due to ill-health.

bc03c88e2093.text:
The News
Africaâs richest man Aliko Dangote is considering plans to list shares of his Nigeria refinery business on a US stock exchange within the next four years following the launch of its initial public offering, the continentâs largest ever.
The share sale, which kicked off in Lagos on Monday, has a fundraising goal of $1.6 billion, with room to add 30% more than the target if the offer is oversubscribed. Plans for a secondary listing would extend ownership in the refinery beyond the millions of Nigerians who have swarmed onto several fintech apps to subscribe to the offer set at 40 cents a share. The refinery is valued at around $50 billion, more than twice the cost of construction.
âIn the next three, four years or thereabout, we will try and also list outside the African continent, most likely in the US,â the billionaire owner of the Dangote refinery said at the IPO launch this week.
The timeframe overlaps with the companyâs plans to double the refineryâs output to 1.4 million barrels a day by early 2029. In an interview last week before Dangoteâs address at the IPO launch, refinery chief financial officer Bruce Tanner told Semafor that the company will âdefinitely be looking for international secondary listings,â and suggested that it would be after the refinery ramps up production. He had declined to give an exact date for the listing.
The companyâs initial intent to roll-out this IPO on multiple African exchanges became unworkable âgiven the timeframe and regulatory hurdles in each of the different environments,â Tanner said. He indicated that some investment houses and pension funds that could have participated in a pan-African IPO have still bought into the offer in its current Nigeria-only form.
Know More
The Nigerian refineryâs daily capacity of 700,000 barrels puts it above every refinery that currently operates in the US. Successfully doubling its size will make it the largest in the world, displacing Indiaâs Jamnagar refinery owned by Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani.
Expansion will enable Dangote to serve African fuel demand beyond Nigeria where it has become the most influential supplier to the domestic market since coming on stream in September 2024. The Dangote group also plans to set up a second refinery in Kenya to form a network capable of fulfilling the continentâs needs. Both projects will cost some $30 billion combined.
Proceeds from the ongoing IPO will be directed towards the Nigeria expansion and further fundraising is planned in future, Tanner said. The refinery recorded $13.9 billion in half-year revenue this year and has forecast annual increases for each full year up to 2030, on the assumption that added refining capacity will boost sales.
Meanwhile, the plantâs 69-year-old billionaire founder, whose decades-old empire includes giant cement and sugar subsidiaries, could see his wealth expand by more than 60% to $58 billion on the strength of the Nigerian refineryâs IPO alone, according to Bloomberg.
Step Back
Dangote is betting that scale, not sentiment, is what finally makes an African-founded company work as a US-listed stock. The refineryâs capacity doubling to 1.4 million barrels a day would mean the plant could produce roughly 10% of US refining capacity. At that scale, a US listing offers him dollar liquidity, index inclusion, and institutional capital the Nigerian Exchange canât match.
But African businessesâ record on US exchanges has been shaky. African ecommerce company Jumiaâs 2019 New York Stock Exchange debut showed how fast âAfrican growth storyâ enthusiasm evaporates even after initially hitting a record high valuation months after IPO. Today the stock still trades roughly 75% below its IPO price. Meanwhile, commodity players including Sasol, AngloGold Ashanti and Gold Fields donât list shares directly in New York but trade as American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) â certificates issued by a US bank representing shares held abroad, letting US investors buy them in dollars without a foreign brokerage account.
But years on, their ADRs still track gold and chemical prices, not business fundamentals â proxies for commodities, not endorsements of the companies themselves. Others, including Flutterwave, have quietly shelved Nasdaq ambitions. Dangoteâs bet is that hard assets, not a growth narrative, will make the difference this time.
The View From Botswana
Neo Mooki, chairperson of the stock exchange in Botswana, said at the Lagos IPO launch that the Dangote refineryâs existence and share sale was proof that âAfricans can own Africaâs ambition.â She implored the company to work with her exchange âto make sure that this ambition can also be owned right across Africa from Gaborone to Nairobi.â
In addition to Kenya, Botswanaâs capital market was a potential destination for the refineryâs shelved pan-African IPO. The Botswana Stock Exchangeâs $70 billion equity value is smaller than Nigeriaâs $120 billion market, but the bourse lists the shares of some large companies like Anglo American, the British mining giant with extensive operations in Southern Africa.

- Published
Colombia has again topped the list of countries with the highest number of killings of land and environmental activists, according to an annual report by campaign group Global Witness, external.
Out of at least 124 activists killed globally in 2025, 39 were murdered in Colombia, followed by Brazil with 26.
Global Witness says that 85% of the documented killings took place in Latin America, making it the deadliest region for every year since the group started publishing its reports in 2012.
Most of the killings were part of land disputes and in many cases they were carried out by hitmen or members of organised crime gangs, the report states.
Colombia has accounted for the highest number of murders of environmental activists for the past four years.
Almost half of those killed in the country were members of indigenous groups, while many of the remaining ones were small-scale farmers, Global Witness's report says.
Many indigenous groups in Colombia have created their own protection networks in the form of indigenous guards, which patrol their territory but are unarmed.
Members of indigenous guards are often targeted by illegal armed groups looking to expand their territory to plant coca - the raw material used to make cocaine - or to engage in illegal mining.
Last week, Jacob GuachetÃ¡ Zambrano, who was part of the indigenous guard in Colombia's Cauca region, was found tortured and killed.
While the possible motive behind his murder is still under investigation and the search for the perpetrator is ongoing, indigenous leaders said that murders, threats and forced disappearances in the area were common as illegal armed groups battled for territory.
Global Witness warned that Brazil had seen a doubling of killings of environmental defenders in 2025 compared to 2024.
As in Colombia, in Brazil most of the cases the group documented were primarily driven by conflict over land, Global Witness's researchers found.
Outside of Latin America, 12% of the murders occurred in Asia, with Philippines top of the list with 12 documented murders.
The group warned that while globally the number of documented killings had gone down from 146 in 2024 to 128 in 2025, its numbers were probably an underestimate as many cases went unreported.

The US Federal Reserve is likely to raise rates today, a move that many economists say is necessary to corral inflation, but which will put the central bankâs chair in conflict with the White House. The Democratic Republic of Congo sought to speed up the implementation of a strategic mining partnership with the US, which is looking to rival Chinaâs influence in Africa. The DRC, the worldâs largest producer of cobalt, a key component in electronics, has already received US investment under the agreement as it seeks to attract more Western funds.
If Washingtonâs plan is fully realized, Congolese minerals will flow west on a US-backed rail line to a port in Angola and then onward to the US. Though China remains by far the biggest investor in African mining, countries across the continent are looking to reduce their reliance on Beijing while expanding their control over more valuable sections of the supply chain.

The European Commission president invited Canada to become the EUâs first-ever âassociate member,â highlighting the global geopolitical realignment underway as a result of US pressure on allies. The move would transform the EU from a bloc defined by geography to one driven, at least ostensibly, by values.
It also risks further worsening Brusselsâ and Ottawaâs relations with Washington: US President Donald Trump has railed against both, and is locked in a trade war with the latter; several EU member states are reportedly wary of the White Houseâs reaction. Still, the announcement could transform the EU and set the stage for more geographically ambitious expansion: âWe are on the same page [as Canada],â Australiaâs trade minister told the Sydney Morning Herald.

444d1f9b4cd4.text:
The News
Somalilandâs president is putting almost everything on the table in his campaign to win US recognition for the breakaway territory of Somalia, offering US investors access to a strategically located port and mineral resources while leaving open the possibility of expanded military access.
âWe are not giving anything for free,â Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi âIrroâ said in an interview with Semafor in Washington. âWe have to offer something. And we expect the other partner [to have] the same or equal opportunities.â
Recognition is the prize, but economic cooperation, trade and investment can proceed in parallel. Somaliland can offer âour facilities and our minerals,â he said.
The US already has a military relationship with Somaliland, including training and security cooperation, but no military base there. The head of US Africa Command visited Hargeisa and Berbera last year as Washington continued to assess the territoryâs strategic importance.
Irro is signaling that the relationship could go further. Military access for the US, Israel or other countries, he said, âis a negotiation.â
âI will not rule out,â he said of a future base agreement, arguing that any deal would depend on what Somaliland receives in return, including greater security and support for its forces.
Yinkaâs view
Israelâs recognition in December changed the diplomatic equation on Somalilandâs status. It gave the breakaway territory its first recognition from a UN member state and, more importantly, demonstrated that the decades-old consensus against recognizing the territory could be broken.
Irro is now trying to turn that breakthrough into momentum. He is spending this week in Washington pressing his case at the White House and on Capitol Hill before heading to New York, where he hopes to meet other world leaders during the UN General Assembly and make the case for recognition.
The US is the next prize. Irro described America as the âbig fishâ Somaliland wants to pursue. âThe earlier, the better is always better,â he said.
His appeal is also tailored to Trump. Somaliland could name Berberaâs airport after him, Irro suggested, or welcome him to build a Trump Tower in Hargeisa.
The message underneath the flattery is more consequential since Somaliland is no longer simply making a historical or moral case for recognition. Irro is trying to show Washington what recognition could buy.
Room for Disagreement
Somalia sees the proposition very differently. Mogadishu rejects Somalilandâs claim to sovereignty and considers Berbera, its coastline and its resources part of Somalia.
That makes Irroâs offer of strategic and commercial access politically contested before any foreign government or company accepts it. Israelâs recognition has sharpened that dispute, turning Somalilandâs push for wider recognition into a more consequential challenge to Somaliaâs territorial claims.
Know More
Geography is central to Irroâs proposition. Berbera sits on the Gulf of Aden, close to the Bab el-Mandeb, the narrow maritime gateway between the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean. As conflict and disruption have put renewed pressure on the regionâs sea lanes, Somaliland sees an opportunity to turn its location into diplomatic leverage.
Diego Garcia, the US military facility in the central Indian Ocean, lies thousands of kilometers away from the Red Sea theater. Berbera offers a far closer location for logistics, resupply or other military operations around the Gulf of Aden and Bab el-Mandab, even if it would not simply replace the much larger US presence on Diego Garcia.
Irro argued that American officials understand that strategic case. âThey know that,â he said, pointing to US training and security cooperation already taking place in Somaliland.
His offer is deliberately open-ended. Somaliland is not announcing a new US base; it is signaling that greater access could be negotiated. âWe are not giving anything for free,â Irro said, returning to the transactional logic behind his recognition campaign.
Step Back
Irro is also trying to sell Somaliland as an economic opportunity rather than simply a strategic outpost.
He points to Berberaâs port and free zone, an 850-kilometer coastline, fisheries and potentially significant oil, gas and mineral resources. Somalilandâs government budget has risen from less than $50 million when he became parliament speaker in 2005 to about $500 million today, he said.
The ambition is considerably bigger. Irro said Somaliland could be âvery richâ within a decade and claimed its budget could eventually reach $3 billion-$4 billion a year if its marine economy and other resources are developed.
Recognition, in his view, would help unlock that potential by making it easier for US and other international investors to treat Somaliland as a conventional investment destination rather than an unrecognized territory.
The View From China
Irroâs push for US recognition does not mean he wants Somaliland locked into a single geopolitical camp.
Taiwanâs representative office will remain in Hargeisa despite Beijingâs opposition. âWe have decided Taiwan to remain,â Irro said, noting that Taiwan was already present when he took office.
China is still welcome to invest. âIf China is coming without condition, we will welcome China,â he said. Chinese companies already operate in Somaliland, he added.
The line Irro draws is political saying no foreign power will decide Somalilandâs diplomatic relationships. âNobody can dictate to us,â he said.

2e066bc7e308.text:
- Published
Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte has appeared in person at the International Criminal Court in The Hague, where he is due to be tried for alleged crimes against humanity.
He is facing charges over his bloody war on drugs, which saw tens of thousands of small-time drug dealers allegedly executed summarily.
The 81-year-old wore a dark suit and white shirt with no tie on Wednesday, the first time he has been seen in person since his arrest in Manila 18 months ago.
Until now he had appeared before the court by video link and subsequently skipped multiple hearings.
The ICC called a status hearing on Wednesday after Duterte's lawyers argued the former leader's deteriorating health had made him unfit to stand trial.
The first trial date is scheduled in November.
The war on drugs was the centrepiece of Duterte's presidency, which ran from 2016 to 2022. He argued peace and order was necessary to grow the economy.
The ICC is looking at killings from 1 November 2011, when Duterte was mayor of Davao, a sprawling southern metropolis, to 16 March 2019, when he withdrew the Philippines' membership in the ICC.
Duterte's lawyer Peter Haynes has told the court his client suffers from "significant memory impairment", making him unable to engage with his legal team. Prosecutors argued otherwise.
In 2019, when he was still president, Duterte revealed he was suffering from myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune condition that causes nerve malfunction. At 71 in 2016, he was the oldest Philippine president at the time of election.
Duterte heads to trial at the ICC as his family is caught in a high-stakes dynasty war for control of the Philippines. His daughter, Vice-President Sara Duterte, has feuded spectacularly with President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos.
The break-up of the Duterte-Marcos alliance, which helped them win the 2022 elections by a landslide, paved the way for the Rodrigo Duterte's arrest at Manila airport in March 2025.
Sara Duterte is a frontrunner to replace Marcos in the 2028 elections, where the incumbent is ineligible under the constitution to stand for a second term.
But she is also fighting for her political survival in an impeachment trial, where if convicted, she will be disqualified from running for public office.
She is charged with misusing public funds and threatening to have Marcos, first lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and Marcos' cousin, congressman Ferdinand Martin Romualdez assassinated.

- Published
Surrey Wildlife Trust has introduced 30 nationally-endangered water voles to a nature reserve near Elstead.
The release on the River Wey comes following a "successful" release on the upper river.
The water voles are being introduced downstream on 10 sites between Frensham and Elstead, the wildlife trust said.
James Herd, director of reserves management at the trust, said: "As we work towards the restoration of natural ecosystems and landscapes county wide, I hope this release is one of many reintroductions of native species that we'll see in the years ahead."
Water voles have been functionally extinct in Surrey since the early 2000s, but co-ordinated reintroduction and habitat improvement efforts by nature restoration groups are working to help the endearing species thrive again.
The trust said in a statement that it hoped that over the coming months, the aquatic rodents will "adapt easily to life on the 16-hectare reserve at Thundry Meadows and establish widely across the top of the Wey catchment".
Their return would also benefit other species which depend on healthy wetland habitats including herons and birds of prey, they added.
David Elliott, National Trust lead ranger for the South Downs West said: "Nature wins when we work together."
"It's so encouraging to see the water voles returning after all this time, they have been locally extinct for decades.
"The return of this enchanting species adds a missing piece to this jigsaw."
The release is part of a wider effort led by the National Trust, River Wey Trust and South East Rivers Trust to reintroduce the locally extinct species back to the River Wey.

46855d867c82.text:
Jasonâs view
On September 15, Saudi Arabia issued alerts for Mecca, Jeddah, and Taif. They were soon lifted and no impact was reported. The threat came after the Houthis, the Iranian-backed militia controlling northern Yemen, swept down Yemenâs Red Sea coast.
They took Mokha, a port city near the coastâs southern end, and Mayun, an island in the Bab el-Mandeb strait, and then moved to the Hanish islands to the north. The Houthis now hold nearly the entire Yemeni side of one of the worldâs most important shipping lanes and sit roughly 20 miles from the main American military base in Africa, in Djibouti.
When I served as the White House Middle East envoy, the Houthis were not my file, but they were never far from it. Few governments treated them as a serious actor. They were seen as a ragtag militia, a Saudi and Emirati problem, and a humanitarian story. Itâs true that the group isnât an impressive military, but they hold Yemenâs capital, the part of the country where most Yemenis live, and now nearly all of its Red Sea coast.
Saudi Arabia and the UAE recognized the danger early and fought the Houthis for years. That coalition frayed: the UAE drew down its forces in 2019, a UN-brokered truce largely halted the war in 2022, and Riyadh resumed direct talks with the Houthis.
The Houthis are a US-designated terror proxy of the Iranian regime. Their rule in Yemen has inflicted suffering on people through corruption, coercion, aid diversion, and war. Their latest offensive reportedly came with direct guidance from Tehran. According to Reuters, Tehran instructed the Houthis to escalate, promising them more money, weapons, and expert Iranian advisers.
The reason behind the timing is clear. For more than six months the US has been raising the cost to Iran of using the Strait of Hormuz as a weapon, and Iran has answered by putting another global energy chokepoint under threat. A drone strike that Riyadh attributes to an Iran-aligned group in Iraq also shut down the pipeline carrying Saudi oil across the kingdom to the Red Sea, bypassing Hormuz.
The Houthis have been hard to stop for reasons that have nothing to do with their quality as soldiers. They fight with cheap drones and missiles against interceptors that can cost a thousand times as much. From mountain strongholds, they have survived years of Saudi-led airstrikes and, more recently, American and British ones. Iranian weapons keep reaching them despite an air and sea blockade. Most of all, no campaign against them has been sustained. Each stopped before it was finished.
This time could be different. The Houthi advance gave their enemies a new set of exposed fixed targets. A militia holding a port city, an airfield, islands, and a long stretch of coastline can be found and hit. The Houthis wanted that ground because it brings their weapons closer to the ships they want to threaten, but holding it also puts them out in the open. This opportunity will not last long as they move to fortify these new coastal positions.
The countries with the most to gain from acting now were together in one room last week. United States Central Command (CENTCOM) confirmed that Admiral Brad Cooper hosted senior military leaders from eight nations in Germany to discuss regional security cooperation. According to reports, they represented Israel, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Jordan, and Egypt.
Six years ago, the Abraham Accords that US President Donald Trump created brought Israel into open partnership with the UAE and Bahrain, clearing the way for the Pentagon to move Israel under CENTCOMâs umbrella alongside its Arab neighbors. Military relationships that began with missile defense have grown into a room where Israel and seven Arab states, most of them not party to the accords, strategize against a shared threat. According to Axios, Cooper told the group that American forces are staying in the Middle East, and discussions are underway about extending to Saudi Arabia the intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance support that Israel already provides to the UAE.
Saudi Arabia says it intercepted a Houthi drone headed toward Mecca, and the Houthis deny it. Whatever the truth of the September 15 alerts, Tehran understands what a threat to Islamâs holiest city does to Sunni opinion while its Shia proxy attacks Saudi Arabia. Iran seeks regional dominance by setting Muslim against Muslim, country against country, and everyone against Israel. To some degree, its pressure is producing the opposite. Regional countries are increasingly coordinating against Iran and its proxies, building a habit of cooperation that will ultimately lead to normalization.
Taking the Houthis head-on requires sustained strikes on their new coastal positions, a joint maritime mission aimed at Iranian resupply, and a declared goal of removing the Houthis from the Red Sea coast, not managing them there.
For years the Houthis were dismissed as a nuisance. They now threaten one of the worldâs most important oil routes while their patron in Tehran squeezes another. This is the moment for the Gulf states, the US, Israel, and their allies to take advantage of a ripe opportunity to act together. Waiting is how the Houthis got this far.
Jason D. Greenblatt served as White House Middle East Envoy in the first Trump administration. He is the author of In the Path of Abraham, the founder of Abraham Venture LLC, and publishes the Substack âHow to Watchâ
Notable
- Saudi Arabiaâs crown prince traveled to Egypt to meet President Abdel-Fattah El-Sisi, who commands the Arab worldâs largest military. The kingdom is reluctant to act alone against the Houthis, Bloomberg reported.

7df50aa57021.text: A new coalition launched Wednesday is seeking a triple win for a data center industry that lately has struggled to notch any wins at all. The big picture: Tech giants Google and Nvidia are partnering with startup Emerald AI to back data centers that can flex their power demand — a strategy they say could curb electricity prices, mollify angry neighbors and grow the economy with more AI infrastructure. The launch comes amid mounting backlash to data centers centered on their resource impacts and power prices, and new polling shows the public-opinion challenge is getting steeper. What they're saying: "It's really a win-win-win solution," said Josh Parker, head of sustainability at Nvidia, in a call with reporters Monday ahead of the official launch of the coalition, called the AI Energy Management Alliance . State of play: The coalition brings together 20 companies and organizations spanning the AI and energy sectors, including Anthropic, utilities National Grid and AES, and power producers Constellation, NRG and RWE. The group is technically a relaunch. An earlier iteration, the Advanced Energy Management Alliance, was founded in 2014 to advocate for demand-response companies but had become largely inactive, Emerald AI CEO Varun Sivaram said on Monday's call. The revamped group is narrowly focused on making AI data centers more flexible power users — and convincing regulators and utilities to reward them for it. Friction point: A whopping 84% of Americans say they're concerned about data centers' impact on local electricity prices, according to new AP-NORC/University of Chicago Energy Policy Institute polling released Wednesday . More than half of Americans are extremely or very concerned about AI's environmental impacts, up from 41% a year ago. In a rare point of bipartisan agreement, roughly equal shares of Democrats and Republicans — 79% and 76%, respectively — support requiring data center developers to pay for the grid upgrades needed to support them. How it works: Data centers have traditionally been treated as giant, round-the-clock power users. The coalition wants to change the rules so facilities that can reliably cut their grid demand when electricity supplies are tight can get connected faster and potentially avoid some costly grid upgrades. The flexibility could come from shifting or pausing AI computing jobs, tapping batteries or nearby power generation, coalition leaders said. Google has committed 1 gigawatt of power demand it can reduce when needed through utility agreements nationwide, said Tyler Norris, Google's head of advanced energy market innovation. The group plans to push the approach with federal and state regulators, regional grid operators and utilities. Yes, but: The bargain depends on data centers actually delivering the flexibility they promise. Sivaram said facilities should qualify for faster or larger connections only if their ability to cut demand is "verifiable and enforceable." Reality check: Convincing communities that this complicated solution can actually address their concerns will be a tall order. "Power-flexible data centers are a wonky topic," Sivaram told Axios. His pitch: Data centers could cut their electricity use when the grid is stressed, helping avoid costly infrastructure while bringing in revenue that can support other electricity users. The goal, Sivaram said, is to turn data centers into "good grid citizens" that communities see as assets rather than burdens. What we're watching: Whether regulators actually create the fast lane the coalition wants. Federal regulators in June directed regional grid operators to examine new options for connecting large, flexible power users, providing an opening for the approach AEMA is advocating. Editor's note: Amy Harder is a fellow at the University of Chicago's Institute for Climate and Sustainable Growth, but was not involved in the polling and received no advance access beyond that provided to other journalists. Editor's note: This story has been corrected to note that 76% of Republicans (not 78%) support requiring data center developers to pay for grid upgrades.

- Published
A wildlife trust has called for a new offshore disposal site to be found for sediment dredged from Brighton Marina, saying it remains concerned about plans being explored off Newhaven.
Brighton Marina has been looking for a long-term disposal site since Sussex Wildlife Trust successfully challenged a licence in 2025 for disposal of sediment at Rottingdean.
The marina has said dredging is needed to maintain safe access and there are limited options available for disposal sites.
Sussex Wildlife Trust said Newhaven was a "protected area" that sat adjacent to the Beachy Head West Marine Conservation Zone (MCZ).
Campaigners previously claimed the silt was a "black, thick, slimy, petrochemically smelling sludge", but Premier Marinas, which owns Brighton Marina, said dredged silt was regularly sampled to confirm it was not harmful.
John Cervenka, Premier Marinas chief operating officer, said: "Maintaining safe navigational access to Brighton Marina is not optional. It is a legal requirement and fundamental to the operation of the marina."
He said the marina was a major centre of economic activity.
According to the marina, about 150 businesses depend on the site, creating jobs for about 1,200 people, with more than eight million visits each year.
Premier Marinas said Newhaven had been identified as a potential alternative by Sussex Wildlife Trust.
However, the trust said in a statement on social media, external: "We have not promoted or endorsed Newhaven over any other option."
The trust said: "Newhaven sits adjacent to Beachy Head West MCZ, and we remain concerned about potential impacts on this protected area.
"Our preferred option is a new offshore disposal site, well away from the MCZ."
The trust said that Newhaven was already used for dredge disposal by Newhaven Port, and there was currently no available data on the impacts of additional disposal there.
Until it saw further evidence, it did not have a view on whether Newhaven was suitable, it added.
"We will respond to any future licence application based on the ecological evidence it contains," it said.
Brighton Marina hopes to submit a marine licence application to the Marine Management Organisation in November.
If approved, maintenance dredging could restart next spring.

WhatsApp groups and social media across Saudi Arabia lit up on Tuesday with variations of the same message: The Houthis are attacking Mecca. Photos of the Kaaba and prayers of âGod protect this countryâ spread after Saudi civil defense issued an alert for Islamâs holiest city, the first since the war began, before lifting it minutes later. Some questioned whether it was an error or a test, while others condemned their âfellow Muslimsâ for threatening what is holy.
Over the past six months, there was a sense that Mecca would provide a shield for western Saudi Arabia. As sirens went off over Riyadh and the Eastern Province, people in the Hejaz assumed no one would dare approach what all Muslims deem sacred. Tuesdayâs alert punctured that logic. While nothing was hit â Saudi authorities said a drone was intercepted â the taboo has been broken. Nothing is holy in war.

Gulf airlines are coming out swinging after a brutal year, fending off opportunistic European rivals and instability at home. Nowhere is this clearer than in Dammam, where Saudi Arabia has ordered a new budget airline and an expansion of King Fahd International Airport. Run by an Air Arabia-led consortium, it will fly Airbus A320s on domestic routes to Riyadh, Jeddah, and Madinah.
In long-haul, Emirates won a coveted Berlin slot this week, strengthening its Europe-Asia foothold. Some European airlines have opened new Middle Eastern routes this year, which Emirates President Tim Clark called âa little bit sad,â and an attempt to exploit the Iran war. The Dubai carrier expects to restore full prewar seat capacity by the end of 2026, returning âhard and fastâ if the conflict subsides. Abu Dhabiâs Etihad is taking the same muscular approach, adding more than 20 aircraft and new routes to Europe, Africa, and China as other long-haul carriers have pulled back.

10ec6ef92d04.text: Kristen Silverberg, a widely respected policy expert and former ambassador, was named the new president and CEO of Business Roundtable , the top policy voice of America's leading CEOs. Silverberg, now BRT's president and chief operating officer, will succeed Josh Bolten , a former White House chief of staff who has led the organization for the past decade , when he steps down on Jan. 31. Why it matters: Business Roundtable is one of Washington's most influential associations. The 200+ members are CEOs of the biggest U.S.-based companies, most with global reach. The CEOs use BRT to amplify what they consider the most important messages business leaders can deliver to government. Silverberg — who worked with Bolten in the White House and is a former U.S. ambassador to the European Union from 2008 to 2009 — said in a statement that a key mission of BRT, American companies and their CEOs is championing and delivering growth and jobs. "The American economy is undergoing a profound transformation," she said. "Leaders in government and business have an extraordinary opportunity and a responsibility to strengthen American growth and competitiveness while expanding opportunity for workers and communities." "Business Roundtable has a critical role to play in advancing policies that make America the best place in the world to build, grow and invest in a business." The backstory: Silverberg, 55, was an assistant secretary of State under President George W. Bush and was a law clerk to Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas and Judge David Sentelle of the U.S. Court of Appeals. She's a graduate of Harvard College and the University of Texas School of Law. What they're saying: BRT chair Chuck Robbins, chair and CEO of Cisco Systems, called Silverberg a "proven and strategic leader, with the deep trust and respect of Business Roundtable's Board and members." "Kristen has been instrumental in positioning the organization and its leaders as effective advocates for policies that help American businesses grow and innovate while expanding opportunity for workers and communities across the country." Bolten told me in an interview: "Kristen Silverberg is one of the finest policy professionals in America today. Over the last several years, she earned broad respect among Business Roundtable members and the enthusiastic support of BRT's board. "I could not be happier that they have selected Kristen to lead BRT through the challenging years ahead." What's next: Bolten, already a member of several major boards, plans a "portfolio" approach for his next phase. 🏟️ On his bucket list: visiting all 30 Major League Baseball ballparks with his son.

4df8f203f22c.text:
Destructive immune cells tied to Alzheimer’s disease may get their marching orders from cells outside the brain rather than within it.
In mice, suppressing a small population of immune cells located in lymph nodes protects against neurodegeneration, researchers report September 3 in Nature Neuroscience. The findings raise the possibility of treating Alzheimer’s disease while bypassing the brain’s siege defenses.
For years, researchers have gone all in on efforts to remove toxic tangles of proteins like amyloid and tau from the brain as a way of halting Alzheimer’s, with limited success. But the immune system also plays an important role in neurodegeneration. What exactly that role is — protector or antagonist — has been unclear.
In 2023, neurologist David Holtzman and colleagues showed that immune system T cells accumulate around tau tangles — implying that they might cause damage. Halting these cells’ entry into the brain reduced inflammation, and also reduced neuronal damage, says Holtzman, of Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis.
Still, it wasn’t known how these T cells accessed the brain in the first place. “A big question has been whether the T cells passively enter the brain or are primed … to do so,” says Rudolph Tanzi, a neurogeneticist at Harvard Medical School who wasn’t involved in the study.
During priming, T cells are ordered to rally and multiply. The generals that bark out these orders are called dendritic cells, which capture signatures of cellular threats called antigens and present them to T cell infantry.
No one had looked closely at what dendritic cells in lymph nodes were doing during neurodegenerative disease, Holtzman says. So in the new study, he and his colleagues compared two groups of mice engineered to have tau-linked neurodegeneration, one of which lacked dendritic cells.
Blocking an attack
Alzheimer’s-like neurodegeneration can ravage a brain, as seen in the slice of a mouse’s brain at left. The attack may be planned in the lymph nodes, new research suggests. The brain slice depicted on the right came from a mouse in which that early stage of attack was blocked.
In old age, mice without dendritic cells still had brains packed with tau. But compared with the other mice, they were protected against neurodegeneration and performed better on cognitive tasks like nest building.
They also had far fewer T cells in their brains. This suggests that tau tangles aren’t working alone in driving neurodegeneration, Holtzman says. “A lot of the damage that tau is causing is due to the inflammatory response that it’s eliciting.” The results would need to be replicated in human brains, he adds.
Despite this seemingly important role, the researchers found few dendritic cells in the mice’s brains. Instead, they detected threat-mimicking brain proteins traveling to the lymph nodes, where dendritic cells used them to rally T cells. The team bred mutant mice with demoted dendritic cell generals that could no longer give commands to T cells. These mice also had fewer T cells in their brains and better-preserved brain structures.
It isn’t practical to disable dendritic cells from birth in people at risk of Alzheimer’s. But Holtzman says his colleagues are working on cellular targets that could suppress them in adulthood. The real promise of the study may be a dementia treatment that bypasses the nervous system’s locked vault — the blood-brain barrier, Holtzman says. “If this panned out, potentially you wouldn’t have to get [therapeutics] into the brain.”

eefa4f4096bb.text: By — Fatima Hussein, Associated Press Fatima Hussein, Associated Press By — Ali Swenson, Associated Press Ali Swenson, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-live-dr-nicole-saphier-testifies-in-confirmation-hearing-for-u-s-surgeon-general Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH LIVE: Dr. Nicole Saphier testifies in confirmation hearing for U.S. surgeon general Politics Sep 16, 2026 10:06 AM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Dr. Nicole Saphier, President Donald Trump's third nominee to serve as surgeon general, will face lawmakers at her confirmation hearing Wednesday in the latest attempt to fill the post known as the nation's doctor. The hearing begins at 10 a.m. EDT. Watch live in the video player above. Saphier, a radiologist and former Fox News Channel contributor, is Trump's newest pick after entrepreneur and wellness influencer Dr. Casey Means saw her path forward stall in the Senate over her background and vaccine views. Trump withdrew his first nominee, Fox News medical contributor Janette Nesheiwat, after questions arose about her academic credentials. READ MORE: Trump pulls Casey Means' stalled surgeon general nomination, picks Nicole Saphier instead Saphier will face questions from the Senate health committee for a position that carries limited policymaking power but a loud megaphone as the nation's top communicator with Americans on public health issues. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. While senators may scrutinize her credentials and background, Saphier will also be in the difficult position of navigating Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s more contentious policies, including his efforts to scale back vaccine guidance when measles outbreaks around the country are alarming the medical community. Lawmakers of both parties have criticized Kennedy's stances and are likely to grill Saphier over whether she'll more fiercely advocate vaccination if confirmed. Saphier is director of breast imaging at Memorial Sloan Kettering Monmouth, according to her profile on the New York-based institution's website. She has a doctor of medicine degree from Ross University School of Medicine in Barbados along with fellowships at the Mayo Clinic, the profile said. Like Means, who is a close Kennedy ally, Saphier has questioned whether every child needs to get the hepatitis B vaccine at birth, a longtime recommendation that the Trump administration has been trying to weaken. Saphier has, however, disagreed with Trump and Kennedy on some issues, telling The Associated Press last fall that Trump's cautions to pregnant women who take Tylenol were oversimplistic and "patronizing." Her latest ethics filing, dated Sept. 7, shows holdings with various healthcare and insurance firms, as well as processed food companies, like Coca-Cola, Yum Brands, the Hershey Co. and cigarette maker Philip Morris. Before entering politics and throughout his tenure at the health department, Kennedy has criticized big pharmaceutical companies and insurance firms for alleged corruption and decried ultraprocessed foods as contributing to a nationwide chronic disease crisis. Additionally, Saphier owns DropRx, a firm that produces controversial, unregulated tinctures — concentrated liquid extracts promoting focus and calm — that contain ingredients, including kava kava root, described by the FDA as potentially causing severe liver injury. Her filing says she will resign from her position with DropRx and Empower MD LLC, which owns DropRx, if she is confirmed. She states in the document that she would partially or fully divest from holdings that would present a conflict to serving as surgeon general. Also facing lawmakers' questions Wednesday is Chris Klomp, chief counselor of the Health and Human Services Department, who has been nominated to serve as Kennedy's second-in-command. Also at the hearing will be Timothy Westlake, chief of staff at the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, who is seeking confirmation to be assistant secretary for mental health and substance use. 1a12fce1de31.text:
Since the dawn of the Space Age, the weaponization of space has been an international concern. Now the United States has announced, with few details, that it has weapons in orbit.
“The United States has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending … against hostile adversary action,” U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said September 14 at the 2026 Air and Space Cyber Conference in National Harbor, Md.
With such limited information, it’s hard to know what to make of the announcement. But “the world should be listening with open ears about this information because of the wide range of consequences,” says astrodynamicist Thomas González Roberts of Georgia Tech in Atlanta.
Space weapons are difficult to define and encompass many different possible technologies. “There’s real ambiguity about the term ‘space weapon,’” Roberts says. These weapons can involve satellites directly attacking other satellites, with projectiles, explosives, lasers or other methods. A satellite could physically grab and manipulate another satellite. Cyberattacks can incapacitate satellites or wrest control away from their operators. Space weapons could also affect life on the ground, for example, by disrupting GPS services.
And space weapons have a long history. In 1962, the United States tested a nuclear weapon at high altitude, which incapacitated many of the satellites orbiting at that time. Soon thereafter, the 1967 Outer Space Treaty banned weapons of mass destruction in space. (Although, recently, the United States has alleged that Russia is testing technology needed to put a nuclear weapon in orbit.)
Multiple nations, including the United States, have also tested antisatellite weapons that can take spacecraft down by launching weapons from the ground or air. Worryingly, some types of space weapons could make orbits unusable, by strewing dangerous debris that can collide with satellites or anything else in its path.
Science News spoke with Roberts about what we know and don’t know about the weapons Meink referred to. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
SN: What do we know about these space weapons?
Roberts: When I saw this news, my first take was that it’s missing a lot of adjectives. The way we describe a space weapon is by its method of attack and the consequences of using that weapon.
So when I think about what a space weapon is, I think about questions like is an attack attributable — can others see who did it? Is it reversible, meaning the effects on the target can be undone? And will there be public awareness about whether it was successful or not? Could the attacker themselves determine if it was successful or not?
And could there be collateral damage, meaning other satellites or other space assets would be damaged or degraded? This is what I’m curious about for these U.S. weapons.
So, what kind of weapon do I think it is? I think it’s one where the benefits in those categories are greatest.
SN: Could it be connected to plans for the Golden Dome missile defense system, which would put missile interceptors in orbit?
Roberts: I had the same thought. Could this be that? Could this be something different?
The hint [Meink gave] of “space control” as an adjective is bothersome to me. I want more information. Are we talking about affecting your adversary’s ability to control their satellites? Are you saying the capability is for the United States to control another satellite? The use of the word “control” really sparks my thought processes. There are weapons where you can steal control away from someone else: cyberattacks, grappling, noncooperative rendezvous and proximity operations. I don’t know what the statement means in this context.
SN: Should we be concerned about space debris if these weapons are used?
Roberts: Some space weapons produce collateral damage. A fragmentation event produces nondiscriminate debris, meaning debris that will run into you no matter what your nationality is. But many, many satellite attacks, you can easily focus them on just your target. I would imagine the U.S. is talking about that. The U.S. is the biggest actor in space. They can’t afford to jeopardize the environment.
SN: How could someone attack another satellite without producing debris?
Roberts: Jamming it is the best idea here. If you’re jamming the signals with which a satellite receives or sends data, that means it’s not useful to its operator. But that doesn’t mean that it’s dead.
A lot of these attacks are targeting certain subsystems. Shining a laser at a satellite is particularly damaging to an optical or infrared sensor. If you think a satellite is taking pictures of Earth, like any spy satellite or reconnaissance satellite, you might be interested in disabling just that optical sensor.
SN: What might the repercussions of this announcement be?
Roberts: It really invites criticism from U.S. adversaries. The global community has been working for some time on preventing an arms race in outer space. It offers evidence to some who might claim that it’s too late.
Right now, states obfuscate. There’s evidence for Russia and China developing space weapons, testing them and demonstrating them. But largely they deny it. In most cases, they pretend they’re not doing anything at all. And the U.S. is taking a different approach. Instead of obfuscating it, they’re telling everyone.
