"A formal agreement or consensus may be near impossible, but they do not need to go that far," said Samm Sacks, a senior fellow at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies' Institute for America, China, and the Future of Global Affairs. "Trump and Xi just need to create political space by acknowledging AI poses risks to both countries." China and the U.S. are increasingly at odds on AI Trump has pushed back on calls to strengthen regulation of the technology, claiming that doing so could cause China to eclipse America on AI. He has repeatedly declared that the nation that leads on the technology "wins." "We are leading China, and all others," Trump said Monday on social media. The two countries are moving the technology forward in different ways. U.S. companies are chasing AI frontiers with computing power supported by cutting-edge chips and the country's rapidly expanding data center infrastructure. China is pursuing wide global adoption of its open-source, more affordable models. Chinese AI models have made major advances and gained traction with American companies even as U.S.-led restrictions bar China from getting the world's most advanced AI chips. While most American frontier models are closed-source, with their design elements kept secret, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday the U.S. needs to develop more open-source models to counter China. The U.S. has accused China of "aggressive, malicious" efforts to extract capabilities from American AI systems. China has hit back, accusing the U.S. of trying to suppress Chinese companies so it can build a "monopoly of the AI industry." David Sacks, a top AI adviser to Trump, said that China has "already rejected" slowing down the pace of developing the most advanced forms of AI. He said on Fox News' "The Ingraham Angle" that unlike the nuclear tensions with the Soviet Union during the Cold War it would be impossible to verify whether China honored any AI commitments. "In this case, we don't have trust and we can't verify," Sacks said. "So let's not be foolish about this and just hand the whole ball game to China." Still, those with ties to the Chinese government see coordination on AI as helpful. At an annual security and defense conference in Beijing, Cui Tiankai, a former Chinese ambassador to the U.S., said Tuesday that AI is an area where "we should go ahead and build up" dialogue between Beijing and Washington. "Because there is a need, a growing need, for cooperation," he told the Xiangshan Forum. "So how can we manage the balance?" American AI leaders call for keeping China in check — and cooperating with China Two leading American AI companies, Anthropic and OpenAI, each restrict access in China and have said the U.S. has a national security imperative to protect its lead on AI technology. But they also have called for cooperation with China to manage safety. In his essay last weekend calling for a slowdown of AI development for safety reasons, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said the U.S. should slow China's progress, including keeping up U.S. restrictions on China's purchases of the world's most advanced AI chips. He also added, however, that "global pacing will require cooperation with China, the autocratic country with by far the most advanced AI capabilities." His essay quickly drew criticism from Beijing, with China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs saying on Monday that "fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance which serves no one's interest." China's state-run Global Times newspaper went further, calling his remarks "packed with containment provisions targeting China and is, in essence, a 'Cold War playbook' for the AI sector." Trump has consulted with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, even calling the maker of the world's most advanced computer chips in the middle of a Monday podcast interview. Nvidia has generally favored some chip exports to China as a way to create an American ecosystem for the technology and a more open relationship on AI given the number of researchers in China. Both countries have been alarmed by emerging AI capabilities In both the U.S. and China, AI's increasingly powerful capabilities have alarmed top officials and policymakers. 915cec96752c.text:
When an immense and inexorable flow of rock, mud and water barreled through northern Nepal on August 26, it killed more than 1,200 people and left thousands still missing. The magnitude of the event caught even experts on the region’s geology off guard.
“The victims, their pain and all the ruined towns … it is almost impossible to believe,” says geological engineer Ranjan Dahal of Tribhuvan University in Kathmandu, Nepal, who has studied geohazards in the Himalaya for nearly 30 years. “I don’t think even Hollywood could make such a movie.”
Satellite imagery helped researchers piece together a rough picture of the event’s origin: An enormous slab of bedrock and ice falling from a mountain called Langtang Lirung spawned a debris flow that hurtled downstream toward India. That dense torrent reached speeds over 160 kilometers (100 miles) per hour and destroyed villages along the way.
“I’ve never seen anything remotely as large as this,” says mountain geographer Alton Byers of the University of Colorado Boulder, who studies the impacts of climate change in the Himalaya.
What caused the bedrock to break in the first place is not entirely clear. But research and insights from scientists suggest that certain geologic, glacial and climate factors probably played a role in the disaster. Those insights underscore the potential threat to other high mountain regions, and how the risk of catastrophe may increase over time.
Human-caused climate warming is melting the ice that holds high mountains together, says glaciologist Ulyana Peña, also of the University of Colorado Boulder. “And it’s not something that’s just limited to Nepal,” she says. “The mountains are crumbling globally.”
Why the bedrock broke
There was early speculation that a collapsing glacier caused the debris flow. But images taken by satellite soon after the event showed a freshly exposed, uniform slope had appeared on Langtang Lirung’s north face, at an elevation of around 5,150 meters. In reality, a slab of bedrock roughly 2.2 square kilometers wide had detached from the mountain, carrying the overlying ice down into the valley below.
At this point, scientists estimate that the detached chunk of glacier and bedrock amounted to a volume somewhere around 110 million cubic meters. That’s roughly 40 times the volume of the Great Pyramid of Giza.
A swath of factors probably contributed to the breaking of bedrock on August 26, scientists say. First, it’s possible that the magnitude 7.8 Gorkha earthquake that hit central Nepal in 2015 may have damaged the bedrock, mountain hydrologist Walter Immerzeel of Utrecht University in the Netherlands said at a Sept. 16 briefing about the factors behind the event. The temblor’s shaking triggered a landslide on Langtang Lirung that killed around 200 people in Langtang Valley.
There’s also the matter of climate warming. The ancient tectonic uplift of the Himalaya is thought to have left fractures now sealed with ice known as permafrost in rocks at the altitude where the bedrock failure occurred. “It’s that cryospheric glue that, for millennia, has held together the glaciers and the rocks and the soils and the boulders up at high altitude,” Byers said September 1 during an online panel discussing the avalanche’s connection to climate change.
Human-caused climate warming has softened much of the permafrost in these regions, he said. “It’s like taking a stick of butter out of the refrigerator and putting it on the counter — it becomes mushy.”
Such softening may have contributed to the August avalanche, Byers and others speculate. Climate change has increased the annual average temperature on the slope and in the region more generally by about 2 degrees Celsius since preindustrial times, according to a report released by World Weather Attribution on September 17. “That’s much faster than the average rate of global warming,” said climate scientist Ben Clarke of Imperial College London during the Sept. 16 briefing.
On top of that, “the period right before the collapse was exceptionally warm,” Immerzeel said. During August 24 to 25, the average temperature at the elevation of the avalanche was about 5° C, with daily maximum temperatures reaching over 10° C. Historically, temperatures at that time of the year average around 2.7° C and don’t typically go above 6° C.
Immerzeel also pointed out that the overlying glacier had retreated more than 300 meters from 2010 to 2026 due to warming, potentially shifting the stresses on the rock wall.
Warming may have facilitated the bedrock breakup in other ways too. If meltwater from the glacier or permafrost trickled deep into fractures in the rock and then refroze, it could have wedged the cracks open even more, says geologist Jeffrey Kargel of the Planetary Science Institute in Tucson, Ariz. Additionally, meltwater may have chemically weathered the bedrock and formed weak, flaky minerals known as phyllosilicates inside of the fractures, he says, which would have made it easier for the rock to slip.
Fragile rock
The type of rock may have also contributed to the destruction downstream. Kargel notes that the scarp left behind appears to consist of rocks that began as hardened layers of mud and sand. These sedimentary rocks were later squeezed by heat and pressure into metamorphic rocks. But the resulting “metasedimentary” rocks still contain their relic layers, he says, which may act as weak zones.
Those weak zones could have helped the rock crumble more easily as it tumbled down the mountain, causing more collisions between pieces of rock and ice during the fall and upon impact with another glacier at the base of the slope, Kargel says. More collisions would mean more frictional heating of ice into water, which would have been crucial in mobilizing the solid debris into the fluid freight train that swept down into the Lhende Khola river valley. It would have picked up more water and sediment on its way downstream, he says.

An Australian athlete who faced criticism for continuing to compete in a Hyrox event after soiling herself has apologised and said she will retroactively withdraw from the race.
Joanna Wietrzyk offered her "sincere apology" for the incident during the indoor fitness competition in Beijing on Saturday, saying she should have "made a different choice" and exited the event.
Footage of Wietrzyk competing after soiling herself raised concerns about hygiene, leading Hyrox co-founder Moritz FÃ¼rste to apologise for the handling of the situation.
In a statement shared on Thursday, Wietrzyk said: "I know my actions had an impact beyond myself, and I am genuinely sorry to everyone who was affected."
After the backlash, Wietrzyk, who won the race in Beijing, said she would forfeit her win.
Wietrzyk said in a social media post: "I want to offer my sincere apology to the people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the HYROX organizers for what happened during the race in Beijing."
She wrote in a social media post, external that she was "completely fit and healthy" at the start of the race, and had "no reason" to expect any illness.
"Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognize that I should have made a different choice. I take responsibility for my decision to continue and am deeply sorry for the discomfort and disruption it caused," Wietrzyk continued.
Hyrox insisted it had "clear biocontaminant and medical procedures in place".
It said "an unforeseen situation arose" during which protocols became blurred, "creating ambiguity in how they were applied and understood".
In a statement posted on Instagram, FÃ¼rste committed to "improving event processes" to "prevent situations like this from happening again".
After Wietrzyk's identity was shared online, Hyrox said anyone sending abuse or threats to the athlete would be banned from any future events.
It said on Monday: "There is no place in our community for threats of violence or encouragement to harm an athlete."
In each Hyrox race, participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing fitness exercises, including a sled push, burpee jumps, indoor rowing, and lunges while carrying a sandbag.
The competition has exploded in popularity since it was founded in 2017 in Hamburg, Germany, and is now held across the world. The sport debuted in mainland China in late 2024.
Some have questioned why those officiating the competition in Beijing last weekend did not intervene when the athlete soiled herself, given that Hyrox penalises acts including "spitting, nostril clearing, littering, and water abuse".

- Published
Footage verified by the BBC shows the wreckage of a Saudi F-15 fighter jet which the Iran-backed Houthi group says it shot down over Yemen.
The US-made aircraft was "downed using a locally manufactured surface-to-air missile" as it "conducted hostile operations" over the Marib region, according to a Houthi statement on Wednesday.
Experts have told BBC Verify the incident is a "propaganda coup" that shows the Houthis' military capability has advanced and they are prepared to further escalate its conflict with Saudi Arabia.
Using satellite imagery to match features in the landscape seen in the footage, BBC Verify was able to pinpoint the crash site to an isolated location in the hills west of the Yemeni city of Marib.
The long-running conflict between a Saudi-led military coalition and the Houthis has escalated in the last week after the armed group launched an offensive against pro-government forces.
This led to the Houthis seizing key territory near the south-west coast, close to vital international shipping channels in the Bab al-Mandab strait.
In one of several video clips released by the Houthis, men with assault rifles can be seen at the crash site inspecting the wreckage. The fighters celebrate as they lift the jet's almost-intact tail fin which features the Saudi flag and a four-digit serial number.
The fate of of the crew is not known.
The Houthis also released a thermal video clip - which cannot be fully verified due to a lack of visual details - that appears to show a fighter jet in mid-flight being struck by a missile.
BBC Verify has contacted the Saudi Ministry of Defence for comment.
Baraa Shiban, Yemen analyst at the Royal United Services Institute, told BBC Verify the incident showed it was "very clear the Houthis have been taking advantage of advice and technological support" from Iran.
"They continue to develop their military arsenal and capabilities to make it more and more painful on Saudi Arabia," he said.
Downing the F-15 is also a "propaganda coup", said Yemen expert Adam Baron from the Washington-based New America think tank, as Saudi air support is considered to be "key to any significant pushback" against recent Houthi gains.
"An eye-for-an-eye has been a huge element of the group's public messaging. This is partially to show that air support will come at a price," he added.
BBC Verify used the position of the sun and satellite imagery to locate the distinctive landscape seen in the footage - including cliff faces and hills - to an isolated mountainous area about 25 miles (40km) west of Marib.
Satellite imagery published on Wednesday also shows a new dark shadow at the same location, which appears consistent with scorch or burn marks at a crash site.
The aircraft in the wreckage has been independently identified by Nick Brown, a weapons expert from military intelligence company Janes, as an F-15 Strike Eagle. He based his analysis on distinctive elements seen in the footage including the tail fin arrangement, radar antenna and missile warning system sensors.
The four-digit tail number visible on the wreckage also appears to be consistent with that of an F-15 Strike Eagle operated by the 55th Squadron of the Royal Saudi Air Force based at King Khalid Air Base near the city of Khamis Mushait in south-west Saudi Arabia.
This base, about 245 miles (392 km) from the crash site, was targeted last week by what the Houthis described as a "barrage of missiles and drones". Satellite imagery analysed by BBC Verify appears to show damage to at least three aircraft hangars or shelters.
The base is one of a series of high-profile Saudi targets struck by the Houthis in recent days including an oil refinery in the city of Jizan.
Saudi Arabia said on Wednesday it had destroyed a Houthi drone close to the Islamic holy city of Mecca on Tuesday, which the Houthis have denied targeting.
The group said on Thursday that Saudi Arabia had launched 40 air strikes against Yemen over the past 24 hours.
Additional reporting by Shayan Sardarizadeh and Alex Murray
Graphics by Tom Shiel

dbb59960b3df.text: Trump officials must give 30 days' written notice before making any changes to the Kennedy Center "including but not limited to any ' demolition '" of the main building, a federal judge ruled Thursday. Why it matters: The ruling reinforces an earlier injunction blocking the Kennedy Center from closing for its planned renovation, after President Trump and administration officials raised the possibility of demolishing the building. The ruling allows the center to continue making "emergency repairs" rather than halt them entirely. Driving the news: District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled Thursday that the defendants must file a "detailed status report, supported by a sworn declaration from a knowledgeable representative of the Kennedy Center, on the 'temporary closure' and emergency repairs described" in the Kennedy Center board's most recent court filing, per a minute order published Thursday. Representatives for the White House and Kennedy Center did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Catch up quick: Trump said on social media Tuesday that the center was going to be closed. Shortly after, an announcement played over the center's loudspeakers telling attendees that it was closed. Legal counsel for the institution initially said someone had improperly triggered a fire alarm, causing the loudspeaker announcement. But when the plaintiff's staff attempted to enter Wednesday during regular operating hours, security denied them entry and said the building was closed for interior construction and safety reasons. The staff member said she later saw workers using forklifts to bring in additional construction-style gates and watched a forklift carrying permanent fencing repeatedly strike the building's structural pillars. Context: Trump was recently pictured looking at a markup reading, "Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED." He told reporters on Wednesday that the Kennedy Center had been bleeding money before he "got involved." "For the Trump administration, for me, to get involved and to take that on long term, and to carry it, or to raise money to carry it, I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition." "Because frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close. It'll end up being ripped out ... You see steel falling down. You see plaster falling off ceiling ...It's been very badly maintained for 25 years." Zoom in: Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio) has been in a legal battle with the administration since the center's board, made up of Trump appointees, began making changes including adding the president's name to the building's facade. Cooper has repeatedly blocked that move, determining that only Congress can change the building's name and that even a small inscription would violate the legislation that christened the building. Trump subsequently announced that the center would close. State of play: Beatty's legal team says it is unclear what construction is underway and has raised concerns that the center could undertake demolition or other work that would make public access impossible and circumvent the court's order. The previous injunction didn't prevent the center from undertaking renovations and repairs without shutting down. But Beatty's attorneys say, "the nature of the construction activities and any potential demolition are unclear. Given the unexplained and unlawful closure, it is possible Defendants intend to undertake immediate steps in order to make public access practically impossible for the foreseeable future," the filing reads. Go deeper: Trump-aligned Kennedy Center board votes to close building Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details throughout.

66f9e6ecfb82.text: Staring into the camera, Rep. Maria Salazar (R-Fla.) cut a new campaign ad that told President Trump what so many of her fellow Hispanic Republicans in Miami are saying: Immigration crackdown has gone too far. Why it matters: The anger at Trump over heavy-handed immigration enforcement is palpable in Miami-Dade County, and there's mounting political worry among Republicans across the state that it could cost the GOP in the midterm elections. Zoom in: A bellwether, Miami-Dade is Florida's most-populous county, which Trump flipped to the Republican column in 2020 and 2024 thanks to strong Latino support, especially among Cuban Americans. "Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far," Salazar says in her ad. "The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today." Trump carried her district by 15 points two years ago. Today, she's tied in polls with newscaster Eliot Rodriguez, a fellow Cuban American, who said her new ad was a sign of desperation. A Trump adviser told Axios: "I'm getting the Trumpiest Cubans sending me videos from Miami of guys getting busted at places like the gas station, for no apparent reason." By the numbers: In Miami-Dade, 62% of the county's 1.3 million registered voters are Hispanic. They account for 76% of the registered Republicans. 63% of Hispanic voters said they supported "deporting illegal immigrants" while 34% were opposed to them, according to a poll conducted last month by a GOP pollster and shared with Axios But those numbers switched when it came to how deportations were being carried out: Just 29% were in favor; 58% were opposed. "The support is just evaporating. The economy sucks and ICE is just out of control," said the pollster, who's from Miami. "People feel they didn't sign up for this." Yes, but: Trump ran on a platform of mass deportations. He promised to target undocumented criminals, but the president's critics warned that his aggressive immigration push would lead to raids, arrests in the streets, racial profiling and separated families. "There was truth in advertising," the pollster said. Trump last year also began revoking Temporary Protected Status for as many as 1.3 million people across the country, some of whom first received the TPS designation in 1998. "Temporary means temporary," a White House official told Axios, noting that President Biden had allowed millions into the country under TPS and a new program that Trump reversed. Ground zero for the Miami-Dade fear and loathing is in Doral. Trump owns a prized golf course there. It's also nicknamed "Doralzuela" because of the large Venezuelan population. Businesses were hit doubly hard last year when Trump canceled TPS for Venezuelans: Legal workers lost the authorization to work, once-legal residents fled, and those who are still there are in hiding or constantly getting picked up by federal agents. "Our sales have dropped 70%. We spend hours empty," Katia Rios of Pipo Burgers, told CBS Miami on Wednesday. Doral Mayor Christi Fraga, a Republican, has been besieged with complaints and has tried to distance herself from the Trump administration. "I don't agree with the way things are handled," she told CBS. Zoom out: Salazar's Republican congressional colleague from Miami, Mario Diaz-Balart, has a district that stretches from Doral on Florida's southeast coast to Naples on its southwest coast. "We've been sending this message to the administration for months," he said of Salazar's ad. Diaz-Balart, however, hasn't spoken publicly against the administration because he prefers to work behind the scenes. Republicans say they're not too worried about conservative Hispanic voters switching to vote for Democrats, but they all believe turnout for the GOP will be low, which could affect legislative and congressional contests, and perhaps the race for governor. "Byron Donalds better watch out," a top Republican consultant said of the Republican congressman locked in a tighter-than-expected gubernatorial race against Democrat David Jolly. (A Donalds spokesman said Jolly will lose.) Friction point: Miami's best-known Cuban American political figure, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, has been publicly supportive of the administration's immigration policies, despite the outcry back home. Rubio was identified with bipartisan immigration reform in 2013, when he served in the Senate. Venezuelans have grown increasingly agitated with Rubio and Trump for not voicing support for an election date in Venezuela and for the administration's transactional relationship with its acting president, Delcy Rodriguez, a socialist who came to power after the U.S. ousted strongman Nicolas Maduro on Jan. 3. "There's a growing feeling that Trump just wanted our oil," a Venezuelan Republican activist said. Between the lines: Miami-Dade has one of the country's most-diverse Latino populations. Cuban Americans are the dominant group, but there are sizable communities with roots elsewhere in Latin America. Cuban Americans tend to be the most conservative because of the exile community that swelled after Fidel Castro took power there in the 1959 revolution. Exiles from families who fled leftist oppression or violence in Nicaragua, Colombia and Venezuela also found common cause with Cuban-American Republicans over the years. Now, these South Florida Hispanic communities are grappling with an immigration system that treats them about the same as Haitians in Miami or arrivals from Mexico in more liberal U.S. cities such as Los Angeles. Cubans once enjoyed expansive immigration protections in the U.S. Under Trump, they're being deported in large numbers to Mexico and even countries in Africa. Behind the scenes: Salazar's broadside against Trump followed days of discussions between her office, Diaz-Balart's and the administration over the arrest of Luis Galeano, a Nicaraguan journalist in Miami with an active asylum application. ba70e01ea12d.text: By — Matt Brown, Associated Press Matt Brown, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/about-35-million-people-have-been-put-into-new-house-districts-in-the-fight-over-congressional-maps-report-says Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter About 35 million people have been put into new House districts in the fight over congressional maps, report says Politics Sep 17, 2026 2:59 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The unprecedented spate of mid-decade redistricting for the U.S. House has changed the congressional districts for one-tenth of Americans and significantly altered the makeup of at least one-fifth of districts, according to a new study. A report by Protect Democracy found that 34.8 million people — about one in 10 Americans — now live in a different district than they did during the 2024 election cycle. And about one-fifth of all Americans now live in a district where more than a quarter of voters are new to the district compared with the last election cycle. READ MORE: Supreme Court again rejects push to use Trump-backed congressional map in Missouri The findings display the stark overhaul that partisan redistricting fights kicked off by President Donald Trump last year have caused for Americans across the country. The new congressional maps are increasingly drawn in ways that favor partisan politics over factors like geography and shared communities. That raises concerns among scholars about how the country's hyperpolarized politics are affecting American democracy. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "If this trend continues, it really brings into question whether or not elected officials are really representing their constituents anymore, or if the voters are being randomly picked by mapmakers to squeeze out partisan advantage," said Ben Raderstorf, a policy advocate at Protect Democracy and one of the paper's co-authors. READ MORE: A whiplash election year enters its final stretch as Trump holds wild cards The bare-knuckled partisan redistricting battle for the House began when Trump urged the Republican-controlled legislature in Texas, the second most populous state, to redraw its congressional map to help the party. The highly unusual plan prompted an immediate response from California, the most populous state, which held a successful referendum to tilt its map toward Democrats. Other states followed, and Republicans are positioned to potentially gain nine seats because of redistricting. The Protect Democracy report warns that such partisan tactics reduce faith in American elections generally and insulate incumbent lawmakers from public opinion. That can make political organizing more difficult, the report cautioned, potentially worsening the country's already highly polarized politics. Both parties may also enter a "doom loop" where they embrace more aggressive and frequent redistricting efforts to avoid ceding any ground to their rivals. In some states such as Missouri, the mid-decade redistricting has created confusion for voters about which district they live in and which candidates will appear on their November ballot. After conflicting lower court rulings, the U.S. Supreme Court last week blocked new Missouri districts backed by Trump that had been used in the primary, leaving the state to revert to its previous districts for the general election. The report concludes with a call for new electoral structures the authors believe would eliminate the potential downsides of partisan redistricting, like proportional representation or a formal truce between the parties to implement nonpartisan districting plans. Nine states already use nonpartisan commissions to draw congressional district lines but those provisions have limits. California, for instance, suspended its nonpartisan maps with a referendum last year in response to Texas' redistricting measures. Such remedies would face long odds in Congress and statehouses, but scholars believe there are few other avenues to turn down the temperature in the partisan redistricting fights. "This is only going to get worse until somebody stops it," Raderstorf said. "The logic of gerrymandering points inevitably towards maximalist partisan advantage on both sides. There is no off-ramp other than reform. It is the only way to break the cycle." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Since 1989, astrophysicist Jonathan McDowell has tracked every human-made object in space. McDowell’s meticulously maintained catalog, updated every few weeks, is more comprehensive and detailed than that of most governments.
From his front-row seat, he has watched with growing alarm as private companies launched dozens, then hundreds, then thousands of satellites over the last decade. So when McDowell heard that a space company called Reflect Orbital plans to launch a satellite to reflect the sun’s light onto the night side of Earth, he heaved a deep sigh.
“It’s an insane project,” says McDowell, who retired from Harvard this year and is now an honorary professor at Durham University in England. “There’s a failure to understand that darkness is a good thing.”
Reflect Orbital, based near Los Angeles, hopes its satellite and others like it some day offer “sunlight on demand,” illuminating disaster areas for search and rescue efforts, lighting up nighttime events and festivals and allowing solar farms to run all hours of the day.
“We believe that exploring how new technologies can help the world forgo fossil fuels is a responsible application of the scientific process,” Christopher Buscombe, a spokesperson for Reflect Orbital, wrote in an email to Science News. “We will continue to work closely with scientific partners who share this belief.”
But many space observers and dark sky enthusiasts are in an uproar. The consequences to astronomy could be catastrophic, they say, and the reflected light could threaten human health and safety and disrupt wildlife. In March, the American Astronomical Society petitioned the Federal Communications Commission to deny Reflect Orbital’s request to operate the test satellite. When the FCC granted approval in July, nonprofit organizations including DarkSky International asked the agency to reverse its decision.
The response to Reflect Orbital reflects growing concerns about the crowding of space more generally. The number of active satellites orbiting Earth has ballooned from 2,000 in 2018 to over 16,000 today, McDowell says. Many more are expected to launch in the years ahead.
This traffic jam, along with the proliferation of space junk from dead satellites and discarded rocket stages, has space scientists worried about collisions that could wipe out GPS navigation and other essential tools. The satellites are also a problem for astronomers, interrupting observations by leaving streaks on telescope images.
But there’s not much scientists can do to appeal the launches, says international environmental lawyer Dana Zartner of the University of San Francisco. Space satellite deployments are governed (sometimes loosely) by a patchwork of domestic regulations and international treaties. “The law has not caught up to the reality of what is happening,” Zartner says.
The Reflect Orbital launch, expected this year, could change that. The satellite’s unique brightness and the risks it may bring could mark an inflection point in the way we regulate the night sky. The project “amplifies the issue to the point where it’s impossible to ignore,” says astronomer Stephen Hummel of the McDonald Observatory in West Texas.
Who’s in charge?
Space law’s roots are planted in the Cold War. Some of the earliest international treaties about activities in outer space grew from agreements banning nuclear tests high in the atmosphere.
“People [were] saying, ‘Let’s not nuke the sky, please,’” says Cristian van Eijk, an expert in international space law at Newcastle University in England.
Over 100 nations have signed the Outer Space Treaty of 1967, which declares space “the province of all mankind.” No nation can occupy or claim sovereignty over any portion of outer space, it says, and space must be used for peaceful purposes and be kept clear of harmful contamination. Four other international treaties have dealt with issues such as the registration of space objects and the liability they might cause.
But such treaties are voluntary, and it’s difficult to enforce compliance. “Nobody can make a state do any of these things,” Zartner says. “You cannot throw a state in jail.”
Individual countries have their own regulations about what goes into space and how. In the United States, the Federal Aviation Administration oversees rocket launches and reentries. But the FCC oversees licensing of commercial satellites that communicate with Earth, and it has become the de facto gatekeeper for satellite approval. The FCC has traditionally been required to consider whether applications serve the public interest, but it has not generally considered factors such as light pollution.
The explosion in satellites in low-Earth orbit, between about 100 and 2,000 kilometers in altitude, has exposed gaps in the system, says astronomer Samantha Lawler of the University of Regina in Saskatchewan, Canada. That’s because current approval processes look at launches one by one without addressing what thousands of satellites mean in aggregate. “There are some serious loopholes,” Lawler says.
Bugs on the windshield
To reduce the impact to science, companies like SpaceX have worked with astronomers to dim the appearance of their commercial satellites, by changing their orbits or painting the satellites black, for example. But there are still problems.
Astronomer Meredith Rawls likens existing satellites to “bugs on the windshield.” She and colleagues have spent years preparing the new Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile to cope with the light streaks left by overhead satellites.
Those streaks can mess with searches for transiting exoplanets, the mysterious sources of gravitational waves, objects in and beyond the distant Kuiper Belt and asteroids that could cross paths with Earth. Satellites in low-Earth orbit, including SpaceX’s Starlink constellations, are mainly visible just before sunrise and after sunset; that’s prime time for many types of astronomical observations.

7d074e1cdc70.text: By — Jacques Billeaud, Associated Press Jacques Billeaud, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/jon-kyl-long-serving-lawmaker-from-arizona-who-shaped-water-policy-dies-at-84 Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Jon Kyl, long-serving lawmaker from Arizona who shaped water policy, dies at 84 Politics Sep 17, 2026 4:23 PM EDT PHOENIX (AP) — Former U.S. Sen. Jon Kyl, a longtime Republican lawmaker from Arizona who shaped landmark water policies in the U.S. West and guided the confirmation of Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, has died. He was 84. Kyl died Wednesday night from a neurological disorder, said Gordon James, a communications professional who is a longtime friend of the Kyl family. Kyl had withdrawn from public life in December 2025 after announcing he had been diagnosed with dementia. Kyl spent almost three decades in Congress, serving in both chambers, and watched his party undergo a drastic transformation, with his career spanning Ronald Reagan's presidency to President Donald Trump's first term. "Arizonans are mourning the loss of former U.S. Senator Jon Kyl," Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs said in a post. "Throughout his decades of public service in the House and Senate, he was a dedicated statesman who always cared deeply for our state." Former Republican Arizona Gov. Doug Ducey, who considered Kyl a mentor, described the former senator in a February 2025 interview with The Associated Press as a true statesman and a "workhorse" among Washington, D.C.'s "showhorses." "If you saw him on the plane, he was sitting in the aisle, in coach, and he was reading," Ducey said. "And he was reading potential bills or Senate business." Kyl returns briefly to Senate to fill McCain seat Kyl rose to a leadership position during his last full term in the Senate, when his Republican colleagues selected him as minority whip. After retiring from politics in 2013 and becoming a lobbyist, Kyl returned to Congress briefly in 2018, when Ducey appointed him to fill the vacancy left by the late U.S. Sen. John McCain. His appointment drew high praise from Trump, who said he was looking forward to working with "the extraordinary senator." Kyl stayed for less than four months before rejoining lobbying firm Covington and Burling. "At the federal level, and I regret to say that this is the case, but probably a lot of my better achievements were in preventing bad things from happening (rather) than forcing good things to happen," Kyl said in a 2012 conversation with former U.S. Supreme Court Justice Sandra Day O'Connor. Lawyer with expertise in water gets elected Kyl was born in Oakland, Nebraska, on April 25, 1942, and grew up in a rural farming district in Iowa that his father represented in the U.S. House. At 18, he headed southwest to attend the University of Arizona, where he met his wife, Caryll, and earned a law degree. Before being elected for the first of his four terms in the House in 1987, Kyl was a key participant in shaping Arizona's 1980 groundwater code as a lawyer representing a large water utility. The first-of-its-kind code created a regulatory framework for managing groundwater in the drought-stricken state, largely centering on the state's population centers, including Phoenix and Tucson. In 2004, Kyl authored legislation that provided one of the largest tribal water rights settlements, which, after a decades-long battle, gave the Gila River Indian Community enough water to fill nearly 313,500 Olympic-sized swimming pools annually. Republican U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, who later served as majority leader, called Kyl's work ethic "legendary" in a 2012 floor speech and said Kyl had labored mostly behind the scenes for 15 years to advance the settlement. Former Arizona Sen. Jeff Flake said he had long admired Kyl and appreciated the advice he offered when Flake started his political career. "The government needs people who are willing to serve a cause greater than their own self-interest, and that personified Jon," Flake said. "He was a true public servant." Arizona State University's Kyl Center for Water Policy takes its name from him. Its director, Sarah Porter, said Kyl was generous with his time and an effective member of the state's congressional delegation who took a practical approach to water policy. "He's always sort of cared about the public good and been able to think about, 'What will this mean for the generations to come?'" Porter said, adding that Kyl remained "quite a dynamo" until recent years, as his wife battled health problems. 'Giant' in the Senate kept Republican caucus together Ducey said Kyl was a "giant" in the Senate, further describing him as serious, engaging, forthright and thoughtful. His biggest impacts, Ducey said, came from the way he kept the Republican caucus together in opposition to Obamacare and his staunch support of Israel. Kyl also backed legislation to authorize construction of a fence stretching hundreds of miles along the U.S.-Mexico border. He later joined with Democrats to support a bill that would provide a path to citizenship and temporary guest-worker status for those in the U.S. without authorization. The proposal ultimately failed. As a lobbyist, Kyl helped guide the confirmation of Trump-picked U.S. Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh. When Kyl returned to the halls of Congress in 2018, he was known as Kavanaugh's chief Sherpa — an informal but widely known term for a nominee's guide to the political tundra in the Senate. In a statement disclosing his dementia diagnosis, Kyl harkened back to the words of Reagan, when the former president revealed his own Alzheimer's diagnosis and said he was starting a journey that would lead him to the end of his life. Kyl said he shared Reagan's confidence for Arizona and the nation's future, and that despite his diagnosis, he was a "very fortunate man." Miriam Levin-Gold likes Prime Minister Mark Carney's idea of Canadians being able to live and work in the European Union under proposed closer ties with the trade bloc.
"I think that's great for young people to explore different parts of the world and work in different places and have different experiences," the commuter told the BBC in Toronto.
Canadians woke up to news of Carney's speech to the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Thursday morning, welcoming the EU's ambition for Canada to become its first "associate member" as he urged closer co-operation on defence and energy.
"We should deepen our people-to-people ties, allowing our youth to live, work and study where they want on either side of the Atlantic," the PM said.
Carney told MEPs that Canada and Europe were "stronger together" in the face of "geopolitical rupture".
But before Canadians start packing their bags, "associate member" status does not currently exist within the EU and could take years to implement, given that all 27 EU member states would have to approve such an arrangement.
Nevertheless, people the BBC spoke to were excited about the potential prospect of working and studying in the EU as news of Carney's speech spread.
Alex Nash, from Montreal, said closer ties would clear away the obstacles of work visas and permits.
"It would certainly be really nice for that to be easier, more convenient and to be able to visit more easily," she said.
Canadian social media has lit up with the topic.
One person on a Facebook group, A Canadian Outlook, said they would love the opportunity for their grandchildren to study at European universities for better rates. Another woman said it would make it much easier for the home she already owns in France.
"Snow birds are going to love it," another person said, referring to Canadians who head to warmer locations for winter.
The sentiments hint at dissatisfaction in Canada over bilateral tensions with the US.
Growing up in Canada, David Jardine thought of the US as not just a neighbour, but an epicentre of culture and cool.
"I remember wanting to go and visit New York all the time," he told the BBC after finishing his overnight shift, not far from one of Toronto's most iconic buildings, the CN tower.
But he's become a lot more sceptical in the light of US President Donald Trump's trade war with Canada and rhetoric about annexation.
"I would say I think not only does it make more sense to associate closely with Europe, it's a place that I would rather be associating with given the way things are these days," he said.
Maggie Stainton, who manages local pub C'est What in Toronto's St Lawrence Market district, became emotional when she spoke about Canada's frayed ties with the US.
"It's too volatile with the United States," she said. "I feel that there's some stability in Europe."
For decades, America has been a cultural centre of gravity that is difficult to avoid, with many Canadian actors working in Hollywood and Canadian radio stations playing US music.
"I think we're forced to feel more American simply by the influences that we have," Stainton added.
"However, I think deep down, I definitely I lean towards feeling more European in my ideas and ideals."
These views were echoed by many other people the BBC spoke to in the centre of Canada's biggest city.
Carney, who used to lead Canada and Britain's central banks, was elected on a promise that he would not only take a tough stance against Trump, but broaden Canada's economic horizons.
Up to 72% of Canadian exports are to the US, and the ongoing trade tensions have spurred Ottawa to seek closer ties with other nations.
The EU, in many ways, would seem a natural fit. Over half of Canada's population reported having European origins, according to the last census, which was taken in 2021.
A recent Abacus Data survey conducted before Carney's speech found that 80% of Canadians say the country should deepen strategic cooperation with the EU, and over half feel closer to Europe than America.
However, details of Carney's proposed plans for greater ties with the EU are scarce.
A pair of opposition Conservative MPs have called on him to elaborate on what he and the bloc plan to work towards.
"It could be a concrete, meaningful proposal. Or it could be just words and vibes," said Adam Chambers, MP for Simcoe North in Ontario, during an interview with the BBC on the eve of Carney's speech on Thursday.
Chambers alluded to the existing Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (Ceta) between the EU and Canada, highlighting that it still awaits ratification by multiple EU nations.
And while deepening ties with Europe would be welcomed by many Canadians, there is still a sense that the country's relationship with the US - however strained - must not crumble.
"I grew up here. I've been here 40 years in Canada, in Ontario, and America's always been the neighbour," says Ahmed Khalil.
Building bridges with Europe makes sense, he said: "I think it brings in more money for Canada and more culture, brings Europeans over, probably solves a lot of problems."
But Canada shouldn't forget its southern neighbour, added Khalil.
"I think both are equally valuable to us," he said. "Both are equally valid."
With additional reporting by Madeline Halpert and James Fitzgerald

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—The Air Force Test Center is prepared to keep up with the Pentagon’s calls to buy, develop, test, and field technology quickly—but safety remains the top priority, the center’s commander said.
“We always want to proceed safely forward. The work that we do, as I've noted, is, can be dangerous. So we don't want to take risks that are unnecessary and unsafe. So that's always something that we're on the lookout for,” Brig. Gen. Mark Massaro, who leads the Air Force Test Center, told reporters during this week’s Air, Space & Cyber conference hosted by the Air and Space Forces Association.
Some context: Massaro’s comments come just three months after eight airmen died during a test flight of Boeing’s B-52 Stratofortress at Edwards Air Force Base in California. They also come nearly a year after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth pushed for sweeping acquisition reform, which includes “being open to buying the 85 percent solution” while achieving the more perfect solution over time. Separately, the Pentagon has slashed staff and reorganized its weapons testing organization, which raised oversight concerns, according to a Government Accountability Office report released earlier this year.
“There's a lot of capabilities out there today that might not be—from a technology perspective—exactly what it looks like in our minds at the end state. But it's at least the same, if not better, than what might be out there today,” Massaro said. “So there's a risk calculus there from an operational and acquisition risk when you do your cost schedule performance and then overlay that on the effectiveness and employability for the combatant and for the operational warfighter.”
The Air Force is currently testing system upgrades for the B-52, one of the service’s oldest aircraft, that could keep it operational through the 2050s.
The center works with program acquisition executives and operators to “understand where those balances are, and design our test programs to accommodate for more rapid” testing and integration, Massaro said.
“A clear example was our rapid integration of Falco, the [Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System], on the F-15E. Our people, processes, and test assets were postured to respond through integrated developmental and operational testing,” he said.
“The Falco was a little bit over a year ago…We had F-15E's. We had the rockets. We just had never connected them together in that way. So we had one technical risk to really get through, and [it] allowed us to go very quickly. So that's balancing the risk of the programmatic side when an operational warfighter needs it really quick, and understanding where you can make those trades. And with safety always as a backdrop.”
Welcome
You’ve reached the Defense Business Brief, where we dig into what the Pentagon buys, who they’re buying from, and why. Send along your tips, feedback, and song recommendations to lwilliams@defenseone.com. Check out the Defense Business Brief archive here, and tell your friends to subscribe!
Here come the MMAs. The Air Force wants Massed Modular Aircraft, or MMAs, to replace General Atomics’ storied MQ-9 Reaper drone, Troy Meink, the service’s secretary announced earlier this week. It’s a call that Swarm Aero has been waiting for—and building toward for the past four years. On Monday, the company unveiled its autonomous Gamera aircraft, a long-range strike aircraft that boasts seven connection points for payloads like missiles and sensors. The UAS is powered by the company’s Legion autonomy software.
- “We thought there would be a need that ultimately…to carry a very large payload like the LRASM that we see here, a long distance, and do so as cost effectively as possible,” Peter Kalogiannis, Swarm Aero’s CEO, told Defense One. “The $10 million listed in the solicitation, that really enables those volumes. And again, we've designed from the very beginning for those volumes, and quite frankly, for that price point, we're very very competitive against them.
- The company is building “several” prototypes in its Oxnard, California, facility and expects the first flight by the end of 2027.
- “This is something that makes the rest of the force—the bombers, the fighters, the B-21s, the F-47s—it makes them more lethal and more survivable. By being able to take some of the mission sets that they would otherwise potentially have to do, and freeing them up where they can be most effective,” Oliver Palmer, the company’s co-founder, told Defense One.
- And while it’s early, the company is looking forward to what the Air Force has in store and the innovation it could spark.
- “Frankly, we need competition in large aircraft production. There has historically been a monopoly structure of awarding programs that are intended to be around for 20-, 30-plus years,” Palmer said. “There have been a lot of really great reasons to do that, but increasingly we need competition because the cycle of technology competition with adversaries like China and others is changing so fast…and the model has to change. They started that with CCA. It sounds like they're gonna do that again with MMA. We absolutely welcome this.”

Steve Hilton, the Republican nominee for governor of California, is facing an acute version of the challenge familiar to GOP candidates nationwide: how to make the most of an endorsement from President Donald Trump as the presidentâs popularity wanes.
In an interview with Semafor, Hilton acknowledged the challenge he faces in a state Trump lost by 20 points two years ago.
âI think the starting point is that weâve got millions of moderate Democrats and independents in California. Thereâs no secret. They donât like the president, to put it mildly, but they are really desperate for change in California,â Hilton said.
In a recent campaign ad, he told voters, âMaybe you hate Trump. Maybe you hate Republicans. I donât care. Politicians screaming doesnât lower gas prices. Our utility bills are insane. Life here has become impossible for anyone who isnât already rich. We are going to fix that.â
At the same time, Hilton said Trumpâs support could help him with the Republican base. He needs all the help he can get: Hilton currently trails Democrat Xavier Becerra by a wide margin.
Know More
Hilton faces a similar balancing act on another defining California issue: artificial intelligence.
California is home to the leading frontier labs driving the AI boom, but a vast majority of state residents share the anti-data center sentiment sweeping the country.
On AI safety, Hilton struck a position closer to Trumpâs, describing what he called a âcompletely ludicrous hysteria going on right nowâ around AI, arguing that California should prioritize the technologyâs economic opportunities rather than rush into new rules.
âI think panic driven policymaking usually ends in disaster with a whole bunch of unintended consequences,â Hilton said. âI would favor the opportunity side of the argument rather than the doom side.â

The closure was based on an inspection of the roof terrace canopy and a partial ceiling collapse earlier this month, Floca said. The closure may be extended after evaluation next week, he added. Trump said the Kennedy Center could be 'ripped down' Trump, who was named the Kennedy Center's chairman last year by loyalists on the board, said Wednesday that his efforts to restore the aging building deserve recognition, "because frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close. It'll end up being ripped down. It's in very, very bad shape, very dangerous shape." WATCH: Kennedy Center board votes to close after judge blocks Trump's name from building The announcement of the closure came in response to a court case filed by a Democratic congresswoman who is a trustee and sought an emergency court hearing to prevent what she called the building's "unlawful closing." Rep. Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat and an ex-officio member of the Kennedy Center board, has led efforts to block Trump's name from being added to the building. Beatty had a verbal confrontation with the Republican president Tuesday during a virtual board meeting. Beatty's lawyers said in a court filing Thursday that the board members' "rationale that they are only temporarily closing the Kennedy Center is a plain pretext to justify shutting down the Center permanently. The facts before the Court are deeply concerning." Cooper denied a request by Beatty's legal team to hold a hearing to clarify the board's actions and intent. But he agreed to their request "to make crystal clear" that his order prohibits demolition of the building without 30 days' notice. The Trump-aligned board, chaired by the president, voted to close the center after Cooper blocked the institution from returning Trump's name to the building. Congress has allocated $257 million to cover the repairs, but Trump said they only would happen if the board was permitted to move forward with plans to add his name to the building. Barbra Streisand calls the dispute 'painful to witness' On Thursday, Barbra Streisand, a Kennedy Center honoree in 2008, questioned the closing of the center for repairs and called the controversy surrounding its operation "galling and painful to witness." Of Trump's attempts to add his name to the center, she said in a statement to The Associated Press: "You can easily imagine my indignation at seeing this revered institution become the subject of such a bitter struggle over one man's name and unchecked ego." The Kennedy Center board voted in August to inscribe Trump's name on the Kennedy Center's facade so it would read "The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated By President Donald J. Trump." If the Trump Kennedy Center Fund reached $100 million, another inscription would be added reading "Endowed by the Trump Kennedy Center Fund." The plaza in front of the Kennedy Center would also have been renamed in Trump's honor. All of those proposals were shot down Tuesday by Cooper, who ruled that nothing could happen "without Congress's blessing." Cooper ruled in May that the Kennedy Center illegally added Trump's name to the building, ordering it removed. The institution's leaders complied in June but left a tarp and scaffolding in place where Trump's name was once displayed. Streisand told AP she was deeply honored to be included in the 31st annual class of Kennedy Center Honorees, adding, "for me, and for so many artists, that honor represented something larger than a career recognition. It represented a belief in the importance of art to the life of a democracy." Associated Press writer Glenn Gamboa in Cleveland contributed to this report. The annual rowing regatta for schools in the Australian state of Queensland usually passes off without too much attention.
Each year more than 600 of the state's most promising teenage rowers battle it out on the crocodile-inhabited Fitzroy River, in the city of Rockhampton.
"We've never had any media wanting to attend here," Anthea O'Loughlin, head of Rowing Queensland, tells the BBC.
But this year is different. In six years' time, the 2032 Brisbane Olympics and Paralympics are set to stage rowing and canoe sprint events in this very stretch of water, which has just passed a technical assessment and been endorsed as safe and fair for athletes.
While sightings of saltwater crocodiles on the river â which number around 500 and can grow to four metres (13ft) long â are not uncommon, state government files going back more than 40 years record no attacks by the reptiles on humans.
And while influential figures at last month's World Rowing congress in Amsterdam made occasional references to "safety", the presence of the reptiles was not their chief concern.
"Fairness" is what's been raised with British Rowing's chief executive Tom Solesbury â a reference to the tidal river's natural bends and currents, which many in the rowing community say make it unsuitable for elite competition.
Drew Ginn, who has won three Olympic gold medals for Australia in rowing, told BBC Radio he had concerns over potential flooding and "fairness and integrity" at the venue.
"Personally, I'm not fearful of the Australian animals but I've never had a crocodile near me," he said.
"I'm sure I'd row faster, I'm sure all the athletes would row faster. That's on the list of concerns, I don't think it's the highest priority in concerns but it was certainly cited very early on."
The German rowing body's president Moritz Petri said athletes had also questioned the sustainability of holding the event some 600km (373 miles) from Brisbane.
But the "so-called impediments" got short shrift from the most senior politician in Queensland, state premier David Crisafulli, who reached for less diplomatic language.
"Let's be honest, let's scratch beneath the surface and call it for what it is," he said days after the Amsterdam meeting.
"It is a group of interstate and overseas elites who are trying to bully their way because they don't want to go to regional Queensland and that's not right."
Rowing chiefs contacted by the BBC before Thursday's decision declined to comment directly on Crisafulli's "elites" remarks.
But both Petri and Simon Wickham, chief executive of Rowing New Zealand, said their concerns had nothing to do with regional or urban preference but with competitors getting fair racing.
Petri added it was about what's best for their athletes who will train four years for the event, "dreaming night [after] night of becoming an Olympic champion".
Whether it was crocs or currents that tipped the balance, ultimately it was the sport's governing body World Rowing and the International Olympic Committee (IOC) that had the final say on the river's suitability.
On Thursday they approved it after a technical assessment by an engineering firm and the Games' infrastructure authority â which looked at the riverbed, competition course, river flows, water levels and likely weather conditions during the Games.
"Based on the extensive analysis undertaken, we now know that the Fitzroy River is capable of providing fair competition conditions during the period of the Games," World Rowing president Jean-Christophe Rolland said.
There was also now "confidence" in the river for canoe sprint athletes, said Thomas Konietzko, president of that sport's governing body, Paddle Worldwide.
The state premier was delighted. "The Fitzroy has passed with flying colours," an upbeat Crisafulli told parliament. "It's official. Signed, sealed and delivered."
In backing Rockhampton, the state government ignored a 2025 report it commissioned itself, which found the location unsuitable and concluded the best option would be to use a course built in Sydney for the 2000 Olympics.
The Fitzroy now needs to pass a final assessment of its design, value for money and long-term community legacy. As the decision rests with the state government, it's unlikely to fall at this hurdle.
But a wider debate will continue over whether Rockhampton is the right place to invest heavily in rowing facilities â and whether it can accommodate the 2032 influx of visitors.
The city is surrounded by cattle producers and normally experiences its peak number of guests every three years during Beef Week.
So what about the crocodiles?
They're not mentioned anywhere in the latest update from the IOC and World Rowing and they weren't considered in the technical assessment.
The safety management plan for this weekend's school regatta does however mention the word "crocodile" 28 times.
"The Fitzroy River is within recognised crocodile country," it says.
"Event planning must therefore assume that a crocodile sighting is possibleâ¦ No natural waterway in crocodile country can be guaranteed to be crocodile-free."
Procedures this weekend include suspending racing and competitors returning to the bank if a croc is spotted. The official signal for a sighting is the call of "crocodile, crocodile, crocodile".
Asked specifically about crocodiles, New Zealand's Wickham told the BBC the primary concern was ensuring the "fairest possible course" for rowers. "We would obviously expect any course chosen to be safe for rowers," he added.
The company owned by Australia's richest person Gina Rinehart, Hancock Prospecting, which supported Rockhampton's bid and has pumped millions into sports including rowing, pointed to "fake media" concerns about risks posed by flooding and crocodiles in the Fitzroy.
"The people of Rocky for many years have sent their own children to train in this river, and for competitions, without a single crocodile incident," a spokesperson said in a statement.

5b131327a8d6.text: By — Sibi Arasu, Associated Press Sibi Arasu, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/climate-change-made-deadly-nepal-glacier-and-rock-collapse-more-likely-analysis-finds Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Climate change made deadly Nepal glacier and rock collapse more likely, analysis finds Science Sep 17, 2026 3:29 PM EDT BENGALURU, India (AP) — Human-caused global warming thinned glaciers and thawed mountain permafrost, likely helping to destabilize the Himalayan slope that collapsed last month and unleashed catastrophic flooding across Nepal, according to a report released Thursday. WATCH: How melting glaciers contributed to the flooding disaster in the Himalayas The report by the World Weather Attribution cautioned that climate change was not the sole cause of the Aug. 26 disaster. A large 2015 Nepal earthquake may have weakened the rock years before the collapse, their analysis found. "This disaster was not an extreme weather event, but the fingerprints of climate change are still clear to see in long-term changes," said Ben Clarke, a climate researcher at Imperial College London who worked on the analysis, in a press statement. More than 1,300 people were killed and over 5,000 remain missing after a massive section of rock and overlying glacier collapsed near Nepal's border with China. The resulting torrent of water, ice, boulders and sediment swept through communities along the Trishuli River corridor and caused billions of dollars in damage. Climate scientists said that across the Himalayas rising temperatures are causing glaciers to retreat and thawing permanently frozen ground that helps bind fractured mountain rock together. That means climate change can alter not only weather hazards such as heat and heavy rain, but the stability of the mountains themselves — threatening communities concentrated in narrow river valleys below. The analysis did not determine whether the collapse would have happened without climate change, caused mainly by the release of greenhouse gases when fuels like oil, gas and coal are burned. However, researchers concluded that warming intensified several processes that made the slope less stable over decades. Global warming weakens high mountain slopes The report found that one of the clearest changes directly linked to climate change was the rising elevation of the freezing threshold. The report found that warming had pushed the altitude at which ground remains consistently frozen upward by roughly 100 meters (328 feet) per decade. This exposes rock at increasingly high elevations to longer periods above freezing, thawing permafrost and causing cracks within the ice, ultimately weakening the rock face under the ice. Jakob Steiner, a geoscientist at the University of Graz who has worked in the Himalayan region since 2006 but is not an author of Thursday's report, said monitoring instruments around 5,000 meters (16,404 feet) now show that some rock and ground no longer remain frozen throughout the year. "This means that the ground that was sitting below ice for hundreds and thousands of years is now becoming exposed," said Steiner. The report found that glacier retreat was another destabilizing force. Glaciers in the region have been losing mass for decades at a rate equivalent to more than half a meter (about 1.6 feet) of thinning each year, the report found. The Langtang Lirung glacier, located in the region where the disaster occurred last month, has retreated about half a kilometer (0.3 miles) since the 1990s, exposing rock once covered by ice. The Himalayan region contains the largest volume of snow and ice outside the polar regions. More than 63,000 glaciers in the area feed at least 10 major Asian river systems and support the food, water, energy and livelihood security of billions of people. However, various studies have found that around 78% of the glacier area, located between 4,500 and 6,000 meters (14,763 to 19,685 feet) above sea level, is highly exposed to warming. United Nations reports have found that between 2000 and 2019, glaciers lost 267 billion tons of ice per year, roughly equivalent to the mass of 46,500 Great Pyramids of Giza. As glaciers shrink, they can remove pressure that helped support adjoining rock walls, while producing additional meltwater. The weeks before the Aug. 26 collapse were also unusually warm. July and August 2026 were the warmest such months recorded locally, according to the analysis. "Other than the potential geological factors like earthquakes that are weakening the bedrock, all these other factors are made worse by human-induced climate change," said Friederike Otto, climate scientist at Imperial College London and one of the report's authors. Disaster exposes limits of adaptation The report said the catastrophe also demonstrates how some climate-related risks in the world's highest mountains may exceed the protection that early warning systems and other adaptation measures can provide. Nepal has developed disaster risk reduction plans and warning systems, but researchers said the size and speed of the collapse overwhelmed those defenses. Unlike a flood caused by rainfall, which can sometimes be forecast hours or days ahead, catastrophic slope failures in remote high mountains can occur suddenly and remain extremely difficult to predict. Otto, the climate scientist, said that the mountain ecosystem and societies are more vulnerable to climate impacts than those living in the plains. "Small changes in temperatures affect the stability of the land itself," she said. Better high-altitude monitoring, earth observation and warning systems could reduce some risks, the report said. But researchers warned there are limits to adaptation in Himalayan valleys where settlements, roads, hydropower projects and other infrastructure are concentrated along rivers. Is Canada about to join the EU?
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney addressed European Parliament on Thursday as discussions continue to swirl about Canada's relationship with the European Union.
Both sides seem to be seeking closer ties, and in his speech today, Carney said he welcomed the EU's "ambition" for Canada to become an "associate member".
The president of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament on Wednesday she wanted to work on "opening the door" for Canada, which would involve closer ties on various key sectors.
US President Donald Trump has threatened to take action against the EU if it makes Canada its first "associate member".
The BBC's Europe editor Katya Alder looks at the EU's future relationship with Canada and what it really means.

The News
The scaffolding thatâs built around an AI model is just as important â if not more important â for AI safety than the model itself, Nvidiaâs VP of agentic AI told Semafor.
âRather than creating fear and FUD, letâs just secure it. We know how. Weâve done these things before,â Adel El Hallak said, referencing the acronym for fear, uncertainty and doubt.
El Hallakâs argument provides insight into the more technical case â as opposed to the geopolitical or ideological ones â for why AI doomerism may be overblown.
Know More
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has emerged as the most prominent tech figure voicing skepticism about recent claims by leaders like Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei that AI labs should slow down model development because the tech is quickly advancing beyond companiesâ abilities to safeguard it. AI agents are central to that fear because they can take actions on their own, though regulation of agentic AI specifically is not discussed as much as is broad oversight of the models.
Huang this week rejected the notion that the industry has to choose between safety and speed, saying âyou could definitely have both at the same time.â
El Hallak said advances in AI models make âharness engineeringâ more critical â a harness is the layer of instructions and code that governs how an AI agent operates in practice.
âIf youâre training a capable agent, it is important that you donât put a lion in and expect to be able to control it in a horseâs pen.â
He couldnât comment on whether government regulation of the agentic layer is needed, but pointed to industry initiatives like the Open Secure AI Alliance as a venue for that kind of work, to figure out âat which part of the layer do we need to add more strengths and more guardrails and more safeguards.â
âThe worldâs not going to slow down.â
Room for Disagreement
Some in Washington argue tech companies canât be trusted to take up these issues on their own.
âThis is not an industry that can regulate itself,â Democratic Rep. Pete Aguilar said this week, arguing for the need for federal industry-wide rules on AI safety.

8f1400af0d07.text: The House's last in-session week before the midterms was beset by furious private finger-pointing between House Democrats following several high-profile rebellions . Why it matters: This dynamic may only worsen if Democrats retake the House, which is set to see an influx of distinctly rebellious and independent lawmakers , particularly on the left. There is even chatter among members contrasting the ability of House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) to control members with that of his top deputy, Minority Whip Katherine Clark (D-Mass.), according to two House Democrats. Said one of the lawmakers, speaking on the condition of anonymity to share details of sensitive private discussions: "People are talking about 'mom and dad'. … Dad is soft." "I think people are asking the question: If this is happening in the minority, are you prepared for what will happen in the majority?" said a third House Democrat. "There is no daylight between the three of us," Jeffries said at a Thursday press conference with Clark and Democratic Caucus chair Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.). "We'll address the situation when we address the situation," he added. A Democratic leadership aide told Axios that everything Jeffries' deputies do is in coordination with him and doesn't represent a break between leaders. Driving the news: Reps. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) and Jared Golden (D-Maine) on Tuesday provided Republican leadership with the necessary votes to advance a package of GOP bills, including a Russia sanctions bill strongly opposed by Democratic leaders. It was the second time this month the pair of centrists defected from leadership on a procedural vote — even after Clark and Jeffries publicly threatened them with punishment the first time. "People thought the first time was a mistake. The second time is defiance," said a fourth House Democrat, telling Axios the two "operate like they are above the caucus." Clark, along with Jeffries, engaged Gluesenkamp Perez in a heated discussion on the House floor during the vote in view of an Axios reporter, which sources said was about her defection. The rebellion came after Rep. Al Green (D-Texas) forced a vote on impeaching President Trump without support from leadership. The vote angered many House Democrats, who complained Green was muddying the party's message on a crucial week. Jeffries and Clark voted "present" along with 44 other Democrats. 147 sided with Green and 18 voted with Republicans to quash the impeachment effort. Leadership's neutrality on that vote drew frustration as well, with a fifth House Democrat telling Axios: "Our constituents don't send us here to be 'present.' They send us here to use our judgment." What they're saying: OurRevolution executive director Joseph Geevarghese said Jeffries "never seems to have this much trouble figuring out what to do when progressives are in his sights." "You cannot demand discipline from progressives while treating defections to the right as an unsolvable procedural dilemma," he told Axios. Rep. Analilia Mejia (D-N.J.) said progressives "catch shit" for being "too ideologic and bold on our ideas," and that it's "curious ... how there isn't an equally vocal attack" on centrists who break from the party line. Usamah Andrabi, a spokesperson for the left-wing Justice Democrats: "Leadership is threatening a Democratic majority in November by refusing to stand up to the corporate Democrats aiding and abetting Republicans' agenda." What we're hearing: Jeffries isn't the only target of rank-and-file backlash — Clark is getting heat from moderates for taking a swipe at Gluesenkamp Perez. The minority whip told reporters Wednesday that "it's team players who should sit on exclusive committees," which was widely interpreted as a reference to Gluesenkamp Perez's seat on the Appropriations Committee. Fumed a sixth House Democrat: "Katherine Clark just declared on moderate Democrats, which is a risky move for leadership going into a potentially tight majority." Jeffries' has been far more muted, repeatedly saying he will "have more to say about the situation when I have more to say about the situation." Much of the fury is also directed at Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez, with some of it is coming from their fellow centrists. "Everyone in the caucus is sick of the bullshit. Everyone has their ... number," a seventh House Democrat, a moderate, told Axios. "Marie is playing with fire," a senior House Democrat told Axios, adding that Jeffries "may not do anything now, but her committee appointment may be in jeopardy for next session." The other side: Gluesenkamp Perez said in a statement to Axios, "I don't worry about that kind of stuff. I will always vote my District and let others play inside DC politics games." Said Golden: "I'm a Mainer and an American. I'm also a proud Democrat, but that team is a distant third." The bottom line: "Members have concerns about those who are not team players," a ninth House Democrat told Axios, and "next year is the best time to address it." Golden, who is retiring, has a warning for his colleagues: "Be careful what you wish for. Next time, it could be you facing punishment for putting your constituency or our country ahead of the party."
