The US government has granted visas to Iranian officials so they can travel to the UN General Assembly in New York next week, as the war between the two countries grinds into its seventh month.
The BBC understands the core delegation permitted to attend includes Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.
A spokesman for the US State Department confirmed the decision on Thursday, saying that the delegation will be placed under travel restrictions and will be banned from purchasing certain American products.
The move comes as the war shows no sign of ending. Since it began in February, it has driven up global energy prices, and expanded into neighbouring countries.
"Consistent with our host country obligations, the core delegation from the Iranian regime will be able to attend UN General Assembly High Level Week," a spokesman for the US State Department told the BBC.
"The delegation will be under travel restrictions and will face prohibitions on the purchase of luxury and other goods per our policy. The delegation is smaller than last year."
Last year, diplomats attending from Iran were banned from shopping at wholesale stores like Costco. They also were required to seek permission from the US before purchasing luxury goods, including jewellery, alcohol and cars.
The 81st session of the UN General Assembly (UNGA) is currently underway. The General Debate - the centrepiece of the annual event - is due to begin on Tuesday.
Tuesday will include speeches from US President Donald Trump, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, and France President Emmanuel Macron.
Wednesday is expected to see speeches from the leaders of Ukraine, Syria and Iran.
Public and political pressure has mounted on the White House to find an end to the conflict with Iran, which began on 28 February when the US and Israel launched joint attacks on the country.
Since the war began, Iran has repeatedly attacked US bases and allied states in the Gulf, as well as Israel.
The BBC recently learned that the US denied a visa to Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas and the Palestinian delegation to attend UNGA.
The White House, which does not recognise the legitimacy of the Palestinian delegation, denied them visas for a second year in a row.

A pro-AI meme campaign is rolling out on government social media accounts, casting âeffective altruistâ as a slur as the White House doubles down on its regulatory light touch.
Amid an international reckoning over the capabilities and dangers of high-level AI, the Trump administration is casting effective altruists â who focus on reducing harm from the tech and heavily weigh advancement versus risk â as the enemy.
Images of a fist-pumping Trump and âAmericanism, Not Effective Altruism!â are appearing on X posts from the Pentagon. The Federal Communications Commission posted a Western-esque graphic with the text âChoose the Frontier â Never Doom.â An account run by the Centre for Effective Altruism replied to one post, âThanks for the mention.â
One person working in AI policy who has been associated with effective altruism told Semafor: âThis is the best publicity EA has gotten in years.â
Know More
Not all AI safety experts and advocates identify as effective altruists, and different groups working on the topic have disparate goals, funding, and membership. Average people who have concerns about the direction of AI development are not likely to even know what effective altruism is.
Using the term as an insult may not prove an effective long-term message for the government, especially since Trump is increasingly alone in his stance that AI companies can figure out how to regulate themselves.
âIt would be a mistake to pigeonhole the emerging pro-human movement,â said Michael Kleinman, head of US policy for the Future of Life Institute (which, he said, is not an effective altruist organization).
His organization helped put on this weekâs Pro-Human Summit featuring both Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and former Trump adviser Steve Bannon: âItâs become crystal-clear that the coalition of people who care about the risks of AI is extraordinarily broad.â

f49f1c541d3f.text: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Thursday returned to the the anti-vaccine group he founded, using a keynote address to signal the Trump administration isn't done questioning the safety of routine shots and expanding carveouts to federal mandates. Why it matters: Though Kennedy avoided some of his most politically incendiary rhetoric, the speech made clear that the Department of Health and Human Services is working hard behind the scenes to continue reshaping federal vaccine policy. He again questioned the safety of routine childhood vaccines and asserted they play a role in the development of chronic illnesses — questions that ignore decades of science supporting the vaccines' safety. Driving the news: Kennedy spoke for more than an hour Thursday afternoon at a Children's Health Defense meeting in Washington, D.C., highlighting the Trump administration's work on healthy food before turning to vaccines. He listed what the federal government is doing to reverse, in vaccine critics' eyes, decades of negligence on the issue. And Kennedy assured the audience that President Trump is fully committed to the cause. "He's directed us to pursue answers to strengthen vaccine safety, to expand options for families who want them and to preserve individual choice without federal mandates," Kennedy said. "Let me be clear: You have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House." Between the lines: Kennedy addressed those frustrated with the administration's pace, in a nod to Make America Healthy Again movement members who feel he hasn't done enough to crack down on vaccines. "In government, a bunch of things have to happen before something else happens, or you get sued, and it's a very laborious system, and there's a lot of inertia built in," he said. "If we were able to overcome it, we would have changed things on day one, but those would have been short lived and I would have been out of a job." He certainly didn't sound like someone who's ready to leave office after the midterm elections, as has been rumored. The backing he appears to have from Trump himself reinforces that. "I didn't come to Washington to protect institutions from uncomfortable questions," he said. "I came to make those institutions answer those questions, and I intend to stay in this fight as long as I am able." Reality check: The vast majority of health experts and scientists say that the question of vaccine safety is settled, pointing to reams of evidence accumulated over many years. "It's a complete fabrication, because there's been so much data on vaccine safety," said Amesh Adalja, senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security and spokesperson for the Infectious Diseases Society of America. "But the overarching point is no matter how much evidence there is or that accumulates, it will not change RFK Jr.'s mind related to vaccines." The big picture: A pre-midterm pause on Kennedy's vaccine rhetoric ended weeks ago, when he stood with the president as Trump signed an executive order calling for fewer childhood vaccinations, splitting the childhood MMR vaccine into three shots and delivering vaccines at separate medical visits. Kennedy's speech mentioned numerous ongoing efforts within HHS to study vaccine safety, "including cumulative effects, longer-term health outcomes, uses of adjuvants, the safety of adjuvants, and many, many other issues." Researchers are also also "examining questions involving adjuvants, timing, vaccination during pregnancy, maternal immunity, timing and a range of health outcomes, from allergies to autoimmune diseases to autism and other neurodevelopmental disorders," he added. The bottom line: Expect, at a minimum, results of Kennedy-requested vaccine safety studies to come out of HHS in the second half of Trump's term. Experts aren't expecting those studies to meet high scientific standards. "Anything RFK Jr. touches, I'm not confident of it's veracity," Adalja said. "I have zero confidence in anything that comes from his department."

US President Donald Trump will reportedly greet Chinaâs leader Xi Jinping as he steps off the plane in Washington, DC next week â the first leader accorded that deference in Trumpâs second term â as preparations ramp up for their summit.
The countriesâ top diplomats spoke Thursday, possibly to finalize an agenda that will center on trade issues, AI governance, and defense ties. Though Washington signaled openness to discussing âshared risksâ on AI, experts have rejected the possibility of major breakthroughs.
Other discussions may involve strengthening military-to-military ties, as well as resuming arms-control talks halted in 2024 over US weapons sales to Taiwan. Asian allies are concerned that Trump could soften US support for Taiwan in exchange for economic concessions.

84f4338235fe.text: President Trump is making plans for a first-ever meeting with Venezuela's interim president, Delcy Rodriguez, as early as next week, sources familiar with the discussions tell Axios. Why it matters: The potential meeting showcases the close relations between the nations under Trump. But it's also fraught with political risks that extend from Miami to Caracas. Driving the news: Trump is already planning to meet with Gulf leaders at the UN General Assembly in New York next week to discuss the Iran War, and those who know his thinking say he wants to make time for a sidelines sit-down with Rodriguez as early as Tuesday, sources said. "Iran is tough, but Venezuela is without a doubt the president's top success and Delcy is a key to that," a Trump adviser said. "Unless something goes really wrong, the president wants to make time." A senior administration official cautioned: "Nothing is finalized. This is up to the president." On Sunday, when asked about meeting Rodriguez, Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One that "I may be, I may be." Zoom in: The New York City meeting could happen just blocks from the federal lockup where Rodriguez's predecessor and onetime ally, socialist Nicolas Maduro, awaits trial on narco-terrorism charges. Maduro was seized Jan. 3 in Caracas in a U.S. military operation authorized by Trump. Rodriguez assumed power after the coup and has worked closely with Trump and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio to normalize relations between the countries, including the inking of a massive but controversial Venezuelan oil deal first reported by Axios. Friction point: Clustered in South Florida, conservative and vocal Venezuelan exile community has expressed increasing agitation with the administration for working so closely with Rodriguez, a lifelong socialist who rose to power along with Maduro under strongman Hugo Chavez, both foes of the U.S. this century. Adding to the anger in the diaspora: neither Trump nor Rubio has called for elections in Venezuela, despite years of bashing Maduro as an election-stealing dictator. Supporters of Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Corina Machado also grew frustrated with administration officials over their criticism of the exiled Venezuelan political leader when she tried to return home after the earthquakes in June. The big picture: In Florrida, politicians, pollsters and consultants say higher gas prices due to the Iran war and the administration's heavy-handed immigration enforcement are bigger political problems for Republicans in the midterm elections than promoting democracy now in Venezuela. Polls in Venezuela show Rodriguez and Trump have low favorability ratings and Machado has the highest, although it's declining . Some in Trump's orbit have expressed concern that the optics of a meeting with Trump will hurt Rodriguez even more at home because she could look like too much of a U.S. puppet. But Trump isn't concerned about that, the administration official said, noting "The fact is POTUS loves Delcy because she's delivering and she's leading."

35cc1b5f4f55.text: By — Fatma Khaled, Associated Press Fatma Khaled, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/tens-of-thousands-flee-as-iran-backed-houthis-draw-yemen-into-wider-war Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Tens of thousands flee as Iran-backed Houthis draw Yemen into wider war World Sep 17, 2026 5:39 PM EDT CAIRO (AP) — As Houthi rebels closed in, Eshraq Abdel Gelil and her husband fled their home, walking through the mountains before catching a ride to a nearby city. Four months pregnant, she feared another miscarriage. They are among an estimated 125,000 people who have fled as the Iran-backed rebels have advanced down the Red Sea coast to a key maritime chokepoint. The offensive, linked to the wider Iran war, has threatened Saudi oil exports, pushed up global fuel prices and rattled markets. READ MORE: Fighting in Yemen intensifies, and Houthis launch more attacks on Saudi Arabia The cost has been far greater for Yemenis caught in the crossfire. Many have fled their homes with only what they could carry. The Arab world's poorest country was pushed to the brink of famine in an earlier phase of the civil war, which killed an estimated 150,000 people. A Saudi-led blockade, along with the Houthis' repressive rule and detention of U.N. and aid workers, has made life miserable in the now-expanding territory under rebel control. Yemen's Saudi-backed government, weak and fragmented, has struggled to push them back. Yemenis describe a harrowing flight from the front lines Abdel Gelil is now sheltering with family in the southwestern city of Taiz, while others are sleeping in the streets or erecting makeshift tents out of plastic. Her husband, Mohamed Thabet, said the latest fighting was "extremely fierce" and more intense than a battle in 2017 that had also forced him to flee. "There was shelling and shrapnel near the house," he said. They walked for 5 kilometers (3 miles) before taking a vehicle for around 60 kilometers (37 miles) on mountain roads. When they arrived in Taiz, a doctor told them that the baby had moved lower in the womb. Abdel Gelil miscarried at the same point in a previous pregnancy. "My wife cried from the shock and was very fearful," Thabet said. Now they are packed into a home with extended family. They can only afford to eat twice a day, and they worry that Abdel Gelil is not getting enough nutrients for her and the baby. Thabet also worries about his sister, who hasn't been able to afford her diabetes medication for over a month. She and her two daughters, 8 and 13, have a blood condition that makes them susceptible to anemia, he said. The renewed fighting is linked to the unresolved Iran war The civil war dates back to 2014, when the Houthis seized much of northern Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa. Saudi Arabia intervened the following year in support of Yemen's internationally recognized government. A 2022 ceasefire largely halted the fighting. Hostilities erupted again in July, when the Houthis renewed attacks on Saudi Arabia in what the rebels said was an attempt to lift the blockade. The attacks on Saudi Arabia's oil industry came as the U.S. was having some success in reopening the Strait of Hormuz. The fighting in Yemen has killed eight civilians and wounded another 32, according to the U.N. humanitarian office, which says at least 125,000 people have fled their homes. The U.N. children's agency, known as UNICEF, says the displaced include more than 57,000 children. "This is one of the most fast-moving and volatile displacement waves Yemen has seen in years," said Obia Achieng, a UNICEF representative in Yemen. "Families are fleeing with little or no warning, often at night, carrying only what they can grab." "The situation is particularly concerning because it comes on top of an already severe humanitarian crisis," Achieng added. There are limited resources for those fleeing Before the latest fighting, the U.N. had warned that around 5 million Yemenis were experiencing "crisis or worse levels of acute food insecurity." Milena Murr, of Prosper Global, a humanitarian group previously known as Mercy Corps, said some people arriving in Taiz had walked for over 16 hours, arriving at displacement camps exhausted, dehydrated and with some of the children appearing malnourished. Iman Abdullahi, country director for CARE, another aid group, said there's an urgent need for food, maternal and newborn healthcare, hygiene supplies, private latrines and mental health support. "One woman had to wash her only clothes and remain inside her tent until they dried because she had nothing else to wear. Another was forced to flee just two weeks after giving birth," he said. Nashwan Ahmed Said was stitching together a tent from plastic wheat sacks. He said this is the third time he's been displaced since the start of the war. "We are in such a state! We have no home, no toilet, no food and nothing to drink," he said. Arwa Ahmed, who was displaced with her five children, said she and her family ate nothing but rice for days. "We need everything. We need tents, we need food and all the essentials, because we were displaced and took nothing with us," she said. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. A spotted cat from the forests of Bolivia has been confirmed as a new species.
The small feline, about the size of a domestic moggy, went under the radar because it was confused with other wild cats that share similar spots and stripes.
But DNA studies show the cat is actually in a class of its own, highlighting how much remains unknown about some of the world's most elusive mammals.
Scientists hope the discovery will draw attention to the conservation of tiger cats, a group of small wild cats found in South and Central America that receives far less public attention than their larger cousins like lions, leopards and tigers.
Tiger cats are small, spotted wild cats found across Central and South America, from Costa Rica to Bolivia and Argentina.
They look remarkably similar and even experts can struggle to tell them apart.
"It's an amazing result that we have a new species for the world, which is the Leopardus tilcayo," said Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz of Universidad Mayor de San Andres in La Paz, Bolivia.
"It's amazing that there are still new species waiting to be discovered: we don't have to go to a volcano, an island, or deep into the sea."
Only one confirmed member of the species is known - a cat living in a rescue sanctuary in Bolivia - but scientists believe others exist.
It was this 10-year-old cat, nicknamed 'Tigrino', that set scientists on the path to discovery.
Bolivian scientist Dr Nogales-Ascarrunz was volunteering at the sanctuary when she noticed the cat looked unusual.
It had been found in the forest by a local resident, who initially thought it was a domestic kitten. As it grew older, however, it became clear that it did not behave like a house cat.
Dr Nogales-Ascarrunz had heard of other sightings of small wild cats in the dense forests of the country's Yungas region, but these had not been investigated by scientists.
To solve the mystery, she joined forces with other researchers from around the world to investigate the family history of tiger cats, using DNA from living animals and museum specimens.
"There's so few records or pictures, no individual in a museum, so it was hiding because nobody was looking," said Eduardo Eizirik, a conservation geneticist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil.
The study, published in Current Biology, external, uncovered further surprises, suggesting there are five rather than three tiger cat species, including the newly described Tilcaya cat (Leopardus tilcayo) of Bolivia.
However, identifying the species is only the first step.
Co-researcher Dr Caroline Sartor, of the Wildlife Conservation Research Unit at the University of Oxford, said the discovery was important for conservation because it is impossible to protect a species if we don't know what it is or where it lives.
"These are animals similar in size to a domestic cat, so you might think we would know them all by now, but this discovery shows how much biodiversity is still to be uncovered in some of the less-studied regions of the world," she said.
Tiger cat species are considered vulnerable to extinction because of deforestation, habitat loss and illegal hunting, although the new species is missing from previous assessments.
The discovery could also have wider implications for the world's cat family.
Both wild and domestic cats belong to the biological family Felidae, which includes every living cat species from tiny house pets to massive tigers.
There are officially 41 species recognised but the new discovery, and the finding that there may be several species of tiger cat, brings the number to 44 or more.
Andrew Kitchener, an expert in mammals at National Museums, Scotland, who was not involved with the research, says the small spotted South American cats known as tiger cats have been a "taxonomic nightmare".
"These cats are confusing because they look so similar and there are few specimens in museums, so even now we are still learning how to tell them apart as genetics reveal more species," he said.

ac683bced537.text: By — Tim Sullivan, Associated Press Tim Sullivan, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/man-who-sprayed-rep-ilhan-omar-with-vinegar-sentenced-to-14-months-in-prison Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Man who sprayed Rep. Ilhan Omar with vinegar sentenced to 14 months in prison Politics Sep 17, 2026 7:07 PM EDT MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — The man who sprayed vinegar at Democratic U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar during a Minneapolis town hall was sentenced Thursday to 14 months in prison after reaching a deal with prosecutors. READ MORE: Man who sprayed vinegar at Rep. Ilhan Omar during town hall pleads guilty to assault The sentencing of 56-year-old Anthony Kazmierczak came nearly eight months after the Jan. 27 assault. At the time, Minneapolis-St. Paul was facing an immigration crackdown that led to angry protests, arrests and the killing of two U.S. citizens by federal officers. Kazmierczak was also sentenced to three years of supervised release, which includes no contact with Omar. U.S. marshals escorted him from the courtroom after he was sentenced. "This wasn't a spur of the moment act," U.S. District Judge Joan N. Ericksen said before handing down the sentence, noting that Kazmierczak had secured tickets for the town hall weeks in advance. "An attack on a public figure is not a political statement. It is misguided, selfish, and inconsistent with any concept of a free or democratic society," Ericksen said. Spraying anything at an elected official "is a terrifying thing, and you knew that when you did it." Omar's attacker apologizes for what he did Kazmierczak, who has been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease, shook visibly at times as he sat at the defense table. He spoke quietly and haltingly, occasionally wiping away tears as he stood before Ericksen. He spoke about being a good neighbor, and how his troubles with insurance companies as well as prison had exacerbated his ailments. His attorney, John Fossum, argued that Kazmierczak had not been taking his mental health medications before the attack, lowering his inhibitions and contributing to what happened. "I've spent enough time in jail thinking," Kazmierczak said, his voice barely audible. "I really apologize to her for having put her through that," he said, referring to Omar. In an earlier hearing, Kazmierczak was unable to explain his actions, saying only "it's fuzzy" when Ericksen asked what he remembered. "I'm sorry if I scared you," he wrote to Omar after the attack. Prosecutors cite evidence of advance planning During the town hall, witnesses saw Kazmierczak jump up from the audience, spraying liquid from a syringe at Omar and saying she was "splitting Minnesota apart." Omar's security officers tackled Kazmierczak and turned him over to police, who arrested him. Omar was not injured and continued with the town hall after the arrest. Authorities later determined he had sprayed her with a mixture of water and apple cider vinegar. He pleaded guilty to assaulting a U.S. officer. The government sentencing memorandum, submitted to the court by prosecutors, said he had texted at least three people indicating he planned to do something at the meeting involving Omar "but would not answer their questions about his intent." He also sent messages to a neighbor to arrange for dog care and asking for bail bond company contact information. The sentencing memo said Kazmierczak had long struggled with alcohol abuse, had "a history of mental and emotional health concerns" and a string of health issues tied to his 2022 Parkinson's disease diagnosis. Omar, a refugee from Somalia, has long been a target of President Donald Trump's anti-immigrant rhetoric. In 2019, after Omar's election to Congress, Trump said she should "go back" to her country of birth. He has described her as "garbage" and said she should be investigated. In social media posts, Kazmierczak had criticized former President Joe Biden and referred to Democrats as "angry and liars." He wrote that Trump wants the U.S. to be "stronger and more prosperous." His attack came as the Minneapolis area was on edge due to the crackdown, with protesters often facing off against convoys of immigration officers and conservatives criticizing protesters. It follows repeated warnings about how rapid advances in AI threaten to outpace the ability to develop the tech safely. One of those warnings came from Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at Anthropic and OpenAI. Coxon joined Geoff Bennett to discuss his concerns. Amna Nawaz: As leaders of the world's largest AI companies are publicly calling for a collective slowdown of the technology's development, late yesterday, OpenAI announced it had discovered six new instances of unexpected or concerning behavior by its artificial intelligence models, including moving files onto the Internet without permission and making up data. Geoff Bennett: OpenAI has now pledged to publicly disclose when its models act without authorization. But the most recent revelations follow repeated warnings about how rapid advances in AI threaten to outpace the ability to develop the tech safely. One of those warnings came from Jacob Coxon, who spent the last three years conducting research at Anthropic and OpenAI before he publicly resigned last week. In a now viral post, Coxon said the companies are -- quote -- "gambling with our lives. Do not underestimate the power of this technology. These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources. "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. No other human activity poses this level of danger." And Jacob Coxon joins us now from San Francisco. Welcome to the "News Hour." Jacob Coxon, Former Anthropic Researcher: Thanks for having me on. Geoff Bennett: We were supposed to speak a few days ago. Circumstances got in the way. I will say, though, I'm glad we're speaking today because so much has transpired since you resigned last week, to include these new disclosures from OpenAI about its own systems behaving in unexpected and potentially troubling ways. When you saw this news, what did you think? Jacob Coxon: So I think this news is entirely to be expected. And, indeed, if you're working on this tech at these companies, then you know that we don't currently have the ability to perfectly control these systems. And currently the systems with the highest level of intelligence will repeatedly behave in ways that we don't fully understand. It is great that they shared these instances and committed to future sharing. But I don't think the instances themselves are that surprising. Geoff Bennett: And, Jacob, why do these AI agents seem to gravitate toward nefarious behavior? Is it something about the way that they're trained, or is the answer even knowable? Jacob Coxon: So it really -- I don't -- I wouldn't phrase it as gravitating towards nefarious behavior. These AIs do many, many things over the course of a day. There's a lot of AI systems doing lots of things. The issue is, we can't perfectly control what drives motivate their behavior and the sorts of things they decide to do, which means, occasionally, these nefarious activities will kind of slip through the cracks. And a sufficiently dangerous bit of nefarious activity could have massive consequences, even if it's just a one-time kind of slip-up, because we can't perfectly control why they do the things they do. Geoff Bennett: So a system doing something that its developers didn't intend isn't necessarily the same as a system trying to escape human control. What evidence do you have, what have you seen that would suggest that these systems are moving toward the more dangerous scenario that you have warned about? Jacob Coxon: So, the big attack that everyone is speaking about and has been speaking about for a while is this Hugging Face attack. And, in this attack, the AIs were behaving in various ways that implied they were thinking about the procedure that was being used to evaluate them. So they were thinking about their situation, the world they found themselves in, the things they were having to try and do. And they were attempting to do things like edit their own memories to make it harder for people to figure out what they'd done. They were attempting to break out of the container they were in. They were attempting to access things on the Internet because they thought it might help them with their tasks. In short, these AIs were trying to do many different things to help them in the situation they found themselves. Geoff Bennett: So when you warn that the next year or two could be crunch time for humanity -- that was the phrase that you used -- walk us through that chain. What specifically has to happen for that to be true? Jacob Coxon: So the main thing that has to happen is for us to enter this phase called recursive self-improvement. So, RSI, or recursive self-improvement, is the idea that we could take the discipline of AI research as currently practiced and automate it with the AIs we're building. So we could let the AIs make themselves smarter. And we have already made strides towards doing that. So, right now, a lot of the research that researchers at these labs do is via AIs that carry out certain tasks or experiments. Currently, we still need the human to provide taste or judgment, but plausibly within a year, certainly, within two years, we're on track to also automating away this nebulous human quality of judgment so that the AIs can rapidly make themselves smarter. And, at that point, things could go very, very fast. Geoff Bennett: So, what would a slowdown actually look like? What kind of intervention are you calling for? ff657c86d6ae.text: By — Adithi Ramakrishnan, Associated Press Adithi Ramakrishnan, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/t-rex-had-a-body-temperature-similar-to-our-own-study-finds Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter T. rex had a body temperature similar to our own, study finds Science Sep 17, 2026 6:50 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — Using fossilized teeth, scientists have finally taken the T. rex's temperature — and it wasn't too different from our own. Researchers once thought that dinosaurs were sluggish, cold-blooded creatures. Later findings challenged that, suggesting that older dinosaurs were warm-blooded and could control their body temperature. READ MORE: Before T. rex became humongous, it learned to hear footsteps Most scientists agree that Tyrannosaurus rex was warm-blooded, but pinning down the exact core temperature of an extinct creature is difficult. "We can't just use a thermometer to do that," said Jasmina Wiemann, a paleobiologist at Johns Hopkins University who had no role in the latest work. Scientists tried other methods like studying how T. rex grew or searching for clues in its bones, but a firm number eluded them. In a new study, researchers hunted for chemical clues in the fearsome predator's teeth. It turns out that atoms within the enamel clump together in different patterns based on an animal's body temperature. "We figured out how warm the most famous animal of all, a T. rex, was," said co-author Aradhna Tripati, a geochemist at the University of California, Los Angeles. Readings from three teeth revealed an average body temperature of about 97 degrees Fahrenheit (36 degrees Celsius). That's similar to modern elephants and not too far from the average body temperature of humans, which ranges from 97 to 99 degrees Fahrenheit (36 to 37 degrees Celsius). The findings were published Wednesday in the journal Science Advances. "I almost would have expected a higher body temperature," Wiemann said. Based on her prior work, she thought the predator could have run a few degrees hotter — similar to modern birds, dinosaurs' warm-blooded descendants. Knowing how hot or cold the T. rex was can help scientists piece together how the dinosaur might have lived. At 97 degrees (36 degrees Celsius), T. rex could have lived across most of prehistoric North America, Tripati said, maintaining a stable internal thermometer across both cooler and hotter regions. The findings could also shed light on the kinds of prey the dinosaur had to hunt in order to keep its energy up. Scientists say it'll be important to test these methods on other dinosaurs to see how warm or cold they ran. It's possible T. rex's temperature could have been one of the keys to its dominance as one of the dinosaur age's top predators. "There's lots of interesting, charismatic species that could be explored using this," said study co-author Robert Eagle, a geobiologist at UCLA. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Major Asian economies are profiting from growing global demand for AI as their manufacturing sectors build the high-end equipment needed for a worldwide data center boom, economists said.
Surging exports are set to drive GDP growth in Malaysia, South Korea, Taiwan, and Vietnam, while Seoulâs and Taipeiâs burgeoning tax receipts â thanks to fast-rising corporate profits â are driving government spending, Goldman Sachs economists noted. Japan, too, is benefitting further up the supply chain by making semiconductor manufacturing equipment for many of these Asian economies, Barclays said.
Not everyone is doing as well, however: Populist policies in Indonesia, AIâs threat to outsourcing jobs in the Philippines, and demographic decline in Thailand have left those Southeast Asian nations particularly vulnerable.

Congress also took action this week on data centers, college sports and the Iran war. Capitol Hill correspondent Lisa Desjardins reports. Amna Nawaz: A bill to impose sweeping new sanctions on Russia and on countries using Russian energy is now on its way to President Trump after the U.S. House of Representatives overwhelmingly passed it last night, this as Congress also took action this week on data centers, college sports, and the Iran war, but also as House Republicans chose to go home early. Covering it all for us is our Capitol Hill correspondent, Lisa Desjardins. So, Lisa, let's start with this Russian sanctions bill. What's the significance of that? Lisa Desjardins: This is easily the most significant step to take on Russia since President Trump returned to office, and some say well beyond that. The bill is named after a key sponsor, the late Senator Lindsey Graham. It would put sanctions on Putin himself, the first time Congress would be doing that, as well as other Russian officials and banks. But it also allows up to 100 percent tariffs on other countries that buy Russian oil and in some cases natural gas. And, now, this is very powerful. It includes China, but also some non-adversaries, potentially like India and the European Union. Here's how Republican Mike McCaul put it: Rep. Michael McCaul (R-TX): This bill will cripple Russia's war machine and finally bring Putin to the negotiating table. It will ensure America's adversaries, not only Russia, but also China and Iran, suffer for their coordinated campaign of aggression. Lisa Desjardins: Now, this bill does give a lot of power to President Trump, and some Democrats voted against it because they think he may use it more widely than it's intended. However, for Ukraine, it is a major victory, and we expect the president to sign it tomorrow. Amna Nawaz: All right, some other big votes this week, tell us about those and also how Republicans are doing on that to-do list you have been keeping track of. Lisa Desjardins: All right, let's start with a big part of American life, college sports. There is a bill to deal with the Wild West of college sports called athletes' pay that has advanced in the U.S. Senate, and it is set for passage this week. Here's what is in this bill. It would regulate college athlete pay, and it would limit them to just one transfer each without a penalty during their college career. It also would limit coaches, who would not able to move in the middle of a season. The college sports bill is waiting on the house to pass it next. But the House, meanwhile, has passed a bill on data centers. This bill would make data centers have to pay for the full costs of their energy. That is a rising concern in American life. Now, it's interesting about that bill. It passed overwhelmingly in the House of Representatives, and that shows just how hot this issue is for voters. But its fate in the Senate is not yet clear. We will be watching in the next week to see what happens. As to that to-do list we have been following, let's take a look to see where Republican leaders are. Here are the seven bills we have been following that the Republicans wanted to get through. You see those first two have passed, funding government. We didn't have that kind of deadline this time. Russian sanctions, that made it through. But then you see in yellow two that are still in progress, that data center bill and the college sports. But you see four of the items on this list are not yet accomplished. That includes funding the war in Iran, the crypto bill, which has hit a rough patch in the Senate, and the farm bill, as well as the SAVE Act that Republicans wanted to get through. Amna Nawaz: You pointed out there Congress has not funded the Iran war, but there was a big vote on Iran in the House this week. Tell us about that. Lisa Desjardins: Right. It was a busy week. The House voted to end the war in Iran. This is the third time that the House majority, a majority in the House has voted that way. But it's notable because of the margin, and also because these seven Republicans, the most yet, voted to bring back troops and end the war in Iran. You will note, of these seven, four of them, you see them highlighted there with yellow, are in competitive House races from Michigan to Iowa to Pennsylvania. Now, these are -- this is a symbolic vote because President Trump can veto. But it shows really the direction and the momentum in Congress is against the Iran war. More are speaking out. And we expect the Senate to take a similar vote next week. Amna Nawaz: Related to the Iran war, I know you have been following a House Republican who filed articles of impeachment against the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth. Lisa Desjardins: Yes. Amna Nawaz: Is that going to get a vote? Lisa Desjardins: It will. It will not until after the election, though, because the House left before that vote was going to ripen. These are impeachment articles introduced surprisingly by Thomas Massie. He did not tell Republican leaders he was going to do this. He is a Republican from Kentucky. He lost his primary. But he felt strongly that he needed to put eight charges against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. Some of those deal with the war in Iran, which he says needs congressional approval, but others include that he accuses the secretary of ignoring the protocols for civilian deaths, killing civilians, including at sea with those strikes that we have seen in the Gulf. Amna Nawaz: So the House has now left. The Senate's here for one more week. Overall, where do things stand with Congress getting things done before the elections? Lisa Desjardins: Well, you will hear a lot of different versions from Republicans, but they have gotten some things done. Avoiding a government shutdown and that fiscal

802f05488795.text: September 17 is Constitution Day, a commemoration of the founding document signed on that date in 1787. But for immigrants seeking U.S. citizenship, the path to naturalization has grown more difficult as the Trump administration has added new requirements and tightened vetting standards.Justice correspondent Ali Rogin reports. Geoff Bennett: Well, today is Citizenship Day, which recognizes everyone who has attained U.S. citizenship and commemorates the signing of the U.S. Constitution on this day back in 1787. Amna Nawaz: But, for immigrants, the path to naturalization has grown more difficult, as the Trump administration has added new requirements and tightened vetting standards. Our justice correspondent, Ali Rogin, has this look. Ali Rogin: In a federal courthouse in Alexandria, Virginia, 60 of the nation's newest Americans take their final steps towards citizenship, sharing where their journeys began. Woman: Venezuela. Woman: El Salvador. Woman: Korea. Ali Rogin: Before they all arrived at this moment. Judge William Fitzpatrick, Eastern District of Virginia: Please rise and raise your right hand. I hereby declare... Men and Women: I hereby declare... Judge William Fitzpatrick: ... on oath. Men and Women: ... on oath. Judge William Fitzpatrick: So help me God. Men and Women: So help me God. Judge William Fitzpatrick: Congratulations. Woman: We're super excited. Me and my husband, we both became citizens. Man: I don't think people realize how daunting this journey is. But it's -- I'm so happy to be here. Ali Rogin: For most, the journey involves applying for and holding a green card for years, lengthy applications, hundreds of dollars in fees, interviews with immigration officers, an English language test, and finally a civics test, for which applicants spend months studying. Lucio Arevalo, Green Card Holder: Definitely am nervous. The nerves are there. The stress is there. Ali Rogin: New Mexico resident Lucio Arevalo is nearing the finish line of his naturalization. A green card holder since 1998, he arrived in the U.S. with his parents from Mexico as a baby. He's awaiting his interview date. Lucio Arevalo: I am, of course, a permanent resident, but I just feel like there's still that thin line between me actually being, I guess, fully part of the country. So, decided to take that step. Ali Rogin: What will it mean to you to take that oath of citizenship? Lucio Arevalo: To be honest, it's -- it would be such a big relief. Ali Rogin: Relief because he hopes to stop living in fear of President Trump's efforts to deport noncitizens. Lucio Arevalo: It is definitely scary to know that there could be that possibility for me to get stopped, I guess, by immigration. Ali Rogin: To help prepare for the civics test, Lucio turned to Welcome.US, a national initiative that emerged after the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan to help new arrivals through the complicated immigration system. That's how he met volunteer Dana Van Ostrand, who lives in Iowa and has been helping Arevalo study in virtual sessions. Dana Van Ostrand, Welcome.US: It's been a really fun process to not only go through the test, but also just hear of Lucio's life and what he's been about. Nazanin Ash, CEO and Co-Founder, Welcome.US: There are a lot of changes happening in our immigration system and in whether and how we welcome newcomers. Ali Rogin: Nazanin Ash is the CEO and co-founder of Welcome.US. Nazanin Ash: It's a process that's rigorous and has always been rigorous, and it's appropriately rigorous. Taking on the responsibilities of citizenship is a commitment that no one takes lightly, least of all the aspiring Americans who are pursuing their dreams. Ali Rogin: That dream of becoming American has become more elusive since President Trump returned to office. In the last year, the administration has introduced a harder civics test with more questions and a higher number of correct answers required to pass, implemented stricter social media vetting, proposed raising the application fee by 75 percent to nearly $1,300, and revived a defunct practice of neighborhood investigations into applicants' moral character. And the government is processing far fewer naturalization applications today than during the Biden administration, a 75 percent drop-off compared to two years ago. And the rejection rate for naturalization has more than doubled since September 2024 from 9.2 percent to more than 18 percent. Sometimes, the roadblocks continue all the way to the courthouse. Since President Trump returned to office, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services has been abruptly canceling naturalization ceremonies, many of them at the last minute. In fact, today, here at this courthouse, there were supposed to be two ceremonies, but the afternoon session was abruptly canceled just last night. Immigration officials say the changes are necessary to tighten the system that has become too lax. In a statement to PBS News, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services said the agency "has implemented reforms to ensure U.S. citizenship is reserved for those who qualify," adding that: "USCIS will not take shortcuts in the naturalization process. Naturalization is a privilege, not a right." Van Ostrand says his volunteerism is a way to respond to what he sees as this administration's hostility towards immigrants. Dana Van Ostrand: The Trump administration's rhetoric and actions have been quite dehumanizing, in my view, and I wanted to be a part of welcoming people who have already been here. Ali Rogin: Back at the Alexandria courthouse, the new citizens receive a parting message from Judge William Fitzpatrick. Judge William Fitzpatrick: What I ask of you is to keep working hard, to give life, to give meaning to the oath that you took today by making your voice heard, by making sure that government, your government, reflects your values and your vision for what America can be. I have signed the final order. It is official. Congratulations to you all. Best

Other efforts to reshape the midterms continue Politics Sep 17, 2026 6:26 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — The Supreme Court this week closed the chapter on one of President Donald Trump's boldest efforts to reshape November's elections — a plan that would have demanded a dramatic overhaul of the nation's mail voting processes on what most election officials agreed was an impossibly short timeline. WATCH: Analyzing the Supreme Court's mail-in voting decision and Trump's reaction But the case was just one example of the Republican president's numerous attempts to assert federal control over the upcoming midterms. Several others remain in various states of play, even as mail ballots have been sent out in at least three states and early voting starts in others this week. Recently, the Department of Justice ordered officials in more than two dozen states to preserve records from the 2024 election as part of a campaign to force them to turn over detailed voter data despite repeated court losses. Please check your inbox to confirm. And lacking the sensitive voter data the administration wants from many states, the Department of Homeland Security has launched its own probe to find noncitizen voters on state rolls, an effort that a federal whistleblower says is rushed, error-ridden and potentially violating state laws. Meanwhile, Trump has continued to falsely claim that mail ballots are corrupt, that noncitizens are abundant on voter lists and that Democratic election fraud is widespread. During the recent Republican convention, the president goaded his fans in a verbal pledge to "cheat like hell, like they do." In response to Monday's Supreme Court ruling, Trump lashed back at the justices, saying they lacked the "courage necessary to save our America." The Constitution gives the power to run elections to states, rather than to the federal government. Election officials have said they're prepared to run a safe, secure election even if Trump continues to fan the flames. Democratic groups have signaled they are building out contingency plans in case Trump sends armed federal officers to the polls or Republicans make other attempts to improperly interfere in the election, a high-stakes contest that will determine which party controls Congress next year. With his mail ballot reforms blocked for now, here's a look at Trump's other, ongoing efforts to reshape election procedures: Trump has pressured states to use a controversial federal voter lookup tool The president insists, contrary to reams of research, that large numbers of noncitizens are illegally voting around the country. In his second term in office, he has sought to use the might of the federal government to crack down on the issue, including through a massive overhaul of a federal voter eligibility database called Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE. The SAVE program was created under an immigration law mandating that the Department of Homeland Security help federal, state and local agencies prevent government benefits from going to noncitizens. Trump last year directed changes to significantly expand its abilities for mass searches by election officials. Then, his administration sent letters and filed lawsuits to push states to run their sensitive voter data through the tool – a prospect some states have agreed to, but many have resisted to keep their residents' personal information secure. Since last year, at least 67 million registrations have been scanned through the program, but critics worry it could end up purging valid voters from the rolls. Some registrants have already been wrongly flagged. A federal judge in June barred the new version of the SAVE program, calling it an illegal violation of Americans' privacy. The Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to intervene and block that ruling with an emergency order. The Supreme Court has yet to weigh in on the case. Meanwhile, the federal government continues to push states to give up voter registration information that contains addresses, dates of birth, driver's license numbers and partial Social Security numbers. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin in July warned that state officials could lose funding or face investigations if they failed to go along with Trump's election security demands. And the DOJ last week sent letters to 29 states and the District of Columbia ordering them to preserve 2024 election documents and advising them that they were "under investigation" and subject to ongoing litigation for their failure to give up the data. Numerous investigations have found that while noncitizens have occasionally appeared on voting rolls and cast ballots, it is extremely rare. DHS is conducting its own noncitizen voter investigation In a last-ditch effort to hunt for noncitizen voters without detailed data from all states, DHS in August ordered a group of U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services staff to pivot to a full-time manual investigation of state voter rolls, according to a whistleblower's report released Monday. The anonymous federal whistleblower said federal employees are being directed to misrepresent themselves on the voter lookup tools in a way that likely violates state laws as they compare DHS-provided data with state records in an attempt to identify noncitizens who are illegally registered. ab0379b1500c.text: By — Steven Sloan, Associated Press Steven Sloan, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/work-has-stopped-on-system-that-was-key-to-trump-effort-to-limit-mail-voting-usps-chief-says Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Work has stopped on system that was key to Trump effort to limit mail voting, USPS chief says Politics Sep 17, 2026 8:19 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The top official at the U.S. Postal Service said Thursday that the agency has stopped work on developing a controversial computer system that was central to President Donald Trump's effort to limit mail voting after the Supreme Court rejected his executive order this week. READ MORE: Trump's push to restrict mail ballots failed. Other efforts to reshape the midterms continue "There's an injunction so we're not doing anything," postmaster general David Steiner told The Associated Press in an interview. Steiner, a onetime chief executive of Waste Management, has spent most of the past year atop the postal service navigating political and financial challenges. He's pressing Congress for changes that would help him resolve what he has called a "liquidity crisis." And Trump's efforts to largely eradicate mail voting turned the postal service into an unlikely arbiter of who is eligible to vote just months before this year's critical midterm elections, a role Steiner seemingly had little interest in playing. Unlike Trump, who was sharply critical of the Supreme Court decision and ridiculed some of the justices, Steiner offered no assessment of the court's action. Steiner also declined to take a position on Trump's policy, presenting himself as the leader of an "independent agency of the executive branch" whose influence over the president's order was limited to operational concerns. "I don't get to decide what rules that are put on us that I decide to accept or not accept," he said. "I looked at it more from the execution side." The postal service has asserted its independence in the past, including during a 2019 standoff when the first Trump administration sought to pressure the agency as the president was in a dispute with Amazon. Steiner said he wouldn't get into the "nuance" of that. But the pressure has grown so intense at points that it's fueled talk of whether Steiner might resign, a notion he denied. "There's no truth to that," he said. "I think I know the motivation behind it. I think it's somebody that would like to see me out of a job." Inserting the Postal Service into elections The executive order Trump signed in March directed several federal agencies to develop state citizenship lists. Those lists would have been delivered to an online portal at the Postal Service, which would have been allowed to send mail ballots only to voters who were cleared through the process. Steiner said he knew about the order about a month before it was unveiled but said his focus was largely on implementation, not the policy's merits. A whistleblower report released earlier this month by Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., argued the system was hastily built and riddled with errors. Steiner said he read "portions" of the whistleblower report and acknowledged the obstacles associated with building such a massive platform quickly. Still, he said he had confidence in colleagues working on the project and had planned to unveil it around Sept. 15. "There's absolutely no doubt that we worked fast," he said. "My personal opinion is it was a monumental task and I'm very proud of our IT department for being able to do it that fast." In addition to the voter list, Trump's order would have required states to adopt a uniform envelope style that included barcodes, something states said would have been arduous so close to the election. Following the Supreme Court's ruling, a memo sent to all postal service employees Wednesday and obtained by the AP said the agency will "not be enforcing any of these new rules in the 2026 federal election." "First and foremost, for Election Mail it is business as usual," according to the memo. "We continue to follow established protocols, and we remain entirely focused on our core mission: delivering the mail safely and securely for voters and election officials across the country." Though the Supreme Court rejected Trump's executive order for this year's election, Justice Brett Kavanaugh indicated he might rule in favor of the administration if the issue comes back before the court at a later time. Steiner encourages voters to cast ballots early Steiner said the postal service would still encourage the use of envelopes and barcodes in future elections, which it has long recommended. He said such changes wouldn't be required but those who don't comply may have to pay more. "If you use the barcode in the envelope, we'll charge you a lower price," he said. "If you don't, we're going to charge you a higher price because it's harder for us to process." While the postal service isn't moving forward on Trump's order, there are still concerns about postmark delays that could have an impact on this year's elections. The number of ballots rejected for late postmarks has soared in the vote-by-mail states of Washington and Oregon, according to recently released data highlighting concerns about recent changes in postal service operations. Steiner said there were no plans to alter those operations and encouraged voters who use mail to get their ballots in early. "We say seven days," he said. "Everything is solved if people vote early." Space Force braces for stalled progress amid lack of full funding
Fiscal 2027 program starts are already on hold until December.
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—Space Force modernization efforts could slow if Congress doesn’t pass a full budget at the end of the year, the service’s leaders said.
“We're on this ramp-up, right, consistent with our overall strategy and the recognition that the space domain is a critical domain, in and of itself, but also for the joint force,” Erich Hernandez-Baquero, the Space Force’s top buyer, told reporters Tuesday. “Now we're going to run into [fiscal year 2027]—and you saw that our budget request was to continue on that—and this [continuing resolution] is definitely going to put the brakes on that for a time period.”
The Space Force has requested $71.1 billion for 2027, including $19.1 billion for procurement. But with little time remaining before fiscal 2027 begins on Oct. 1, Congress has passed stopgap legislation—a continuing resolution—to keep funding the Pentagon at 2026 levels through Dec. 11. The CR permits no new programs to begin.
“We certainly appreciate at least not being shut down. So…that's a good thing, but on the CR, it really does pace us at a time where we really need to go faster. So we are obviously encouraging Congress to do what they can to help support the president's budget on that,” Hernandez-Baquero said. “In the meantime, we'll just do what we always do: prioritize the things that will yield the most mission capability soonest, and make sure we're executing on those.”
Hernandez-Baquero, who was sworn into the chief space acquisition role last month, declined to specify which priorities could be most affected by a continuing resolution because things were “pre-decision at this point.”
Gen. Doug Schiess, the chief of space operations, said about 10 percent of the service’s programs could be slowed down due continuing resolution.
“About 90 percent of the programs we have are programs from last year—so we can still get after those,” but there’s a remaining 10 percent of programs that require full budget funding, Schiess said. “It's going to slow us down, and the threat is not slowing down.”
Amid a broader push for acquisition reform, Hernandez-Baquero said he’s focused on streamlining and speeding up military purchasing. And when it comes to technology initiatives, there will be a new senior leadership role dedicated to it.
The Air Force’s new program acquisition executives, or PAEs, are “establishing those pathways for onboarding new technology, but I'm just conscious that that by itself is not going to support drawing in the right technologies,” he said. “I want somebody that's focused—100 percent—on looking at the most promising tech and driving the prototyping initiatives that are going to help mature it to the level where a PAE can say, ‘Ah, it meets my criteria for this onboard path, and I can go do that’.”
That person is a technology portfolio executive, who “will have the most promising technology coming out of the [research and development] side, and…will work with industry to ensure that we have the right pathways to do that. Conceptually, there would be prototype efforts that get executed out of that to support the mission areas.”
The technology portfolio executive office already exists but the role hasn’t yet been filled, he said.
“When I designate a TPE, for example, that person is going to report directly to me and represent my authority when it comes to the technology transition,” Hernandez-Baquero said. “I cannot do this without the buy-in of the PAEs that are executing the mission areas, and so my charter to them is going to be not only to deliver on those missionaries, but be part of the enterprise team that's going to deliver on those cross-cutting capabilities.”

Air Force contemplates unmanned tankers
The technology isn’t yet available to give autonomy to very large aircraft—but it’s coming.
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—With an eye on the Navy’s progress toward an unmanned aerial tanker, Air Force planners are asking questions about their own future tanker fleet.
“Thinking beyond the current KC-46 buy and the program extension. Whatever that next tanker looks like—our advanced tanker system—it's got to be connected. It's got to be able to defend itself. But it begs the question: Does it need to be manned? Could it be optionally manned, or could it be autonomous, or is there a family of solutions maybe that would answer that question?” Lt. Gen. Daniel Tulley, who leads Air Mobility Command, told reporters at the Air, Space, & Cyber 2026 conference.
The Air Force is currently buying Boeing KC-46 Pegasus tankers and spent $12 million to explore buying a new tanker this year. But it zeroed out funding to continue those explorations in the 2027 budget request and is asking instead for $13 million for “advanced tanker systems.”
Tulley said the Navy’s work on the Boeing MQ-25 Stingray suggests that his own service might eventually not need manned tankers. The Navy announced on Thursday that the MQ-25, which first flew earlier this year, has received approval to enter low-rate production. The service also ordered three more aircraft, bringing its total to 14.
“I do not believe that it has to be manned, a future air-refueling solution,” he said. “But then, how do we, the U.S. Air Force, bring that to bear in scope, scale, and range?”
A drone tanker for the Air Force would need to be a very large aircraft with the capacity for fuel and the ability to fly for a long time. The KC-46, for example, can fly nearly 7,400 miles and carry more than a thousand tons of fuel. The MQ-25 can fly about 500 miles and carry up to 7.5 tons of fuel.
“An optionally manned or an unmanned tanker at the ranges we need it to operate at is a very large aircraft. And we're not yet to where we're employing fully autonomous large aircraft,” Tulley said.
“Just about any large aircraft these days made by Boeing can take itself off with very little help, can fly on a programmed route and pretty much land itself on autopilot, bring itself to a stop on the runway. But we don't employ it that way with a system that's controlling it and then taxiing it in and making it a part of a more effective, broader system.”
One maker of autonomous-aircraft control systems said the vision of autonomy for large aircraft was getting clearer. And while the technology isn’t there yet, there’s progress, said Matthew George, CEO of Merlin Labs.
“We’re the furthest along in the world on making that real—in our opinion,” said Matthew George, CEO of Merlin Labs. “So we're going to be implementing autonomy on the C-130J, which is the same general size class” as the Boeing KC-135 Stratotanker.
“And the advantage with those aircraft is you can start to implement autonomy still with human crews aboard, and you can supplement those human crews in a way that's pretty helpful. That's a way that you can start to chip away at that without actually going fully to the unmanned tanker right away,” George said. “The goal is that the unmanned tanker is ready, and the autonomy ends up being ready at the same time.”
George agreed with Tulley’s point that many aircraft can somewhat fly themselves, but there are instances, such as emergency situations, when a human needs to make a decision.
“What's really hard is those edge cases and those emergencies—or those things where there are decisions to be made. So, for instance, if you're going to a destination and then there's weather in between, how do you get around the weather?” he said.
And beyond technology, there are policy challenges.
“None of this matters unless it's certified and safe. So for us, getting certification done is important, and that's what we're working really closely with the Air Force on this year,” George said. “We're taking that [autonomous pilot] brain and putting it onto the C-130J. And as far as we know, that's going to be the first time autonomy fully takes control of an operational U.S. Air Force aircraft.”
No date was provided for when that flight will occur, but the company’s technology completed a critical design review, George said.

69bdd3e58296.text: Violence has spread across the Middle East since the U.S. and Israel launched the war in Iran. Qatar has spent months mediating between Iran and the U.S. while also being targeted by Iranian strikes. Nick Schifrin sat down with Dr. Majed al-Ansari, adviser to Qatar’s prime minister, to discuss regional tensions and whether there is a way back to negotiations. Amna Nawaz: Today, Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis in Yemen traded new strikes. The fighting is just one example of violence that's spread across the region since the U.S. and Israel launched the war in Iran. Geoff Bennett: The country of Qatar has spent months mediating between Iran and the U.S. and Iran and the region while also being targeted by Iranian strikes. This week, Nick Schifrin sat down with a key adviser to Qatar's prime minister to discuss regional tensions and whether there is a way back to negotiations. Nick Schifrin: Thank you very much, Mr. Ansari. Thanks very much. Welcome to the "News Hour." Majed Al-Ansari, Adviser to Qatari Prime Minister: Thank you for having me. Nick Schifrin: You have been in the middle of negotiations this year between Iran and the United States. Qatar was largely confident about this when the MOU was signed. But, since then, we haven't seen any progress. Iran has maintained its choke hold over the Strait of Hormuz. From where you sit, is there a path back to U.S.-Iran negotiations or not? Majed Al-Ansari: You know, Nick, one thing we can't afford to do in the region right now is despair about the diplomatic solution. There is no way out of this unless it is a diplomatic solution. And, therefore, we have been working with all our partners 24/7. Our mediation teams have been running between each capital in the region trying to get it forward, and we won't give up. We will just continue doing it until we have a solution. Nick Schifrin: Negotiations is not just U.S.-Iran. It's also Iran-GCC. It's also the Gulf Cooperation Council. We were supposed to have a meeting earlier this week. And the regional officials I was talking to before this meeting was supposed to happen on Monday were saying Iran was asking for too much. Iran was asking for control or at least some kind of access of all ships going in and out of the strait in Iranian waters. Is Iran asking for too much? Majed Al-Ansari: Now, first of all, this is -- this was supposed to be an interim solution, not the new status quo. The new status quo cannot be to deal with the Strait of Hormuz, something that can be open or closed by any... (Crosstalk) Nick Schifrin: Meaning it needs to be open, period. Majed Al-Ansari: Exactly. We need to go back. It's a matter of international maritime law. It's where all the littoral states have the right to use the Strait of Hormuz openly and not creating a new status quo that would give any of the littoral states any power over the strait. Nick Schifrin: Reuters a few weeks ago reported that Qatar's liquefied natural gas exports, which, of course, count for a large share of Qatar's GDP, have dropped 96 percent since the U.S. and Israel launched this war. Firstly, is that accurate? And, secondly, how existential a threat is it to Qatar if this war continues, if the strait continues to be closed? Majed Al-Ansari: I won't come into the specific numbers. I will leave that to QatarEnergy and the people in our energy sector. I can tell you, of course, that all of our LNG used to go through the Strait of Hormuz. And Strait of Hormuz being closed basically means that no LNG is going through. Let me say it very clearly. The effects -- we have not yet to see the real effects on international economy of this crisis. We have yet to reach the tip of the iceberg. We are looking now... Nick Schifrin: Why do you say that? Majed Al-Ansari: Because the economic effects of this war is going to go on -- if it continues like this, going to go on and affect every other sector. We have already -- are already getting reports of reduced yields from crops in countries like Somalia and other countries in Asia, where this is an issue of famine. It's not an issue of luxury, right? I think it's an existential threat for all of us collectively in the international economy. And, of course, Qatar is heavy -- heavily dependent on the Strait of Hormuz. But let me say it also very clearly. Our economy is not fragile. Those who are living in Qatar, thankfully, other than the fact that missiles were being intercepted every other day, but when it comes to commodities, when it comes to security, when it comes to everyday needs, when it comes to salaries and the economic situation, nothing was affected. Nick Schifrin: Iran hit the Al Udeid Air Base, the largest air base across the region. Do you have faith that the United States can defend the U.S. Qatari base, one of the most important spots in Doha? Majed Al-Ansari: You know, the metric that we need to consider here is the fact that more than 95 percent of every projectile that was sent towards our countries was deterred through the work of the men and women in uniform, and it's not an easy an easy number to deal with. The -- our militaries proved their worth. The cooperation with the United States proved its worth. We see the coordination and the interoperability between our militaries and the U.S. military on all fronts when it comes to defending our countries. I think we have shown that we are not an easy pill to swallow. Nick Schifrin: But do you have faith that 95 percent can be repeated if there's another cycle of Iowa? Majed Al-Ansari: One hundred percent. I can tell you that our militaries are standing ready right now for any kind of escalation. Of course, we're working diplomatically to make sure that there is no other escalation. But you have to remember 40 percent of the attacks on Qatar, for example, were on energy facilities, right? More than 80 percent of the missiles launched were on -- by Iran were on our countries, not on Israel or the American forces. So, for us,

2a83846840e0.text: Professional wheelchair tennis players are competing for their countries this week in the World Team Cup at the U.S. Tennis Association’s National Campus in Orlando. It’s part of the 50th anniversary of the sport’s creation and comes at a time when popularity is growing. Amna Nawaz reports for our ongoing coverage of the culture of sport, part of our CANVAS series. Amna Nawaz: This week, professional wheelchair tennis players are competing for their countries, part of the World Team Cup at the U.S. Tennis Association's national campus in Orlando. It's all part of the 50th anniversary of the sport's creation and comes at a time when popularity is growing. I recently took a close-up look at the U.S. Open in Flushing Meadows, New York, for our ongoing coverage of the culture of sport, part of our Canvas series. All the agility, speed, and power of tennis supercharged on two wheels. (Cheering) Amna Nawaz: The sport of wheelchair tennis has come a very long way in just 50 years. Brad Parks, Wheelchair Tennis Co-Founder: Everybody, they're just so darn good. I mean, it's just so fantastic to see how it has progressed and improved over the years. Amna Nawaz: Brad Parks, who founded the sport back in 1976, has a lot to celebrate. Today, wheelchair tennis is in more top-tier professional tournaments than ever before, including all four Grand Slams. A player development pipeline is being built, and sponsorships and broadcast deals mean the fan base continues to grow. Parks himself never expected to be here after being paralyzed in a freestyle skiing accident at the age of 18. Brad Parks: Somebody came and told me about wheelchair basketball when I was in the hospital. And I'm thinking, well, if you play wheelchair basketball, why can't you play tennis? And tennis was on my mind because I wanted to be a better tennis player than I was. Sliding into a shot, hitting a ball, recovering, coming back around, that whole feeling of movement and everything else is really, really great. Amna Nawaz: Acceptance was built one match at a time. Brad Parks: When I was first injured, we would go to a tennis court, and sometimes the pro would come over and go, what are you guys doing? Everybody was always worried we were going to damage the courts. And they -- we weren't really even accepted. Nobody could believe that we were actually wheelchair athletes, that we were athletes. Amna Nawaz: The game differs slightly from the able-bodied sport. Players use the same courts, balls, and rackets, but they're allowed two bounces of the ball. The chair is considered part of the player's body. So the same rules that apply to the body in able-bodied tennis apply to the chair. Dana Mathewson was the first American woman to win a major wheelchair tennis title, the 2022 Wimbledon doubles championship. She retired in 2024 ranked number one in the U.S. and number seven in the world. She left the court at the top of her game, but found a new role just a few feet away, hosting and commentating. Seven years ago, when you last spoke to us, you had this to say. I want to put it back to you now and get your reaction. Dana Mathewson, Professional Wheelchair Tennis Player: That's crazy it was seven years ago. Amna Nawaz: I know. You said: "The more and more I get exposed to different things..." Dana Mathewson: The more that I realize that I can do with this disability and the things that it's afforded in my life. Amna Nawaz: "The more I actually feel really grateful for it." You still feel that way? Dana Mathewson: It's a hot take, isn't it? (Laughter) Dana Mathewson: Yes. I would be lying to you if I said that I woke up every day and I saw my chair and I was like, yay. Like, that's kind of -- that's a reach. But the sentiment of what I said definitely still rings true. I think that I can guarantee that, without a disability, I wouldn't have been a professional athlete. I wouldn't have represented my country. I wouldn't have set records within a sport. I wouldn't have got the opportunity to do things like this. I wouldn't get to be an advocate for a marginalized group of people. Amna Nawaz: Advocating for and mentoring the next generation of players. Did you have the kind of mentors when you were coming up that you're trying to be for them now? Dana Mathewson: I want to say yes, but the honest answer is not really. When I first started and I went to my first ever wheelchair tennis camp, there were a couple Paralympians that I met, and they made such an impact on me, but I only got to see them for that week. The little amount that I had was so impactful to me that, if I can do that for someone else, that that means more to me than any -- it sounds cliche, but, honestly, I mean it -- any Slams or anything like that. Amna Nawaz: Among the sport's new stars, Japan's Tokito Oda, a 20-year-old with multiple sponsors who's known as much for his sartorial flair as he is for his killer serve. Oda was just 17 when he won the French Open in 2023, becoming the youngest man ever to win a Grand Slam title.
