f152572142e8.text: House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) is staring at a scary political environment for Republicans and claiming to see something very different: a path to 225 seats . Why it matters: Republican leaders insist they can retain the majority, but only if they drive their voters to the polls by manufacturing the kind of voter enthusiasm Democrats are generating organically. "If we make it a contrast election, we win," Scalise told Axios in an interview Thursday. "We could get to 225. It would be a good night for us if we did, but it's possible," he said. "235 is not," he said. "You're literally doing coin tosses in a couple of seats." Between the lines: Asked if he saw any signs of a blue wave forming or the map expanding, Scalise said: "Not right now. No." Reality check: Republicans know that history — and many of the indicators heading into November — is working against them. "I know what history says, you know, but history's not on the ballot," Scalise said. Still, Democrats are turning out in primaries — and special elections — as if they're getting free gas cards for showing up. Democrats lead by nearly nine percentage points on the generic ballot. President Trump's approval rating is below 40%, according to the RealClearPolitics average . And Trump is underwater by a whopping 61 percentage points on inflation in a recent poll, an apparent record . Zoom in: Republicans are examining the map with a jeweler's loupe and insist the picture isn't as bleak in the pivotal battleground seats. "We're not looking at national polls; we go district by district," Scalise said. That means trench warfare in 35 seats, where Republicans say they have proven winners, plenty of money and new rules to spend it . "We've got 20 [seats] on our side that we're fighting to hold on to that are real competitive, and 15 [seats] that we have a real chance to flip," he said. "These are knock-down, drag-out fights." What we're hearing: The White House has long thought of the midterms as a "hate election." Scalise uses the more genteel term "contrast election." But before Republicans can dream about growing their majority, they need to fix their enthusiasm problem — and match the Democratic energy showing up in many of the preelection indicators. The GOP's midterm convention in Dallas last week was the first step. "If we are able to capitalize on that kind of enthusiasm and carry that momentum into November, then we'll have the same turnout as the other side, and we'll hold the majority," Scalise said. Now comes the road show: Congressional leaders — and the president — are hitting the campaign trail. In the next two weeks, Scalise will travel to 11 states to campaign for 16 Republicans — incumbents and challengers. The bottom line: The 225-seat scenario is Scalise's high-water mark. At another point in the interview, he suggested the majority could be smaller — closer to the 220–215 split Republicans won in 2024. "This isn't going to be a 10-seat majority, but it could be a six-seat majority."

7b7dca8cc811.text: President Trump told Axios Thursday that he's approaching a critical juncture in the Iran war over whether to restart massive attacks in an effort to bring the conflict to a close. "I have a big decision coming up. Do I want to go in and annihilate them [the Iranian regime] or do I not? It's a big decision. Anything could happen with me." Why it matters: Though Trump has made similar threats before, his comments come ahead of a planned meeting Tuesday with leaders from six Gulf countries — Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman — on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. The meeting could shape the next phase of the war, including whether to make another push for diplomacy or intensify military action. If Trump wants to resume major combat operations, he would need buy-in from his regional allies. The president has said several times in recent days that the war will end soon. Some U.S. officials warn that the conflict has settled into an unsustainable, neither-war-nor-peace stalemate, and they believe Trump could return to major combat operations after the midterms if a deal isn't reached by then. What he's saying: Trump made clear in the interview that he wants to use the meeting at the UN to hear directly from regional allies about the war's next steps. "I want to find out where they are and how they are doing. We have been very protective of them," Trump said. Trump declined to say whether he'll decide on the path forward before or after the midterms. Driving the news: In early August, Trump held off on resuming major combat operations after Saudi Arabia and Qatar expressed concern that Iran would bomb Saudi oil and gas facilities in retaliation. Since then, Trump has taken a "low-key" approach : suspending negotiations with Iran, launching a new economic sanctions campaign , continuing a naval blockade on Iranian ports, and focusing the U.S. military on reopening the Strait of Hormuz and increasing oil flow to the global energy market. The U.S. military has significantly increased oil and gas tanker transit through the strait. But traffic is still below pre-war levels, and oil prices remain high. State of play: Trump and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth have ordered the military to maintain its level of forces in the Middle East until the end of the year, U.S. officials say, to remain ready for a potential return to full-scale combat. The officials say Trump needs to decide soon on the way forward, partly because the U.S. military can't stay in its current holding pattern much longer. "At some point, you have to decide what is the endgame," one of the officials said. Trump told Axios he's very satisfied that the naval blockade has prevented Iran from exporting its oil. "Not one ship has gone to Iran since we started. They tried and we blew them up," he said. The president added that Iran is in direct contact with the U.S. and said the Iranians still want to reach a deal. The big picture: The White House has also been working on a post-war strategy that calls for a regional effort to contain Iran while expanding normalization of relations between Israel and its neighbors. While the plan is still in the early stages of drafting, it's intended to guide the U.S. approach in the Middle East after the Iran war ends and in the final two years of Trump's term. Two big events loom over the planning: the Oct. 27 election in Israel and the U.S. midterms in November. What to watch: When asked if he will meet with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in New York next week, Trump said, "I may."

Swedish pop star Zara Larsson has condemned the White House for using one of her most recognisable songs in a social media reel.
The clip used Larsson's Midnight Sun in a video appearing to show immigration enforcement raids. The song has since been removed from the post, but the video is still visible on the White House's TikTok feed.
The video is captioned "never ending deportations", riffing on Larsson's lyrics "never-ending midnight sun".
In a three-minute reaction video posted on social media, Larsson described the clip as "dehumanising", joining a growing list of singers, including Sabrina Carpenter and Ariana Grande, who have told the Trump administration to not use their music.
The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.
The reel splices together multiple videos of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, as well as other US law enforcement personnel, handcuffing men and putting them into vehicles.
Larsson reposted part of the original clip, which then cuts to a selfie video of her using her fingers to hold an 'L' shape against her forehead.
In the reaction video that has already clocked up more than 4.2 million views on TikTok, she tells her followers the White House video is "so dehumanising".
Larsson continues: "These people in this video â they're real people."
"The vast majority of these people who are undocumented are regular people with jobs and they're just trying to have a better future".
"It's so crazy how everything is so memefied and so 'ha-ha-ha'," she says, accusing the White House of using her song to sow "division", despite the lyrics reflecting a connection between people and nature, according to Larsson.
Earlier this year, Larsson condemned a video of President Donald Trump dancing at various events overlayed with her hit Lush Life.
White House social media accounts have been forced to remove various songs from their feed following interventions from artists.
Taylor Swift's seasonal track August disappeared from a reel shared by the Trump administration in August, while one of Olivia Rodrigo's songs vanished from a video after the singer condemned its use for what she called "hateful propaganda".
Sabrina Carpenter and Ariana Grande have also warned the Trump administration in separate incidents to not use their music in social media content after the White House posted videos featuring their songs.

A US federal judge has ordered the Trump administration must give 30 days' notice before any "demolition" occurs to the Kennedy Center, as President Donald Trump warns the Washington DC performing arts venue could be "ripped down".
The order comes after Trump was photographed onboard Air Force One looking at a poster with a headline that appeared to tout the demolition of the site.
On Thursday, US District Judge Christopher Cooper ordered a detailed report of the centre's "temporary closure" for emergency repairs, and for written notice of any change to the scope of the project.
In May, Cooper ordered the removal of Trump's name from the building.
In a document filed to court on Thursday before the judge's ruling, Kennedy Center executive director, Matt Floca, said the temporary closure was to repair safety hazards and would last seven days, "unless extended".
On Tuesday, the Kennedy Center's board of trustees voted - for the third time since February - to close the venue down for two years.
Trump then took to Truth Social to write that the board, which is chaired by Trump and includes his cabinet members and allies, voted "almost unanimously" to close the venue "for safety reasons".
He has argued that the venue is badly in need of repair, and that by adding his name to the building it will be able to secure renovation funding.
"I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition because, frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close," he told reporters in Charlotte, North Carolina, on Wednesday. "It'll end up being ripped down."
On Wednesday, Trump was photographed through a window of Air Force One looking at a poster with the words "Kennedy Center DEMOLIS" visible.
On Thursday, Cooper ordered the Trump administration to provide at least 30 days' notice ahead of any change in construction plans.
That order came after congresswoman Joyce Beatty, an ex officio Kennedy Center board member, asked the judge to make "crystal clear that its order prohibits demolishing the structure".
Beatty, a Democrat, had previously sued to halt changes to the Kennedy Center, and to strip Trump's name from the building.
Congress established the centre as a memorial to President John F Kennedy, who was assassinated in 1963.
Some critics argue that congressional action is required to make changes to the building, and that the need for renovations is exaggerated.

The snowballing controversy over pro-Palestinian rapper Macklemore being dropped as a support act for Ed Sheeran has plunged the tour into crisis and left concert-goers in the middle of the fraught Israel-Gaza debate.
Fans who spoke to the BBC - including those who have tickets to see Sheeran's next show - have been split since Macklemore was dropped from the Loop Tour this week after his "free Palestine" protest on stage.
All of Sheeran's opening acts have since quit in solidarity.
"I'm still torn," Damien Given told the BBC on whether he would attend Sheeran's show on Saturday, calling the artist's response disingenuous. Another fan called it a "no-win situation".
Since the controversy blew up earlier this week, ticket prices, external for his remaining shows in the US, Mexico and South America have dropped, as calls for boycotts spread.
Sheeran has responded, saying he's been "appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine", but would not be drawn into a political debate.
He argued that "those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum" and stressed he was not responsible for Macklemore being removed from the tour.
Still, the backlash has come from all sides.
Some are upset Sheeran's tour is continuing without all the listed acts and they want refunds. It's no longer the show they paid for, they said.
Given, who is from Northern Ireland, said he's felt in two minds over the tickets he has on Saturday to see the show in Philadelphia.
It will mark Sheeran's first time back on stage since the controversy spiralled.
Given said he's felt that Macklemore was treated "very, very wrong" and thought Sheeran was not being transparent with fans.
"[Sheeran] said he was in support of Ukraine when the Ukraine-Russia war started," said Given.
"You can't just say now suddenly, 'I'm not political.'"
But he explained the poignant connection he's felt to Sheeran's music that has drawn him to Saturday's show.
The singer's hit Thinking Out Loud was the first dance at Given's wedding.
"When she danced," Given, 52, said, recalling the moment with his bride, "the first words of the song were, 'When your legs don't work like they used to before.'"
His wife, Kellie, had been diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and could barely walk. She died four years later, in 2024.
Given said if it wasn't for "that connection, I would absolutely" not be attending, but "I'm probably leaning towards going".
Fellow fan Patti Ann has felt less conflicted over the backlash and instead said Sheeran was in a "no-win situation".
"I back [Sheeran] 100% for his decision," she said. "I feel like he has an obligation and a contract with his venues, and sometimes, financially, you can't get out of those types of things."
Ann, who has been a Sheeran fan for years, said she thinks a concert venue is not the place for politics.
Believe what you want, she said, "just don't press it on me".
She still plans to attend his show in Atlanta, Georgia, in October.
Matt Jaye, a Jewish-American from Florida, said he was outraged watching Macklemore's comments on a New Jersey stage earlier this month in support of Palestine.
He contacted Ticketmaster and asked for a refund for tickets he has to Sheeran's November show in Tampa, Florida.
His request was denied, which he said was "pretty upsetting".
His mood changed, though, after Macklemore was removed from Sheeran's line-up.
"I'm not in favour of a one-sided presentation of things from an artist," Jaye, 48, said. "That's not why I'm going to the concert."
Jaye said he believed Sheeran bore some culpability for Macklemore's pro-Palestinian protest.
"If [Sheeran's] saying that he's apolitical, I would expect him to maintain those same standards for the artists that he's bringing on," he said.
"I don't think he handled it in the best way possible."
He added that he would have liked Sheeran to issue an apology to the Jewish community for making part of his audience "very uncomfortable".
Some fans are worried what will become of the tour by the time Sheeran is set to play in their city.
Heather Park, who has tickets this weekend, said she's worried some shows might be cancelled.
"My main thing was to go see Ed Sheeran," she said. "Macklemore was just a bonus."
While Park, 49, believes Macklemore's ouster was unfair and a violation of free speech, she said she's mostly unbothered by the drama and prefers to separate the artist from the art.
"I still like the music," she says.

395bb8863dd8.text: By — Fatima Hussein, Associated Press Fatima Hussein, Associated Press By — Mike Stobbe, Associated Press Mike Stobbe, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-rfk-jr-speaks-at-conference-for-anti-vaccine-group-he-founded Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: RFK Jr. speaks at conference for anti-vaccine group he founded Politics Sep 17, 2026 8:34 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. gave the keynote address Thursday at a conference of an anti-vaccine activist group he once chaired, telling the hundreds in attendance that they had a friend in President Donald Trump's White House. Watch Kennedy's remarks in the video player above. It was Kennedy's first time appearing at the Children's Health Defense conference since he became secretary. Kennedy took leave from the group when he launched his bid to become president in 2023, but his speech Thursday served as a sort of homecoming, offering him a platform from which to hail the administration's steps to scale back vaccine guidance and reassure the activists in attendance that he was working to turn their priorities into policy. "Let me be clear: You have a strong and steadfast friend in the White House. We've accomplished in 19 months things that would have seemed unthinkable two years ago," he said. The speech, peppered with questions about long established vaccine safety, also highlighted how once fringe views on vaccines have been given a prominent pulpit under the Trump administration. Kennedy boasted about the administration's moves to downsize the childhood vaccination schedule and reshape a key vaccine advisory board — steps that have since been halted by a judge. Kennedy lauded Trump for pushing ahead with attempts to overhaul vaccine guidance, including an executive order last month calling for spacing out the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, against medical groups' recommendations. WATCH: Pediatrician says RFK Jr. sowing doubt about measles-associated deaths That executive order and now Kennedy's keynote speech at the Children's Health Defense conference mark a pivot by the White House and the Department of Health and Human Services, who earlier this year had appeared to be moving beyond vaccine efforts and toward a less contentious agenda on healthy food ahead of November's midterm elections. HHS promoted the speech on its social media channels. Kennedy, a longtime anti-vaccine activist, chaired Children's Health Defense for years. He served as the group's chief legal counsel and expanded it. After becoming health secretary last year, Kennedy moved at a blistering pace to overhaul public health guidance and revamp long-held precedents in vaccine policymaking. Critics, among them many of the country's top medical associations, have said the moves risk stoking vaccine hesitancy and sowing confusion among Americans who endured a crisis of trust in their public health agencies following the COVID-19 pandemic. That public confidence continues to erode. "We have not taken vaccines away from anybody. We have preserved access. But we have started asking the questions that you and millions of American parents have been asking for years," Kennedy told the group. Mary Holland, the CEO of Children's Health Defense, referred to Kennedy as "Bobby" and said the group has "gratitude beyond words" to the HHS secretary for "recognizing there are real consequential issues around childhood vaccinations." Kennedy's appearance Thursday comes as the country faces its worst year for measles since 1991 and has seen seven reported measles-associated deaths in the last two years — more than the combined total of reported deaths over the previous three decades. Pennsylvania officials have reported four measles-associated deaths this year. None of the four were vaccinated, according to the state health department. When state officials last month announced the first two of those deaths, it ignited a public feud between Gov. Josh Shapiro and Kennedy. Shapiro blasted Kennedy's appearance on the social media site X Thursday, saying Kennedy "chose to spend his time today addressing the premier vaccine-denial conference in America." Shapiro said the HHS secretary should have encouraged people to get vaccinated for measles, "yet he couldn't bring himself to do it. Instead, he pushed a narrative that continues to stoke fear and mistrust." A representative from the White House did not respond to an Associated Press request for comment on Kennedy's appearance at the event. Following Kennedy onstage Thursday was Andrew Wakefield, an author of a since-discredited study that linked the MMR vaccine to autism, which has fueled the anti-vaccine movement even though it was retracted. Widespread scientific consensus and decades of studies have firmly concluded there is no link between vaccines and autism. Shaughnessy Naughton, founder of 314 Action, a group that recruits scientists to run for public office, said Kennedy's decision to give a speech at the conference shows "the lack of seriousness he brings to HHS." "With a deadly measles outbreak killing people in Pennsylvania, the best thing Kennedy can do for Americans is step aside." Stobbe contributed from New York. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. In a border city stadium, US NFL fans sing Canada anthem with gusto
At a match between the Buffalo Bills and Detroit Lions football teams in Orchard Park, New York, both the American and Canadian national anthems played.
The Bills chose to honour their Canadian fans amid rising tensions between the US and Canada.
President Donald Trump, who is currently locked in an escalating tariff tussle with Ottawa, has, on a number of occasions, declared his ambition to make Canada the 51st American state. He blames Canada for taking advantage of the US through unfair trade practices and trade deficits.
The BBC's Robin Levinson-King spoke to fans ahead of kickoff about the symbolism of the anthem being played.

See tiny organisms on show in microscopic video competition
Nikon's annual Small World In Motion competition is open to anyone around the world with an interest in film or time-lapse photography through a microscope.
This year's winning video was magnified to 100 times in size, and featured tiny hair-like structures, called cilia, in the airways of a child with a rare genetic disease.
It was submitted by Dr Ning Xu, a researcher at Tsinghua University in China, who used a series of complicated light waves to illuminate different parts of the sample in colour.
Runners up in the competition included videos of a roundworm encountering a single-celled organism and microscopic jellyfish larvae suspended in droplets of water. Clips of bioluminescent algae and a tiny sea slug were among the highly commended.

The White House has withdrawn President Donald Trump's nominee to lead Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after a Republican senator joined Democrats in opposing his confirmation.
Richard Schroyer was serving as a senior aide to the secretary of Homeland Security when Trump picked him to lead the immigration enforcement agency in June.
The White House withdrew his nomination on Thursday in a short memo, which did not explain the decision. The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.
Republican Sen Rand Paul had stalled the nomination as he pressed for more information about ICE and Border Patrol shootings that killed two Americans in Minneapolis in January.
Schroyer had worked with the Oklahoma Highway Patrol for 29 years, and also served in the US Marines. He is a close ally of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, whose department oversees ICE and other immigration and border agencies. His selection by Trump was seen as a surprise given his lack of experience overseeing such a large law enforcement agency.
The position is one of many that needs to be confirmed by the US Senate. Schroyer's nomination did not manage to make it to a full Senate vote and had stalled in the Senate's Homeland Security committee.
ICE has not been led by Senate-confirmed leader since 2017 and instead has had a host of temporary chiefs. It is currently led by David Venturella, a former private prison executive, after Todd Lyon announced his departure from the top job in April.
The withdrawal on Thursday marks a defeat for Trump and Mullin, as the White House continues Trump's campaign pledge to lead the largest deportation effort in US history.
Paul, who serves as chairman of the Senate Homeland Security Committee, said he would not advance the nomination to a full vote until the White House provided more information about the Minneapolis killings.
National protests took place earlier this year following the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis.
Both US citizens, the two were protesting when they were fatally shot in separate confrontations with ICE agents in January.
One of the promises that helped Trump take the White House in 2024 - cracking down on illegal immigration - has now divided voters going into the congressional midterm elections less than two months from now.
At the same time, Representative Maria Elvira Salazar, a Republican from Florida, is warning that the crackdown could cause many of the Hispanic voters who supported him to turn their backs on the party when they go to the polls in November.
"Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far," she said in an advertisement filmed outside the White House that was released on Thursday. "Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy. The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today."

The Royal Observatory Greenwich has announced the winner of its Astronomy Photographer of the Year competition for an image of the Shark Nebula.
The dark nebula is made from interstellar dust dense enough to block starlight and is 650 light years away.
Steve Marsh, one of the judges and art editor at BBC Sky at Night Magazine, said the image by Ali Alobaidly showed "flawless presentation, pin-sharp details and dynamic contrast".
He added: "The Shark Nebula is already a striking object, but when it is resolved to the point where even detail-rich distant galaxies can be seen through it, you know you're looking at something very special."
Alobaidly, who won Â£10,000 for winning the competition overall, said he hoped to use his photographs "to make astronomy more accessible, engaging and meaningful through science communication and education", and described the award as a "tremendous honour".
For the 2026 competition there were almost 4,000 entries from 66 countries.
Alobaidly's entry, taken in Kuwait, was entered in the Stars and Nebulae category.
Nikolaos Strimpoulis, 15, won for ZWO Young Astronomy Photographer of the Year for his image Mineral Moon, taken in Palaio Faliro, Athens, Greece.
The close-up image of the Moon's surface includes dark areas known as maria and bright areas known as the highlands.
The orange and blue colours on the lunar surface are caused by iron and titanium deposits and it was for that reason that the image was given its title.
Marsh said: "Many of us start our astrophotography journey with the Moon â some of us stay there forever! But often we don't delve deep into the subtle colours of its mineral deposits until much later. This amazing young astrophotographer has achieved perfectly developed colouring in this photograph."
Dr Greg Brown, astronomer at the Royal Observatory Greenwich, said the entries from the 18th year of the competition demonstrated "skill and innovation" coupled with improvements in technology.
See more of the winning images:
An exhibition of the winning and highly commended images will be on display at the National Maritime Museum, London from 18 September.

- Published
A wildlife charity fears it could lose a funding grant after a burst pipe prevented vital conservation work.
It is the fourth time Long Mead Local Wildlife Site, at Swinford in Oxfordshire, has been flooded because of a mains failure.
Although the meadow by the River Thames naturally floods in the winter, standing water at this time of year can cause damage to the rare habitat.
Thames Water said the latest leak had been fixed and it remained committed to protecting local wildlife sites.
"It's already starting to stagnate, so that's serious," said Catriona Bass, director of the Long Mead Foundation.
"Floodplain meadows are used to flooding in winter when the plants are dormant.
"These meadows don't flood typically in summer and when they do it's a disaster because the plants are growing - so it kills off the plants."
The site is central to a restoration programme that aims to boost this type of specialist habitat across the county.
There are only four square miles in total of floodplain meadow in the country - the equivalent in size to Heathrow Airport.
The rare habitat is home to deep-rooting wild flowers and grasses like great burnet and devil's-bit scabious.
Long Mead meadow acts as a donor site where seeds are gathered to help restore other similar habitats around Oxfordshire.
Volunteers have hand-grown more than 11,500 individual specialist plants.
The latest flooding was discovered on the day that restoration works were due to start after the last incident.
Conservationists have said they are worried a grant the charity had secured is at risk if the work is not completed in time.
"We planned on the 1st September to do this massive restoration project to deal with the previous floods and now we're not going to be able to," Bass said.
A Thames Water spokesperson said: "We are sorry for the disruption caused and remain committed to protecting local wildlife sites.
"We have repaired a recent burst in Bettys Meadow and traffic management equipment is due to be removed shortly.
"The repair took longer than anticipated due to heavy rainfall and the volume of water, which meant our engineers were unable to safely access and repair the pipework until conditions improved.
"We will continue to assess the condition of the water main and review any further measures needed to help safeguard the area in the future."

Every Nigerian is now an oil magnate.
At least that is what the social media memes would have you believe as investor fever hits the country.
Nigerians have been eager to have a piece of the energy business that was built up by the country's â and continent's â richest man: Aliko Dangote.
More than four billion shares in his giant oil refinery â representing just over 3% of the company - went on the market on Monday in Africa's biggest-ever sale of its kind.
The minimum purchase was 10 shares for about $4 (Â£3) and despite this only representing a miniscule portion of the firm, many are now celebrating and joking about their new-found (part-)owner status.
One popular social media video has a Nigerian narrating how he stopped a speeding Dangote company lorry driver, telling him not to be reckless with company property.
Other memes show investors trying to phone up Dangote to discuss business matters.
And the term "Yangote" â a pun in the Hausa language essentially meaning "we all have a share now" - has been trending on social media.
On the first day of the Initial Public Offering (IPO), investment apps crashed as they could not handle the high demand.
Bamboo, which runs one of the most popular investor tools here, later apologised, saying: "We know we let you down."
Public affairs analyst Jamil Ubah said he had rarely seen Nigerians as excited about something as this. He argued that it fed the dream that it could lead to greater riches for a population that is often battling to make ends meet.
"I think the hope for the common man is that his money will grow into something big, and don't forget this is coming at a time when many are struggling as the economy is not doing great," he told the BBC.
Dangote wanted this to be "the people's IPO" with drivers, cooks, cleaners and servants having the chance to be part of something big.
And they took him at his word.
Twenty-five-year-old clothes seller Idris Lawal Musa made his first-ever stock exchange purchase and told the BBC he was happy after investing 21,000 naira ($16; Â£12) in 40 shares.
"It is no longer Dangote but 'Yangote', the company belongs to us now," he said while laughing.
But he may make a quick sale.
"I am a trader by profession and when I see that the shares have increased in price I will sell," he noted.
The popularity also reflects a growing investment culture among younger Nigerians who have embraced mobile trading platforms, cryptocurrencies and digital savings products.
But fear of missing out may have also pushed some to get into the investment business.
In the build-up to the IPO, social media platforms were awash with financial conversations. People shared subscription guides, debated valuation metrics and encouraged friends and family to participate.
But amid the frenzy, experts have warned that there are risks â shares can go down in value, as well as up, meaning people could lose some, or all, of their investment.
Financial analyst Shuaib Uwais said prospective investors should avoid thinking of the IPO as a guaranteed route to wealth.
He urged people to consider a number of factors that could impact the refinery's future performance, including disruptions to crude oil supply, operational challenges, regulatory changes and fluctuations in demand for refined petroleum products.
"If for any reason the company experiences difficulty in sourcing its raw materials, there could be challenges," he told the BBC.
Nevertheless, the IPO has given people the chance to be part of this home-grown success story.
Dangote's sprawling refinery on the outskirts of Lagos, which began operating two years ago and now processes around 700,000 barrels of crude a day, has transformed the fortunes of Nigeria's oil sector.
Until recently, Africa's largest crude oil producer had no refining capacity and had to import the finished product. Now the Dangote refinery is feeding much of the domestic demand.
But for Dangote, the share offer is about raising cash to fund the growth of the business, something that the country's mini-magnates may now be able to get behind.

Three people have been killed and eight injured in a shooting at a high school in Banga in the province of Mindanao, southern Philippines.
Two of the victims were 14-year-old students, Banga mayor Albert Palencia told the BBC. The gunman, 16, is among the dead, he said, while four of those injured are in a critical condition.
The incident happened on Friday afternoon at Banga National High School.
The Department of Education said in a statement that it was "deeply concerned by the reported shooting incident".
This is the third deadly school shooting in the Philippines since June this year.
"Our immediate priority is the safety and well-being of our learners, teachers and school personnel," the education ministry said, adding it was coordinating with authorities to verify the incident and provide necessary support.
"We urge everyone to remain calm and refrain from sharing unverified information as authorities continue their investigation."
Palencia told the Reuters news agency that during a lunchtime conversation on Friday, the gunman had urged friends to go home "because after lunch, [he would] be executing [his] plan".
"His friends laughed because the shooter was a known joker," Palencia told the news agency.
"After lunch, he started shooting students. He hit 10 students before killing himself."
Classes have been suspended "in all levels in the entire municipality of Banga" due to the shooting, the Banga disaster management authorities said in a statement.
The Philippines Red Cross said it was alerted to the incident at 14:00 local time and had dispatched an ambulance with four paramedics to provide life-saving assistance.
Police are at the site investigating the shooting, local media reported.
Gun crime is not uncommon in the Philippines, which has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in the region. Broadly speaking, school shootings are rare, but today's incident marks the third deadly campus shooting in the last four months.
In June, three students were killed and more were injured after their peers opened fire at a high school in central Philippines. Investigators believed the deadly shooting had been motivated by a "grudge" over bullying.
In August, a student at a Catholic junior high school in the southern Philippines shot dead a fellow student and later took his own life. In this case, the suspect had fired at the teacher, but missed, then moved to another classroom and shot a student, who later died.
Following the shooting on Friday, Reynaldo Tamayo, the South Cotabato governor, urged adult gun owners to "be responsible in storing firearms" and ensuring that minors do not get access to them.
"We cannot expect a handful of security personnel to monitor thousands of students. We need to work together because otherwise this will be very difficult for us to address," he told Reuters.

AI safety worries are hanging over Chinese leader Xi Jinpingâs visit to Washington next week, which is attracting big names in the tech world.
OpenAIâs Sam Altman will attend the Sept. 24 state dinner that President Donald Trump is hosting for Xi, Semafor has confirmed, and Nvidiaâs Jensen Huang and Appleâs Tim Cook are reportedly attending, too.
There are also discussions about an adjacent White House meeting with AI CEOs next week, which House Majority Leader Mike Johnson referenced, but a representative for the speaker declined to provide further details.
Still, it remains to be seen whether Trump and Xi will respond to calls for both countries to cooperate on AI safety.
Officials from both sides have expressed skepticism about AI regulation in recent days, with Trump citing the need to stay ahead of China in AI development as a reason for avoiding guardrails.
Chinese officials also rebuked Anthropic CEO Dario Amodeiâs essay about regulation as âfearmongering.â Axios earlier reported that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was open to discussing âshared risksâ around AI during his own meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng this weekend in New York City, which will help lay the groundwork for the Trump-Xi summit.
The White House declined to comment.

cd70e15aa345.text: Left-wing streamer Hasan Piker said he "absolutely" wants to campaign for New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez if she runs for president in 2028 and said he has talked with AOC and her team, he said in the new episode of "The Axios Show." Why it matters: Piker, who has millions of followers online, has been a high-profile campaign surrogate this year for a new generation of left-wing candidates, and wants to do the same in 2028. Driving the news: Despite Piker's ambitions, some Democratic politicians have begun distancing themselves from him because of his controversial commentary. Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan's Democratic nominee for the Senate, campaigned with Piker during the Senate primary. But after Piker told Axios that he believed America's long history of attacks in the Middle East that have killed civilians made it worse than al-Qaeda "pound for pound," El-Sayed said he disagreed and that Piker didn't speak for his campaign. El-Sayed has said Piker won't appear with him in the final weeks of the race before the Nov. 3 election. In an hour-long interview with Axios, Piker explained his worldview and defended his stances that some Democrats are distancing themselves from: China: Piker traveled to China last year and has said that the country is the closest government model he would like to see adopted in the U.S. He also thinks that "trajectory-wise, I worry that a Chinese child might have better conditions in the next decade or next two decades than an American one. And I think that should worry every American citizen." Asked about his past praise of Mao Zedong, Piker said "he's a great man of history. Of course, there were a lot of excesses." When asked to clarify what he meant as "excesses," Piker said: "Deaths borne out of mismanagement and famine." Political violence: Axios asked Piker about several of his past statements about killing or harming political opponents, and he said they amounted to "three or four choice quotes." He said he consistently says that the "appropriate way to deal with political problems, even violent ones, is to advocate, organize, and create a response that is borne out of labor militancy, work stoppages and the like, to apply political pressure that way." Talking with a friend on his stream, Piker once said of landlords who don't rent their properties: "Kill those motherf*ckers and murder those motherf*ckers in the streets. Let the streets soak in their f*cking red capitalist blood, dude." He told Axios that "we were messing around. It wasn't a serious call to violence." Piker — a frequent and aggressive critic of Israel's government — said he believes "Zionism is fascism" and that it was equivalent to neo-Nazism. Asked about the potential danger of his rhetoric, Piker said: "I'm not worried that [my followers are] going to be violent against Zionists. No, I'm not."

5362d8f082d1.text: A host of industry players, policy wonks and businesses are grappling with the question of how to regulate AI in a trustworthy manner. Inside the White House, it's mostly business as usual. Why it matters: The industry's mad dash is the product of an ad hoc regulatory apparatus and a general consensus that swift action from Washington is unlikely in the near term . State of play: AI CEOs have been grappling with how to test advanced AI and work with Beijing on safety standards, while the White House favors a solution where the industry finds ways to police itself. That means the race is on to decide who will be anointed as third-party evaluators of AI systems and controls as the companies await legislation or White House action beyond the current voluntary process. A robust ecosystem of safety and benchmarking groups already exists, but some White House officials and AI execs see them as too closely tied to top AI companies. Other options include businesses and startups that already do evaluations, as well as some more unorthodox suggestions. What they're saying: Companies have the most expertise when it comes to AI and understand what the White House's AI voluntary framework requires, according to a White House official. "These people are not 12-year-olds," the official said. "The top frontier companies need to come to a consensus on what they want because they haven't agreed on anything," the official continued. "If these companies feel it's such a dire situation, they have every right, reason, and ability to throttle their models." Friction point: Some third-party evaluators — including individuals at METR, which investigated the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident — have been singled out for having close ties to the effective altruism movement , as well as to companies they would be policing. One of the lead outside investigators of the Hugging Face episode is married to Paul Christiano , a seasoned AI safety and technology official who recently joined the board of OpenAI's non-profit foundation. An Anthropic employee recently left the startup to work at METR as well. METR has said it doesn't take funding from frontier labs. A spokesperson said Christiano joined the OpenAI board after the investigation concluded. AI companies and safety officials say the AI research community has always been small and close-knit, and employees from frontier labs are well-suited to evaluate model capabilities. Between the lines: Some facets of existing AI evaluation systems grew out of efforts to market the capabilities of new models, including how they perform on coding benchmarks and math tests. A wide array of companies, including defense and tech contractor Booz Allen, evaluate AI systems for clients. Many evaluations lack critical components, such as gauging how often models create software vulnerabilities or the variability in how they respond to prompts, said Eric Syphard, Booz Allen's head of AI. "They all lean in to that performance-only view of the world," Syphard told Axios in an interview. Elon Musk this week suggested labs in the U.S. and China could review each other's models, a prospect some see as unlikely due to the ferocious competition between top players. Other ideas have surfaced as well, including one former Trump adviser's call for legendary "coding god" and programmer John Carmack to step in. OpenAI offered a public incident reporting playbook this week after identifying six new incidents . Like the White House's AI framework, OpenAI's idea for public incident reporting is voluntary, as is Musk's peer review approach. OpenAI's public incident reporting idea involves third party auditors for more complex cases. Yes, but: "Public transparency is really important here. What these companies are doing is good, but it's only based on their goodwill and I don't think that's sufficient," SaferAI executive director Henry Papadatos said in an interview. What we're watching: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who will lead talks with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng this weekend, said there's an opening for safety talks with Beijing.

The warnings follow two recent flashpoints: In Equatorial Guinea, police were filmed pointing guns at migrants deported from the US during a dispute at a hotel housing deportees.

One of the manâs brothers served in the Afghan National Army while another was a US-trained pilot killed by the Taliban.

Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee. He pledged to âcontinue to investigate this matter.â
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., a Senate Foreign Relations Committee member, told Semafor he is âextremely disturbed and alarmedâ and said the administration has ânot been very responsiveâ to inquiries about the deportations.
âWe will be demanding accountabilityâ if Democrats flip the Senate in the midterms, he said.
âCruelty is so often the point for this administration, and there few better examples of this than the administrationâs deportation flight strategy that sends migrants back home to face persecution and imminent danger or to third countries where they have no history or support and that may imprison them or send them back home to face persecution and imminent danger,â said a spokesperson for Sen. On a weekday morning in a quiet Boston neighborhood, a kitchen bustled with activity. Volunteers sliced chicken breasts, stuffed bell peppers, filled trays, and carefully labeled each item. It was part of an experiment to offer nutritious and medically tailored meals to Medicaid patients who are unable to shop for groceries and cook for themselves.
“Once I started to eat these meals that were geared toward my illness, I built up my muscle mass again, built up my strength, built up my confidence in myself,” said Vanessa Georges, who is in remission from throat cancer and said she would struggle to consume enough calories without the deliveries. “These meals have given me a second chance.”
Georges said she noticed another benefit from the meals: She spends less time at the doctor’s office.
Researchers have found evidence backing her observation. About 1,900 Massachusetts residents who, like Georges, received medically tailored meals for at least three months needed less medical care, according to a study published in the journal Nature Medicine. They had 20% fewer emergency department visits and 31% fewer hospitalizations than similar patients who did not receive meals.
“It actually saves the healthcare system money,” said Dariush Mozaffarian, a cardiologist and professor at Tufts University who led the study. “That’s a really big deal, because most things in healthcare don’t.”
The research from Massachusetts adds to evidence that medically tailored meals could save states money — in addition to improving health. Yet such programs could land on the chopping block as states look to tighten spending under Trump administration budget cuts, even as federal officials argue that food is a critical component of health.
Medicaid Budget Cuts Loom
The 2025 law known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act slashed projected Medicaid funding by more than $900 billion. Many Republicans who backed the bill believe federal health spending is too high and riddled with fraud. Sen. John Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican, for example, has accused California of “outrageous fraud” for using Medicaid dollars to fund housing and nutrition programs.
Amaya Diana, a policy analyst at KFF, said states will have to make tough choices in the next few years as they figure out how to fill funding gaps. “If states are not able to offset the loss of federal funds with new taxes or reductions in other state spending, they may have to make program cuts,” she said. (KFF is a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News.)
Thirteen states have received federal waivers to use Medicaid dollars to pay for meals — part of an approach known as “food is medicine.” Three other programs are awaiting federal approval.
President Donald Trump’s support for social services has wavered. While the first Trump administration allowed states to pursue medically tailored meals and other social supports, the second Trump administration rescinded Biden-era guidance for Medicaid initiatives that address social needs. It hasn’t detailed a new policy. Administration officials have warned that they will be more focused on the budget impacts of such initiatives.
“They signaled they’re going to be a lot more skeptical,” said Kurt Hager, an assistant professor at the University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School who studies nutrition programs and helped lead the Massachusetts study. “Instead of using a broad-based approach nationwide, they’re going to make decisions on a state-by-state basis.”
At the same time, health leaders in Trump’s administration have made nutrition a major focus, including by promoting less-processed foods. Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who leads the Department of Health and Human Services, and Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, have pushed hospitals to serve healthier foods to boost patient outcomes.
The healthcare system is often willing to pay for surgeries, Oz said in a social media video in June, “but not always willing to pay for the nutrition that might help prevent those outcomes in the first place. That’s bothered me my whole career.” He added that the agency is evaluating several strategies, including medically tailored meals, to prevent illness and hospitalization. CMS officials did not respond to several emailed requests for comment for this article.
Katie Garfield, who studies social determinants of health at Harvard Law School’s Center for Health Law and Policy Innovation, said the lack of federal guidance is stirring uncertainty for states that want to pursue nutrition programs in Medicaid. “We’re still waiting to see that big step forward around ‘food is medicine’ interventions,” she said. “We need to see that step forward to resolve some of the uncertainty.”
Lawmakers have had a hard time engaging administration officials on medically tailored meals, said U.S. Rep. Jim McGovern, a Massachusetts Democrat who sponsored a bill that would pilot meal deliveries for some chronically ill seniors on Medicare. The legislation has yet to come up for a vote.
“I had thought, based on some of his rhetoric before he entered the Trump administration, that RFK Jr. would be a natural ally on this,” McGovern said. “But we can’t seem to get his attention.”
The Costs of Poor Nutrition
Some companies have been accused of billing Medicaid for meals that were neither healthy nor nutritious, raising concerns about lax regulation of these programs.
But at Community Servings in Boston, the food is prepared with specific attention to sugar, salt, fat, vitamins, and minerals and is based on a person’s health needs, said David Waters, chief executive of the nonprofit. Many recipients require food that is mild or low in fiber, for example.
“What we’re able to do is to work with your healthcare provider to understand your health realities — what your diagnoses are, what your medications are, side effects, food allergies, cultural norms — and then prescribe a diet for you that is scratch-made,” Waters said

The Drugs and Devices Have Been on the Market for Years. But FDA-Ordered Studies Still Aren’t Done.
When the FDA was deciding whether to approve the drug Tavneos several years ago to treat a set of rare autoimmune diseases, agency experts argued that would be a mistake, according to FDA records.
One problem cited: The manufacturer had provided only “limited safety data.”
As it often does, the FDA in 2021 approved the drug with a proviso: It required the manufacturer to conduct an additional years-long safety study once the drug was on the market.
Today, like many similar “postmarket” studies mandated by the FDA, that additional study is delayed, according to a federal database. As of last fall, only 21 of the planned 300 patients had been enrolled, the FDA said in an April letter and regulatory posting.
Meanwhile, the FDA has identified dozens of cases of liver damage “possibly” or “probably causally associated” with the drug. That was one of the potential side effects the postmarket study was meant to evaluate.
Tavneos illustrates the perils of the FDA’s approach to many drugs and medical devices — and the frequent lapses in follow-through.
A KFF Health News analysis of Food and Drug Administration data found hundreds of postmarket studies listed as delayed. In some cases, the work was delayed by more than a decade or the manufacturer was still developing a plan for the study.
As a result of delays, patients, doctors, and others could be left in a fog about the risks and benefits of the drugs or devices, even as they stake their money, their health, or their lives on the products.
Postmarket study requirements “have often proven toothless,” said cardiologist Sanket Dhruva, an associate professor of medicine at the University of California-San Francisco who has published related research.
The FDA’s reliance on postmarket studies reflects a balancing act.
Making new treatments available faster can save or improve lives, especially when patients with grim prognoses and no good options have little to lose. The full risks and benefits may be revealed only over the long term, and when therapies are used by far more people than even large clinical trials enroll.
But relying on post-approval studies to resolve questions risks exposing patients to products that do more harm than good. Whoever is paying the bills — patients, insurance companies, employers, or government health programs such as Medicare and Medicaid — can end up wasting money and rewarding manufacturers for useless or risky products.
“Doctors rely on this evidence, patients rely on this evidence, and if that evidence is not there, it’s going to lead to a lot of uncertainty,” Dhruva said.
Trump administration policy changes designed to hasten drugs through FDA review could leave more riding on postmarket studies, medical researchers say.
For example, in February, FDA leaders announced that “the default requirement” for agency approvals will be one clinical trial instead of two.
Reducing pre-approval testing “will inevitably put a lot of pressure on the post-approval system,” said Aaron Kesselheim, a professor at Harvard Medical School who has analyzed postmarket studies.
FDA officials said the new policy would “substantially reduce costs” for manufacturers and “speed drugs to market.” Writing in The New England Journal of Medicine, they denied the change would compromise safety or efficacy, saying that “erroneous conclusions may be reached even with two, three, or four studies.”
In response to questions for this article, a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, which includes the FDA, said postmarket studies can experience delays for legitimate reasons. “Assessing the significance of any delay requires a case-specific review,” said the spokesperson, Emily Hilliard.
The fact that a study is delayed “should not be treated as evidence that a product has an unresolved safety or effectiveness issue,” Hilliard said.
Amgen, the company that makes Tavneos, is still working on the postmarket research the FDA mandated, company spokesperson Alison Chartan said, adding, “We remain committed to completing this important study.”
Behind Schedule
An FDA database downloaded by KFF Health News in August tracks the progress of postmarket studies that makers of drugs or biologics — such as vaccines and gene therapies — were required to perform or promised to perform.
The database showed almost 600 were running behind schedule.
Of those, more than 250 originally had final reports due before July 31, 2026 — the date that, according to an FDA webpage, the database last had been updated.
About a third of ongoing studies were listed as delayed.
In some cases, the FDA has granted extensions. In others, it has denied them. And in rare instances, the products were discontinued before the studies ran their course.
Postmarket studies can involve clinical trials or other analyses of patient data. They can look at safety or efficacy. A product can be the subject of more than one postmarket study.
The nearly 600 delayed studies involved almost 350 products, KFF Health News found.
The FDA has defined delayed as behind the original schedule. That can mean off track or overdue.
As of August, other FDA databases tracking medical devices listed dozens of postmarket studies as behind schedule.
Products included:
The CustomFlex Artificial Iris, a prosthesis implanted in the eye in place of damaged, defective, or congenitally missing irises. The protocol for a study in children was accepted in 2019, the database said. The study was meant to follow patients for five years. According to an FDA page downloaded in August, zero patients were enrolled.
Barbara Fant of Clinical Research Consultants, to whom the FDA’s 2018 letter approving the product was addressed, said the rarity of an eye disease called aniridia poses challenges for post-approval studies. Healthcare prices are likely to keep increasing next year. As midterm elections approach, candidates are laying out their plans to tackle these growing expenses.
KFF Health News chief Washington correspondent Julie Rovner joined WAMU’s Health Hub on Sept. 16 to explain how healthcare could play a critical role in the midterm elections. She said similar cost increases in the early 2000s led to the debate that became the Affordable Care Act.
“We’re seeing people have to pay more in their — not just premiums — but their deductibles, how much they pay before their insurance kicks in, and how much they pay when they go to the doctor,” said Rovner, host of the What the Health? From KFF Health News podcast.
In recent years, it’s not uncommon for healthcare providers to ask for payment upfront.
“Now you get there, and they say, ‘Can we have your credit card?’ before you even get to go in and get your care,” Rovner said.

The California valley with the most dairy farms in the state will follow stricter water pollution requirements following years of advocacy and a marathon six-hour meeting this week.
The State Water Resources Control Board unanimously agreed to adopt the regulations under what several environmental groups call a long overdue dairy order.
Nitrogen from the manure dairies produce turns into excess nitrate in soil, waterways and groundwater, and can eventually contaminate drinking water.
Families and children in the Central Valley “are living in crisis,” said Leslie Martinez, of the Leadership Counsel for Justice and Accountability and Defensores del Valle Central para el Aire y Agua Límpio (Central Valley Defenders of Clean Air and Water), a group of San Joaquin Valley residents.
“Low-income rural communities of color rely heavily on shallow groundwater and face the greatest exposure,” Martinez said during Tuesday’s meeting in Sacramento.
More than 700 dairies in the state—concentrated in the Central Valley—are within 1 mile of an area at high risk for nitrate groundwater contamination, according to state figures from last September.
A 2024 state tally estimated that more than 1.7 million cows generated over $8 billion worth of milk in California. But dairy farms here also pollute nearby waters.
In a 2017 study, the University of California, Davis, concluded that agricultural lands, including those with dairy operations, “are the largest contributor of nitrate to groundwater in the Central Valley.”
The 131-page order that was adopted Tuesday was released at the start of September as a draft and detailed the new requirements limiting water pollution from dairies. In the order, officials acknowledged the “outsized contribution” of dairies to nitrate pollution in the valley.
Environmental groups, while not satisfied with every aspect of the regulations, were happy to see them approved. Some advocates have fought since the early 2000s to increase oversight and management of water pollution from dairy facilities.
In an October 2024 first draft of the new regulations, water board officials proposed requiring that Central Valley dairies comply with a nitrate drinking water standard of 10 milligrams per liter and meet new rules for storing waste, applying manure to fields of crops and providing alternative drinking water to residents when nitrate levels in their water supplies are unsafe. Those requirements held in the newly approved order.
Still, during Tuesday’s meeting, even supporters of the new requirements worried about public participation and whether Spanish-first speakers had been given ample opportunity to comment on the rules being outlined.
The new dairy draft order was released online to the public Sept. 4 and feedback on the latest version was only gathered in-person or via video during the meeting Tuesday. No written comments were accepted.
Environmental groups were also uneasy about whether tribal communities got an appropriate chance to weigh in.
Dairy industry representatives in Sacramento were wary about the new regulations and what impacts they may have going forward.
Michael Boccadoro, executive director of the industry group Dairy Cares, worried the order was “inconsistent” with the Central Valley Salinity Alternatives for Long-Term Sustainability, a collaboration that has worked for 20 years to tackle nitrate and salt accumulation affecting water supplies in the region.
Kevin Abernathy, general manager of the Milk Producers Council, another industry group, believes the new rules will leave smaller dairy farms vulnerable to takeovers by bigger operations.
“This has the potential to further consolidate the dairy industry into the Costco and Walmart world that we all live,” said Abernathy, noting he was concerned about small- and medium-sized family dairies. “Mark my words, what you guys do here today will further consolidate the industry.”
He added, “Ag and dairy has always done our part to protect the environment for all of us and be good stewards of all of our land.”
A Long List of Health Risks
The Central Valley water board oversees dairy farms under a 2013 waste discharge rule. Current state estimates list between 900 and 1,000 regulated dairies in California.
Existing regulations of dairy farms were adopted at the urging of the Environmental Law Foundation and the Asociación de Gente Unida por el Agua, known as AGUA, which sued the regional board claiming its 2007 dairy regulations were inadequate.
A Sacramento court of appeals ruled in 2012 that the board was out of compliance with California’s law to protect clean water.
Under the state Safe Drinking Water Act, the maximum contaminant level for nitrate is 10 milligrams per liter, said Peter Thorne, an environmental health professor at the University of Iowa.
“There’s evidence that if you’re consuming water in the range of, say, 5 to 10 milligrams per liter there’s still an elevated risk of cancer that has been documented in a number of different studies,” Thorne said. “Especially for gastrointestinal cancers, stomach cancer and colorectal cancer.”
Earlier this year, Stanford University researchers released a white paper outlining frequently underreported levels of wastewater and manure from large dairy facilities in the Central Valley.
The researchers highlighted failures by dairy owners to document where waste goes and by the regulators to properly enforce reporting requirements.
Drinking water contaminated by nitrates “can interfere with red blood cells’ ability to carry oxygen throughout the body,” the Stanford experts noted.
Infants are acutely susceptible to low oxygen levels, including from nitrate impacts to water, which can lead to the potentially fatal “blue baby syndrome.”
Some counties in the Central Valley have seen 40 percent of drinking wells with nitrate levels above the safe limit established by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, posing health risks such as miscarriages and infant mortality.

The State Departmentâs approval of the proposed $24.3 billion sale of 48 Lockheed Martin F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia represents a major victory for the kingdom, as Riyadh seeks US support amid increased attacks from Iran-backed groups.
The sale must still undergo congressional review, where it will likely face opposition.

Senators want to hit the campaign trail for the fall, but first they have to figure out how much they want to get done before the election.
Negotiators are close to agreeing on a bipartisan permitting reform deal, but they also have to get through a college sports bill that will take up all of next week âÂ absent a deal among all 100 senators to speed things up.
Senate Environment and Public Works Chair Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., told Semafor that while sheâs âoptimisticâ about the permitting deal, âitâs got to pop out of here in the next 48 hours.â
Asked about that timeline, ranking member Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., âwouldnât rule it out.â
And Majority Leader John Thune still could hold a roll-call vote on a data center power bill that Democrats blocked on Thursday.
Know More
Republican leaders are preparing for Democratic opponents of the college sports bill to dig in, dragging out the rest of the schedule. Majority Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., said he expects Sens. Cory Booker, D-N.J., and Chris Murphy, D-Conn., âare going to try to prevent it and slow us down in every possible way.â
Murphy said if GOP leaders agree to amendment votes, Democrats could probably reach an agreement to speed things up. The permitting reform bill would need to be ready to go as soon as the sports bill is done to get in the queue.
And Thune said passing the Ratepayer Protection Act â a bill from Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, that Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., blocked because it only includes voluntary language on data center power consumption â hinges on how those other big bills are doing.
âIt depends on next week â how quickly we move through [college sports] â¦ and then whether or not permitting comes together. It would take some cooperation,â Thune said.
If there is a bipartisan permitting deal, it would take up even more floor time and keep senators in Washington longer. The chamber is scheduled to go on recess on Oct. 2. Even getting that deal may require commitments from across the Capitol.
Whitehouse said heâd like Thune and Speaker Mike Johnson to present a bicameral road map for a potential permitting reform deal. He said that it âdoesnât matter what we do in the Senate, now or later, if they donât have an understanding in the House about when it gets taken up.â
âWill they come back before the election? Will they schedule something solid, a fixed date after the election? I donât have a program from them yet. Itâs not my call. But I do think itâs important that there be a Senate and House voting plan that the White House has checked off, and so thatâs what weâre looking at,â Whitehouse said.

The Signal Interview
Kai-Fu Leeâs AI Superpowers, an influential book published in 2018, largely predicted the current tech battle between the US and China. Now, Leeâs forecasting that AI will unleash more radical changes inside the worldâs companies than most CEOs expect â and this could reshape the competition between those two economies once again.
The former head of Google China, who has also held senior executive roles at Microsoft and Apple, understands intimately how Silicon Valley leaders think. But now that Anthropicâs Dario Amodei has called on the industry and its regulators to âpace the frontier,â Lee says he would reframe that call: âMove fast, but make sure safety keeps pace.â
Lee says he agrees with the principle that developments in AI capability must be matched by advances in safety and governance, adding that industry collaboration will be âparticularly important at this stage,â given how governance and regulatory frameworks âinevitably lag behind technological development.â
He is now deeply embedded in Chinaâs AI industry as chairman of the Beijing-based venture capital firm Sinovation Ventures and founder-CEO of 01.AI, a Chinese âAI tigerâ that has pivoted from building AI models to helping enterprises deploy the technology effectively.
Leeâs transpacific perspective has given him a unique insight into the challenges that global companies face in realizing AIâs potential. In a video interview, he says two things are clear from his conversations with other chief executives: âOne is that they all want to do AI transformation. Two is theyâre mostly doing it wrong.â
Lee is pitching his new book, AI Native, as a road map for doing it right. CEOs hoping to build an âAI-nativeâ company must take personal charge of their technology strategy, he says, and use âradical transparency,â enabled by AI, to give them unprecedented insights into what is actually happening inside their organization. That conscious echo of the management mantra of Bridgewater Associates founder Ray Dalio, he adds, is an idea that Chinese employees will embrace faster than Western workforces.
Why transformation starts at the top
CEOs everywhere face âa Darwinian choice,â Lee says: Embrace AI or accept the consequences. They have little time to do so, he adds; companies whose assets are largely digital, like entertainment, gaming, and internet businesses, will be âdead in the waterâ if they do not adapt, he says. CEOs operating businesses further from the AI frontier â like coal mines, farms, or manufacturing plants â may have a three-to-five-year âbufferâ before they feel the pain of AI disruption.
That means executives need to ask now whether they are passing âthe earnings call test,â Lee says: If their companyâs AI efforts have not yet boosted their profits, then they are mere âAI theater.â
Where chief executives go wrong, in any industry, is when they delegate and defer to their chief information officer, Lee argues. âOnly the CEO can define the ambition, concentrate resources, redesign the operating model, remove barriers, and remain accountable for the result,â he writes in AI Native, so AI transformation âcan only be done from the top.â
That also means that each CEO needs to be using AI effectively themselves, he adds. Doing so demonstrates that the companyâs leader understands AIâs importance to the bottom line.
The radical transparency of Boss AI
Lee has taken his own advice, designing a âdecision assistantâ made up of 19 agents to help him run 01.AI. His company has since packaged this up into a product to sell to other companies, called Boss AI.
At its heart is what Lee calls a âtruth engineâ that records, organizes, and analyzes every internal meeting, sales call, and customer service request to show what is getting in the way of the company meeting its goals. That gives a CEO visibility into all corners of their company â and a âpromise ledgerâ to hold people accountable for following through on what they say theyâll do.
âMiddle managers often hope that the CEO will forget. And the CEO does forget, but the CEOâs AI does not,â Lee says. It is at this tier of most companies that the bossesâ plans meet the most resistance, he adds.
âThere are a lot of antibodies in the company, people who just donât want to do AI transformation. Middle managers feel vulnerable because theyâre not technology experts, [and] theyâre afraid the boss will put in someone who is,â he explains. Those managers also fear losing their power if their company lays off their direct reports, he adds.
Still, even as he says that AI is dividing workforces into âirreplaceable humansâ and âdisplaceable humans,â Lee does not think that CEOs should measure AI success by the number of jobs they eliminate.
âThe winners will not measure success by payroll cuts. They will measure it by what their best people, amplified 10 times, can now do that was previously impossible,â he writes in his book. Most people will not be laid off if theyâre willing to learn new AI skills, he adds, âbut they might be paid three or five times moreâ than before.
But he still believes that companies should flatten the hierarchies that protect people who resist change. âWhen the company is transparent, thereâs no need to hide, nowhere to hide, and everybody talks about the real issues and tries to solve the problems.â
Where clashing cultures meet AI superpowers
Lee presents his ideas as âexhilaratingâ for employees who are willing to sign up for them. âThe company will have a better morale, better culture, better execution, better results, better stock price, and everything will be a virtuous cycle and the company will grow,â he predicts.
Even so, Lee admits that radical transparency âtakes [some] getting used to.â Some corporate cultures will be more reluctant than others to expose themselves to the bossâ all-seeing AI, he adds, bringing his argument around to a point which converges with his earlier predictions about AIâs impact on geopolitical competition.
