British singer Ed Sheeran is facing growing backlash over a controversial decision to drop rapper Macklemore from the rest of his US tour after Macklemore made pro-Palestinian comments on stage.
The decision - which Sheeran said was made by his promoter, not by himself - has caused ticket sales to decline, supporting acts to drop out, and fans to express frustration.
Sheeran's first show since the debacle began will be on Saturday in Philadelphia, and pro-Palestinian groups are planning to protest outside the venue.
Here's everything you need to know about the controversy.
What happened?
While performing as the opening act for Sheeran at a concert in early September in New Jersey, Macklemore said: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine."
The Thrift Shop rapper then performed a song dedicated to pro-Palestinian protesters at Columbia University. The lyrics are critical of Israel's military actions in Gaza following the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel.
The following night, Macklemore referred to the death toll as a genocide, a claim that Israel rejects.
In response, the Israeli American Council launched a petition demanding his removal from the tour, and the campaign group StopAntisemitism said the musician had ambushed fans with propaganda.
Pop star Pink, who is Jewish, reposted an anti-Macklemore meme and then her own message, explaining her criticism of the rapper's comments.
Macklemore then posted on Instagram that the media attention "surrounding Pink and what I said" had caused billionaire stadium owner Robert Kraft to call Sheeran.
"Ed told me that Kraft said I would not be allowed to perform in his stadium," Macklemore wrote of Kraft, who also owns the New England Patriots American football team.
Concert promoter Messina Touring Group said Macklemore was dropped because some venues - such as Kraft's Gillette Stadium - would cancel Sheeran's planned concerts if Macklemore remained on the bill.
Kraft, who is Jewish, confirmed he banned the US rapper from performing at Gillette, accusing Macklemore of hate speech and antisemitic rhetoric.
"I agree with Macklemore, too many lives have been lost and there has been too much suffering, but only sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas is not honest and only advances more divisiveness and hate," Kraft said.
Macklemore was removed from Sheeran's tour on 14 September.
What have Ed Sheeran and Macklemore said?
The rapper said in a lengthy Instagram statement that after a week of "difficult conversations" with Sheeran that ultimately ended "in a place of fundamental disagreement", he was dropped from the lineup.
Sheeran said the call was made by Messina Touring Group. The Bad Habits and Shape of You singer said he respected "Macklemore's strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes", adding that while he doesn't use his own platform for politics, that "doesn't mean I don't care" or "support causes in my own, personal way".
In his statement, Macklemore said he empathised with the difficult position Sheeran was in but criticised the English singer for not taking a stance.
"Taking a side can cost you. Money, brand deals, sponsorships, festivals, private shows, relationships and access. I've lost all of those things. But there is no neutral position between the oppressor and the oppressed," he wrote.
The rapper, who in 2014 apologised for a costume he wore on stage which critics said was anti-Semitic, also addressed the accusations of antisemitism, writing that "one of the most effective ways to enforce silence has been to weaponize the accusation of antisemitism".
How have fans reacted
In his statement earlier this week, Sheeran said: "There is a reason I do not use my professional platform for politics - my audience includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds."
The singer-songwriter also said he did not want to let down his fans or crew by cancelling the tour.
Sheeran fans and ticket holders are torn about the situation. Some have said that without all the supporting acts, the show is no longer what they paid for.
Damien Given, who is from Northern Ireland and has tickets to Saturday's show, told the BBC that he felt that Macklemore was treated "very, very wrong" and thought Sheeran was not being transparent with fans.
Given said that Sheeran can't suddenly say he's not political because he had previously voiced support for Ukraine after Russia invaded the country.
But another fan named Patti Ann told the BBC that Sheeran was in a "no-win situation".
"I back [Sheeran] 100% for his decision," she said. "I feel like he has an obligation and a contract with his venues, and sometimes, financially, you can't get out of those types of things."
Ticket resale prices for Sheeran's remaining US concert dates have decreased since the controversy began, with some going for below market value.
The controversy has also snowballed into other areas of Sheeran's career. Ireland's Classic Hits Radio announced it was removing Sheeran's music from its playlists because of feedback from listeners who had expressed "disappointment and concern" over his US tour. Sheeran was raised in England but has said he identifies culturally as Irish.
Who were Ed Sheeran's support acts and why did they pull out?
Irish singer-songwriter Aaron Rowe, Danish band Lukas Graham, American singer-songwriter Finneas, and Irish folk band Beoga quit Sheeran's tour following Macklemore's departure.
In a post on Instagram, Rowe thanked Sheeran for the opportunity but said he "cannot stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power" to silence people who criticise Israel's actions in Gaza. "Free Palestine," he added.

President Donald Trump has said his son paid back a Russian oligarch with close ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin for hosting post-wedding festivities in the Bahamas.
Asked in the Oval Office about Umar Kremlev's involvement in Donald Trump Jr's celebrations, Trump said it is "totally allowed" and that it is "very common" to give wedding parties for others.
After an investigation said Kremlev paid "hundreds of thousands of dollars", the couple confirmed he partially funded two nights of their three-day festivities on a private island as a gift.
Trump did not say how he knew the Putin ally was paid back. The BBC has not verified payment was made and has contacted Trump Jr.
Trump Jr, the president's eldest son, is a private citizen, so it is not illegal for him to accept gifts from a foreign national.
But ethics watchdog groups have said that the president's son accepting an expensive gift from someone associated with a foreign head of state presents the appearance of a conflict of interest â even if Trump Jr is not a US government employee.
President Trump's ties to Russia have raised questions since his 2016 campaign, and led to a special counsel investigation into a meeting attended by Trump Jr with a Russian operative at Trump Tower.
Kremlev runs the International Boxing Association (IBA), which is funded by the state-backed Gazprom energy company. The organisation was suspended by the Olympic Committee in part over its failure to report its ties to the Russian energy giant.
Kremlev was also a member of a delegation that visited China with Putin in May. He has been given the Order of Friendship, a top state honour, by the Russian president, according to ProPublica, which published the investigation about the wedding events.
Trump Jr's spokesperson told the news outlet that the president's son and Kremlev were personal friends and did not have "a business relationship".
Kremlev's office told ProPublica that he and Trump Jr met a few years ago and "have a friendly relationship".
The BBC has contacted representatives for Kremlev for comment.

Residents in Saudi Arabia's Riyadh have been given the all-clear after air raid alerts were issued and explosions were reported in the capital.
It was the first time alerts have been issued in Riyadh since the Houthis increased their attacks and declared a "maritime embargo" on the Saudis in July.
The Saudi Civil Defence sent alerts for the capital and several other regions late on Friday night and Saturday morning (local time) as the Kingdom's conflict with the Iran-backed Houthis continued to escalate.
Journalists from Reuters and AFP reported hearing explosions in the capital, but authorities have since said the danger has passed. Residents were urged to avoid gathering in crowds.
The Houthis recently seized control of the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island, a gateway to a key shipping route used by the Gulf state to export to Asia and Europe.
The Iran-backed group's military spokesman said the naval blockade was in retaliation for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled north-western Yemen.
Saudi vessels have relied on that stretch of the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.
Last week, the Houthis attacked several Saudi oil facilities with drones and missiles, causing fires which led to operations being temporarily halted.
The attacks on Saudi oil assets have directly impacted global energy markets and the price of petrol and diesel in many countries has sharply risen in recent weeks, compounding already elevated costs caused by the blockades of the Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the country's de facto ruler, has personally asked US President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News, the BBC's US media partner.
Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, offering instead to assist with intelligence and targeting support, the sources said.
A senior Trump administration official told the BBC: "We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen government regarding regional stability."
Earlier this week, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said the Houthis had launched drones and missiles at Saudi Arabia in retaliation for more than 450 Saudi air strikes on their territory over the past week.
The United Nations Security Council held an emergency meeting on Tuesday, during which both Yemen's government and Saudi Arabia called for more decisive action against the Houthis, who they accused of choking the Bab al-Mandab Strait as a way of applying economic pressure.
Council members agreed that freedom of navigation in the Red Sea must be maintained to prevent disruption to global supply chains.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
The fighting has reportedly left more than 150,000 people dead and triggered one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, with more than 22 million people in need of some form of aid, according to the UN.
Additional reporting by Tabby Wilson.

Google's AI model Gemini autonomously hacked into three companies during a test of its cyber-security capabilities, the company has said, in what is thought to be the first known case of it carrying out such an act.
Gemini found "public information online and guessed credentials to access websites it thought were part of the test", a Google official told the BBC, noting that in each instance "the model stopped".
The affected companies have been informed about the breach.
It comes after renewed public scrutiny over the pace of AI development, with some tech firms calling for a slowdown as they raise concerns over its potential threat to humanity - though not all companies agree.
The hacks first reported by the Wall Street Journal, occurred in May during a test conducted by an independent company that carries out cyber-security evaluations.
Heather Adkins, vice president of Security Engineering at Google, told the BBC in a statement: "We ensured the three entities were made aware, and we worked with our training partner on the changes they've now made to their testing processes."
She added: "These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly."
Other AI systems have recently reported similar instances of breaches.
In July, Anthropic's Claude escaped its test environment to hack three organisations on its own just days after OpenAI said its models had carried out cyber-attacks against several "publicly available services".
As public debate continues to grow over the safety of developing the tech, so too does conversation around regulation.
Both Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang and OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman are expected to attend a White House state dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping next Friday. Altman will then brief the UN Security Council next week.
On Friday, Huang told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, "we should go as fast as we can" with AI development.

As parts of the West Midlands baked in warmer temperatures this summer, species once considered unusual in the region, such as hummingbird hawk moths, ivy bees and the wasp spider have been spotted in growing numbers.
The hummingbird hawk moth, known for its furry grey body, orange hindwings and long proboscis, migrates to the UK from southern Europe and north Africa in the summer months.
James Benwell, from the Birmingham and Black Country Wildlife Trust, said 2026 was a "record year" for sightings of the species, which was often mistaken for a small bird.
The moth, which can be seen hovering over flowers, has wings that beat about 80 times per second, external, according to Benwell.
"They've had a really good year this year," he said. "Normally they would come in small numbers. We'd normally hear of a few maybe. But this year, we've seen loads of records of them.
"They're absolutely amazing but I somehow haven't seen one this year, so I'm jealous of anybody else that has."
Ivy bees, which feed mainly on the nectar of ivy flowers, had also become more prevalent in the Midlands, Benwell said, adding they were easy to find on buildings.
The bees, first recorded in the UK in 2001, are slowly spreading north, after first being recorded in the region in Stourbridge in 2015.
"There's nothing that distinguishes them from other bees really, they're not that kind of attention-grabbing species, but, you know, were you to look for them, go to ivy and you'll see them," Benwell said.
Other insects that had seen an increase in their numbers locally included the clouded yellow butterfly, a European migratory species known to have "peak" years during unusually hot summers.
"Most individuals are unable to survive the British winter, but if temperatures continue to rise as a result of climate change, we may well see them becoming permanent residents," Benwell said.
"There's numerous species that we could point out that weren't here 20 years ago... and now they're quite abundant."
Others once more commonly associated with southern England have also spread further north.
The trust said the hornet hoverfly, with yellow markings that mimic a hornet to protect against predators, although it cannot sting, had become really common after it was first recorded in Birmingham and the Black Country in 2004.
Another species, the cricket bat spider, which gets its name from its cricket bat-like markings, has also become more common in grassland since it was first spotted in the region in 2019.
The sightings come as one of the UK's largest spider species, the wasp spider, was spotted in the Midlands as warmer temperatures pushed it more than 100 miles away from its usual habitat.
The spider has recently been recorded in Worcestershire, alongside sightings in Herefordshire and Warwickshire, said the Worcestershire Wildlife Trust.
Rosemary Winnall, from the Wyre Forest Study Group, which maps the wildlife and ecology of the forest in Worcestershire, said the arrival of the wasp spider was to be celebrated.
She said the group was always on the lookout for new arrivals and had already recorded the willow emerald damselfly, the southern oak bush cricket and the purple emperor butterfly, as more species travelled north.
"The impressive western conifer seed bug is here as is the box bug," she added.
Hot weather had also benefited butterflies that loved sunshine, such as the holly blue and the pearl-bordered fritillary, which the Butterfly Conservation charity, external said was once "very widespread" but had rapidly declined in recent decades.
However, despite an increase in some species appearing in the region, there were others whose numbers were dwindling.
"The once-common small tortoiseshell butterfly is now rarely seen for example, and there are far fewer records of the two-spot ladybird," Winnall explained.
"We are encouraging folk to record the common species of today as they may be the rarities of the future."

- Published
US President Donald Trump has signed a sweeping sanctions bill, taking aim at Russia's economy by punishing major purchasers of its oil and gas.
The bill, passed by the US House of Representatives earlier this week, gives Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas â most significantly China and India.
At Trump's behest, the bill also extends to Iran's energy and weapons sectors.
The bill is named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, one of Ukraine's staunchest defenders in Washington before his death on 11 July.
The 48-page bill, formally titled the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, includes exceptions for countries that import less than 15% of their natural gas from Russia and are working to lessen their dependency.
Additionally, the bill includes sanctions against Russian President Vladimir Putin, senior figures within the Russian government as well as banks and other financial institutions and Russia's "shadow fleet" of tankers used to circumvent existing sanctions.
Senator Richard Blumenthal, a New York Democrat, previously described the legislation as "scorching sanctions" which would "throttle Putin's war machine".
Data from the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, or CREA, shows that China accounted for 50% of Russian crude exports between December 2022 and August 2026, followed by India at 37%.
Turkey and the European Union each accounted for 5% during the same time period, although Russian energy exports to the EU have been decreasing.
Senator Graham had long sought to push the Trump administration to do more to punish Russia for the war that followed its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
The bill also had the support of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who praised its passage by the House of Representatives earlier this week.
"It is symbolic that the US House of Representatives' passage of Lindsey Graham's sanctions bill took place on the night of yet another Russian attack on Ukraine involving ballistic missiles, other missiles, and drones," Zelensky wrote on Telegram on 17 September.
Graham, 71, died on 11 July of an "aortic dissection" caused by cardiovascular disease shortly after returning from a trip to Kyiv.
"He died doing the work he was born to do," Trump said at the time.
Prior to his death, he was widely considered one of Ukraine's fiercest allies on Capitol Hill, at a time when Republicans were bitterly divided over the extent of US involvement abroad and the amount of aid being given to Ukraine.

From our collaborating partner “Living on Earth,” public radio’s environmental news magazine, an interview by host Steve Curwood with climate scientist Michael Mann.
As the United Nations prepares to hold a climate summit in late September, it’s warning that current climate policies will lead to at least 1.8 degrees Celsius of global warming, well beyond the 1.5 degrees of the Paris Agreement. This year recorded one of the hottest summers globally, with deadly heat waves in Europe and catastrophic floods in Nepal, and July became the single-hottest month ever recorded in the U.S. Despite the evidence of growing danger, the Trump administration is moving to dismantle regulations that constrain warming emissions from power plants and other sources.
Michael Mann is the presidential distinguished professor of Earth and Environmental Science and director of the Penn Center for Science, Sustainability, and the Media at the University of Pennsylvania, and author of the book “Science Under Siege.” He recently shared his assessment of where we stand in the climate emergency, and what the newest numbers mean. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. The full interview can be heard on Living on Earth.
STEVE CURWOOD: One and a half degrees centigrade above pre-industrial levels is the number that many in the climate space are quite familiar with, especially in association with the Paris Agreement. Keeping the average rise in global temperatures ideally at that level or at least below two degrees centigrade is what we’re hoping for. What’s the harm of going above those numbers?
MICHAEL MANN: It might sound like a small amount of warming, right? But when the human body warms up that much, it’s called a pretty serious fever. Even though you’re only talking about a couple degrees on the thermometer, you know what the consequences of that fever are. Coughing, difficulty breathing, you’re delirious. You’re suffering all sorts of health consequences, and in a sense, that’s the same thing here.
That thermometer scale is telling us that Earth is running a fever, and we’re seeing the consequence of that fever in terms of the heat domes, the wildfires, the floods and all of the impacts that it’s already having. We’re not even at 1.5 Celsius yet—3 degrees Fahrenheit, basically—and already we’re seeing dangerous climate change. At this point, it’s not like we’re going to avoid dangerous climate change. It’s here, and it’s a matter of limiting it as much as we can.
“When you put all that together, the climate crisis and fossil fuel dependence is more deadly than the deadliest pandemic that we’ve experienced yet.”
We may miss the 1.5 degrees Celsius exit; it looks very likely that will happen now, especially because of two years of inaction here in the U.S. with the current administration. That next exit, 1.8 degrees Celsius, would be a whole lot better than two, and it’s still absolutely achievable … We can get there.
CURWOOD: Talk to me about the health and social implications of increases at this scale in climate disruption.
MANN: Extreme heat is a killer, and thousands of people are dying from just extreme heat events here in the United States that have been made more extreme because of human-caused warming; you have dangerous and deadly flood events, superstorms. We saw several thousand with that Tibetan flood, that glacial collapse, and we can say that was caused by climate change. Those floods were directly related to the melting of a glacier that only happened because of human-caused warming of this planet. That’s not even getting into all of the wildfires and the extreme heat events that we saw this summer; thousands of people died in Europe because of extreme heat.
Now, when you take into account the health consequences of fossil fuel extraction and processing, I think the estimate is that 20 percent of all excess mortality today can be tied to air and water pollution that’s linked to fossil fuels. When you put all that together, the climate crisis and fossil fuel dependence is more deadly than the deadliest pandemic that we’ve experienced yet.
CURWOOD: To what extent is the planet warming faster than many scientists had predicted?
MANN: There’s a lot of misinformation out there about this, and there are some scientists who are making extravagant claims that I would argue don’t actually match the evidence. The planet’s average temperature right now has increased almost exactly as much as the models said it would, given our continued burning of fossil fuels. If you look at the global average temperature record, along with the spread among the models that the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change used in their last assessment, the observations are right in the center of those model simulations. I like to say, “The truth is bad enough.” We don’t have to exaggerate that. The reality is that the planet is warming up exactly as we said it would, and those models tell us it will continue to warm more if we continue to burn fossil fuels. The models have gotten right the overall warming of the planet.
CURWOOD: To what extent are the impacts coming faster than what science had predicted? What about the impacts of the glaciers cutting loose, these heat waves and fires? To what extent did science predict that?
MANN: That’s exactly right; many of these impacts are actually happening earlier, or the magnitude of the impact is greater than what we predicted. The planet is warming up as much as we expected, and the consequences of that warming are worse than expected with regard to extreme weather events, the disintegration of ice sheets, sea level rise and any array of impacts.
CURWOOD: What do you think it would take to get the public level of concern about the climate to equal what’s being said loudly about artificial intelligence risks?

On a recent canoe trip to the remote upper reaches of the Narraguagus River, Ellie Mason saw prime Atlantic salmon habitat everywhere.
Though small, the river and its tributaries are some of the wildest in Maine, largely undeveloped and surrounded by forest. There are shady refuges for fish on hot summer days, and the rocky river bottom offers plenty of nesting spots for eggs.
But the salmon are missing.
The Gulf of Maine’s Atlantic salmon are listed as endangered under the federal Endangered Species Act. In recent decades, only about 25 wild adult salmon have returned to the Narraguagus each year to spawn.
The main stem of the river runs about 40 miles from its source in the downeast lakes to its head-of-tide in Cherryfield, where an ice-control dam that stood for more than 60 years has just come down. It’s being replaced with a “nature-like” set of stair-stepping pools that will still slow down the ice jams that used to flood Cherryfield, but shouldn’t slow down salmon, river herring, shad and other migrating fish. Construction began in June and is set to wrap up by November.
Mason, a 29-year-old habitat restoration project manager at the Downeast Salmon Federation, is running the show day to day. She fields calls from government agencies about permits one minute and answers questions from engineers the next.
Although Mason grew up nearby on Mount Desert Island, she had never seen an adult salmon until last year.
“The thing about growing up here is there are no salmon,” she said. “I think there’s really little understanding of what a river of this scale actually historically held.”
Scientists estimate that in centuries past, before their decline—caused largely by dams and log driving on rivers—hundreds of thousands of salmon would return to Maine’s waters each spring to spawn. These days, only about 1,000 come back to the state from the sea each year.
Mason and other young conservationists are the latest of multiple generations of people in Maine and Canada who have pitched in to help these fish. Some have dedicated their whole lives to the cause, including many in downeast Maine.
“This fish gets under your skin,” said Christopher Federico, the executive director of a regional coalition of landowners and conservationists called Project SHARE, which stands for Salmon Habitat and River Enhancement.
The group has been working for more than two decades to improve habitat on the Narraguagus River. As a result, the Cherryfield dam was the only remaining barrier for sea-run fish on the main stem of the Narraguagus.
The rest of the river is ready and waiting. But there’s no guarantee Atlantic salmon will come back. Other challenges remain.
These endangered fish have been dying in large numbers at sea. Researchers have different theories, but many of them fall “under the broad brush of climate change,” said Rory Saunders, a fisheries biologist with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
Maine’s remaining salmon population has also become dependent on hatcheries, which produce eggs and juveniles that humans then stock in rivers to prop up the wild population. While the hatchery system has helped keep Atlantic salmon from extinction, it hasn’t succeeded in growing their numbers, according to Saunders’ NOAA colleague James Hawkes, who recently co-authored a study on the salmon in the Narraguagus.
In order for Atlantic salmon to be reclassified from endangered to threatened, Maine would need to see at least 1,500 wild adult salmon returning to its rivers each year for multiple years, among other criteria. In order to be delisted entirely, at least 6,000 wild adults would need to return annually, spread over different watersheds from the Androscoggin up to the Dennys; their offspring would need enough suitable habitat; and the population would need to be growing.
Whether Atlantic salmon and the people who care about them will reach those goals remains an open question.
“The Connectivity Business”
Before the salmon were officially listed as endangered in 1999, the people and companies who own much of the land Downeast—working forests and blueberry barrens—saw the writing on the wall. They wanted to avoid repeating what Federico described as a debacle between the timber industry, conservationists and the federal government that followed the listing of the spotted owl in the Pacific Northwest.
So a group of these landowners—including regional giants American Forest Management and Wyman’s—formed Project SHARE. They got involved in the conversation about how to help Atlantic salmon, and eventually they got involved in the work.
In the early 2000s, the group identified 61 culverts on the Narraguagus River that were blocking the passage of fish and began replacing them one by one. They also began working with the state to “chop and drop” large trees into the river, aiming to make the river narrower, deeper and cooler once again.
Ernie Atkinson, a fisheries biologist with the Maine Department of Marine Resources, said his agency is “in the connectivity business.” Clearing the way for salmon and other sea-run fish to move freely up rivers is the first priority. After that, the goal is to rehabilitate the habitats the fish will find along the way.
While people can’t restore the river back to wilderness, they can rehabilitate it so it functions as a healthy coldwater habitat again, Atkinson said.
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers built the main barrier on the Narraguagus, the Cherryfield dam, in 1961 to hold back ice jams that used to flood the town.
The dam had a fish ladder on one side, which alewives navigated relatively well. Some salmon passed through, but fisheries officials often saw adult salmon schooling on the side without the ladder, unable to find their way. Shad are even more sensitive, and few got through.
The dam held back the ice for decades, but inspections over the years revealed it was aging.
“Something had to be done,” said Cherryfield selectman Corey Smith.

A rare catch-and-kill order has been issued for a great white shark off the coast of Western Australia, after a man was killed while on a morning swim at a popular beach on Friday. His body has still not been found.
Authorities have said that beaches along the state's coast, including in the capital Perth, will remain closed until at least Sunday as the search for the shark continues.
It is the second shark attack in Western Australia (WA) this week, and the third fatal attack in the state this year.
The incident, at Sorrento Beach in Perth's north, has reignited debate about how to keep beachgoers safe in Australia.
The swimmer has been identified as 63-year-old Greg O'Neill, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) has reported.
"Greg loved the ocean and was known as a passionate swimmer, sports lover, dedicated worker and an all-round generous, witty guy," his family said in a statement to the broadcaster.
Witness Jacqui Rapaic told the ABC that two men were swimming, but only one made it back to shore, and that she could see "a pool of blood" in the water.
Another witness told WAtoday that she saw the man being "mauled" as the shark "tossed him around like a fish".
Members of the public reported seeing a 2.5m-long (8ft 2in) shark at around the same time.
Authorities in Perth's Joondalup area, where Sorrento is located, said all beaches were closed "as a precautionary measure" and would remain so until at least midday on Sunday.
Pictures on Saturday showed the coastline being patrolled by a police boat and helicopter.
Catch-and-kill orders are rare and controversial in Australia, where great white sharks are a protected species.
WA Fisheries Minister Jackie Jarvis said that she took the "extraordinary step" of issuing the order after the shark was spotted by water police on Saturday morning, and "positively identified as the shark involved in the incident".
The minister said she authorised fisheries officers to "destroy the shark" if it could be captured because of the "exceptional circumstances" of the attack and the "hazard posed by the shark".
It is believed to be the first time in 10 years that such an order had been issued in WA, Jarvis added, emphasising that the order was not a widespread cull as the state has seen in the past.
The minister also said that the use of drones and tagging would be increased to help protect beachgoers.
Catching and killing sharks has a long and controversial history in Western Australia - there were months of huge protests in 2014 when the state government authorised a cull after a spate of attacks.
The incident in Sorrento is the second in WA this week - on Monday a 56-year-old man was bitten while surfing off the coast of Geraldton, 430km (270 miles) north of Perth. He survived but lost part of his leg, another surfer who rescued him told the ABC.
There have been five fatal shark attacks in Australia this year.
A 12-year-old boy died after he was bitten in Sydney Harbour in January, and three divers were fatally mauled in separate incidents between May and June - two in Western Australia and the third in Queensland.

Jaques and Paulina Sebastiao were the first residents on their street to rebuild their two-bedroom house two years after Hurricane Michael’s 155 mile-per-hour winds leveled almost every building in Mexico Beach in 2018.
Few of their old neighbors in the Panhandle fishing village followed their lead. Some didn’t have insurance, and others battled their insurance companies over claims. Some neighbors just didn’t want to go through the lengthy and expensive headaches involved with building a new house from the ground up under stricter building codes, especially when many of them were in their early 60s.“I think age had a lot to do with it,” Jaques Sebastiao said.
New owners soon scooped up beachside lots that had once held modest homes around the Sebastiaos. They built multimillion-dollar McMansions with a half-dozen bedrooms or more that they often rent out to vacationers when they’re not using the homes themselves. The Sebastiaos’ tight-knit neighborhood group fell away as former neighbors decided not to move back.
“It went from a middle-class neighborhood to now a lot of multimillion-dollar investment properties,” Jaques Sebastiao said recently. “None of the people who said they were going to move back here, moved here.”
Although the Florida hurricane season this year has been comparatively quiet so far, up and down the state’s coastlines, populations of communities that were recently thrashed by more frequent and intense storms have been remade economically and socially in what has been dubbed “post-disaster gentrification.” Beachside neighborhoods that were once home to working-class or middle-class people are being replaced by younger, wealthier residents who can afford the higher costs of rebuilding and through-the-roof homeowners’ insurance.
Who Doesn’t Come Back
In the early 2020s, U.S. Census Bureau surveys identified who was least likely to return to a community following a natural disaster. Black and Latino households were more likely never to return compared to white households. Renters, the poorest households and people who didn’t finish high school were less likely to return than households in higher income and educational brackets. People with disabilities and members of the LGBTQ community also were more likely never to return, according to the bureau’s Household Pulse Survey.
The reasons include a lack of insurance, limited access to assistance and unaffordable housing after a storm, according to research from Ther Aung and Ashwini Sehgal at the MetroHealth Institute for Health, Opportunity, Partnership and Empowerment in Cleveland.
“People of color and with lower income also are likely to live in places that increase their exposure to hazards, such as areas more prone to flooding,” Aung said in an email.
Post-disaster gentrification also has been taking place in communities decimated by wildfires in recent years, according to a working paper published last month by researchers from the University of British Columbia, the University of California San Diego, the University of Virginia and the Census Bureau.
On average, half of destroyed homes remained unoccupied four years after a wildfire, they found. In homes that were rebuilt, the incomes of residents were higher than those of residents before the fire, and the share of people over age 65 was lower. The incomes of residents living in destroyed homes that had been rebuilt started climbing in the second year after the wildfire, according to the researchers.
Local officials’ desire to rebuild neighborhoods under stricter codes, so that new homes can withstand future storms, often conflicts with the need to find housing for displaced residents. The cost of rebuilding also goes up when materials and workers are in short supply.
“Whereas institutions and business interests tend to benefit from hazard gentrification, residents at the lower end of the socioeconomic ladder tend to bear the brunt of its negative effects,” researchers led by Justin Stoler at the University of Miami wrote last year.
Few Options After a Hurricane
Bridget Fown was living with her two children in Cape Coral when Hurricane Ian’s more than 12-foot storm surge flooded her three-bedroom rental just a few blocks from the southwest Florida coast in September 2022. Her landlords were told by city officials that they couldn’t rehabilitate the house since it was too old and didn’t comply with new codes requiring elevated foundations, even though its cinderblock walls and foundation were still intact. Fown and her family were left without a roof over their heads.
“Like many other people who got caught up with losing everything during Ian from the flooding, there were no rehousing options,” Fown said recently. “I mean, there was nothing to aid you in getting back into another place.”
Fown stayed with a friend, and her children stayed with other friends in a camper on the friends’ property. Fown searched for a new rental up and down Florida’s southwest coast but couldn’t find anything because a substantial chunk of the rental market had been wiped out. More infuriating for her, each time she filled out an application, she had to pay a nonrefundable fee, ranging from $100 to $175 per adult in her household. Her daughter was 19.
“I blew through $5,000 looking for housing, just like everybody else did, and nobody got their money back,” Fown said.
As Christmas approached that year, Fown had enough.
“I just couldn’t do this because we were separated on two different ends of town,” Fown said of her kids.

The countries most vulnerable to climate change are spending nearly 25 times more on repaying debt than on climate action, according to a new ActionAid report released Wednesday.
The report, “Debt Fuels the Climate Crisis: How the Finance Flows,” is “really unpacking the narrative about how the climate and debt crises are supercharging each other,” said Teresa Anderson, one of the authors and global lead on climate justice for ActionAid International, a nonprofit global federation focused on poverty eradication and social justice.
Across 65 highly climate-vulnerable countries analyzed, debt servicing is expected to consume 65 percent of government revenue in 2026. “They are only getting to keep one third of the money that they are actually raising, but that’s for climate, healthcare, education and public services,” said Anderson.
The imbalance comes as many of those countries are already struggling with both mounting debt and intensifying climate impacts. More than 93 percent of the climate-vulnerable countries are either in debt crisis or at significant risk of one, according to the report. “A lot of that debt was taken on very unfair, illegitimate terms and shouldn’t really be part of the economic picture today,” said Anderson.
Compounding the problem, much of the international funding intended to help developing countries address climate change comes in the form of loans. According to the report, two-thirds of the money labeled as climate finance by Global North countries has been provided through loans, potentially adding to countries’ existing debt burdens.
Countries in the Global South have to pay back their external debt in dollars, pounds or euros, which are stronger currencies than their own.
Countries may also pursue exports that are harmful to the environment—including fossil fuels—because they need to earn the foreign currency required to service their debts, Anderson said. In other words, fossil fuel production can become not only an energy issue but a fiscal one: exports provide the foreign currency governments need to repay creditors.
Climate disasters deepen that cycle. In the aftermath of a major flood, drought or other disaster, foreign investors may withdraw capital or become more reluctant to invest, weakening demand for the country’s currency. “When there is a decrease in demand, that makes your currency depreciate more, so you have to come up with much more local currency to pay your debts,” said Kevin Gallagher, director of the Boston University Global Development Policy Center.
Zambia offers a stark example of how that vicious cycle can play out.
Between 2023 and 2024, an El Niño-driven drought devastated crops across the southern African country, affecting more than 9 million people and contributing to severe food and water shortages. Cereal production fell sharply, while drought-driven power shortages disrupted businesses and livelihoods.
As the crisis deepened, some families turned to increasingly desperate ways of coping. “We saw quite a number of barter exchanges happening where, for example, child marriages went up because in Zambia, when you marry a young girl, you get in return some resources,” said Michael Mwansa, ActionAid Zambia’s thematic lead on climate justice.
At the same time, Zambia has little room in its budget to prepare for the next climate shock. According to ActionAid’s analysis, the country is spending more than 60 percent of its government budget on debt repayment this year, while just 0.32 percent is budgeted for climate resilience and adaptation.
The report proposes several ways to break the cycle.
One recommendation is to cancel unpayable or unjust external debts, with the goal of ensuring that no climate-vulnerable country spends more than 10 percent of its national revenue on external debt repayments. “Is it realistic, based on current political will? No. But can you do it? Sure,” said Niranjali Amerasinghe, executive director of ActionAid USA, based in Washington, D.C.
For Zambia, Mwansa said that canceling unpayable or unjust external debts would be a real game changer. “If Zambia’s debt were to be canceled, it would have the capacity not only to respond to the current climate crisis, but also to address other social amenities,” he said. “We are talking about social protection programs, health and education.”
Gallagher cautioned that outright debt cancellation could have unintended consequences. “The majority of their debt is from multilateral development banks, such as the Asian Development Bank or the World Bank. The problem is if you just cancel that debt outright the banks will get their credit ratings downgraded and then they won’t be able to lend affordably—which might make further debt distress inevitable,” he said.
Instead, Gallagher pointed to another option, also cited in the report: renegotiating the terms of existing debt. That could include reducing the amount countries owe without eliminating the debt entirely.
The report argues that today’s crisis calls for a deep relief, exceeding the scale of the major debt-cancellation initiatives of the late 1990s and 2000s. The goal, Amerasinghe said, is to “ensure that countries are in a place where they can balance debt repayment in fair terms with what they need to spend on.”
Overall, the burden is greatest in sub-Saharan Africa, which is the region hardest hit by the cycle of climate shocks and debt distress.
Gallagher hopes that this report will be read by decision-makers in the International Monetary Fund-World Bank meeting in Bangkok next month. He is also hoping that the United Kingdom “steps back into a leadership position as they host the G20 on debt next year,” looking beyond this year’s G20 in the United States.

Millions in Cuba were left without power on Friday as the country was plunged into yet another major blackout.
The country's entire electricity grid suffered "total disconnection" that triggered a nationwide outage, Cuba's energy ministry said.
Power was restored to some priority areas by late evening, including those near hospitals and water pumping stations in the capital Havana, grid operator UNE said.
It is at least the sixth partial or total blackout to hit Cuba this year, where ageing electricity infrastructure and chronic fuel shortages have been placed under further strain by a US blockade on oil shipments to the communist-run nation.
UNE said the outage started just before 14:00 local time on Friday (18:00 GMT) due to a transmission fault coupled with poor weather conditions in central Cuba.
Protocols to begin the "gradual restoration" of power were activated, the operator's national load dispatch director Felix Estrada said, with the process ongoing on Saturday.
Cuba relies heavily on fuel imports, meaning tight US sanctions and an oil blockade since the start of the year have exacerbated existing shortages.
Food and medicine have also become more scarce, with hospitals struggling to function normally and schools and government offices having to close.
"Lately, it's becoming a habit," Havana resident Frank Lorenzo told news agency Reuters on Friday.
"Before it happened less frequently - once a monthâ¦ just yesterday we were 24 hours without electricity, they turned it on for just an hour and it went down again."
"It's one thing after another: no water, no gas for cooking, no electricity," 36-year-old schoolteacher Lidia Fernandez told news agency AFP. "Honestly, I don't know how we haven't gone crazy."
Francisco Rodriguez, 78, said his home had already gone without power for 28 hours on Friday and feared he would not have light "for several days".
The repeated blackouts have prompted rare protests in Cuba, where unauthorised demonstrations are illegal and those who defy the ban risk being jailed.
Havana has blamed its fuel crisis on the Trump administration and denounced all of its sanctions - including a new round announced in August - which are part of a wider pressure campaign against the Caribbean island's leadership.
Cuba's regional ally Venezuela was believed to have sent it around 35,000 barrels of oil a day - about half of its oil needs - until Venezuela's own supplies were cut off following the US seizure of its President NicolÃ¡s Maduro in January.
US President Donald Trump has threatened tariffs on countries shipping oil to Havana, and a number of such shipments have been seized by the US.
Washington meanwhile attributes Cuba's energy crisis to poor internal management and has accused it of posing a "national security threat". Trump has openly discussed toppling its leadership, including threatening a "friendly takeover" in March this year.

0a3cca8e1bf8.text: Republicans scrambling for midterm momentum are making a massive bet on football, pouring millions into advertising during the country's biggest NFL and college games. Why it matters: Across the country, Republicans are trying to hold onto male voters — football's core audience and a critical part of President Trump's 2024 coalition. After winning 55% of the male vote in 2024, Trump has seen his standing with men deteriorate. A new Fox News poll puts his approval among them at 42%, down 9 points from a year ago. The signs of slippage are particularly clear among young men. A spring Harvard Youth Poll found men ages 18–29 favored a Democratic congressional candidate by 8 points, after reporting an even split between Trump and Harris in 2024. By the numbers: Part of Republicans' plan to try to change the midterm vibe is to capitalize on their financial advantage by dominating the football airwaves. They ran 5,546 TV spots during the NFL and college games and pre-and-postgame programming where they advertised most heavily last weekend, compared with 471 for Democrats — nearly 12 times as many, according to ad-tracking data obtained by Axios. Republicans' biggest presence was during the blockbuster Texas-Ohio State matchup, which featured teams from two states with competitive Senate races. The pro-GOP Senate Leadership Fund (SLF) super PAC spent $2 million, airing ads in every quarter before 14 million viewers on ABC. The national coverage meant viewers nationwide saw Senate ads that were targeted to Texas or Ohio. Zoom in: Nowhere is the GOP's football strategy more apparent than in Michigan, where the Senate race could determine control of that chamber. SLF struck a deal with a vendor that manages sports programming in Michigan bars, putting its ads on more than 1,000 TVs at 150 bars across the state. Republicans launched the effort after Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed made critical remarks about football, which became the focus of the ads. A super PAC supporting Republican Mike Rogers premiered its latest ad attacking El-Sayed during Thursday night's Lions-Bills game and will air it again during Saturday's Michigan State-Notre Dame game on NBC. Zoom out: The push extends beyond advertising. Turning Point USA, the conservative group once led by Charlie Kirk, launched "Grand American Tailgate," a get-out-the-vote tour of college campuses on football Saturdays. This weekend it heads to Oxford, Miss., ahead of the Ole Miss-LSU game. Minnesota Senate candidate Michelle Tafoya is spotlighting her career as an NFL sideline reporter, while Arizona House candidate and former NFL kicker Jay Feely highlighted his football career during his speech at the GOP's midterm convention. Rogers campaigned at last weekend's Michigan-Oklahoma game in Ann Arbor and gave an interview outside Michigan Stadium — the "Big House" — noting that his dad had been a high school coach. The White House is joining in with football-themed social posts, including one showing Trump dancing to Fox's NFL theme. Flashback: In 2024, Republicans spent millions on ads during football games attacking Kamala Harris over transgender issues, including transgender women participating in women's sports. Trump advisers credited the ads with helping him make inroads with young men. The presidential margin among men under 50 swung 11 points toward Trump between 2020 and 2024, according to Pew Research . Republicans are reviving the strategy. The pro-GOP Congressional Leadership Fund ran two ads during last weekend's Iowa-Iowa State game, including one attacking a Democratic candidate on transgender issues. Texas Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, who faces Democrat James Talarico in November, is airing ads on the same issue during NFL games. Yes, but: Democrats aren't abandoning football. Talarico will advertise during Sunday's Dallas Cowboys-Washington Commanders NFL game, for which a 30-second candidate spot costs $200,000, according to the ad buying company Medium Buying . What they're saying: Republicans say football's enormous reach is worth the price. "Smart campaigns and organizations recognize that live sports remain one of the last few remaining shared cultural events where millions of Americans watch live," SLF Political Director Domenic Re told Axios.

062e32e6ad36.text: Data: Axios research. Note: Some countries use a quota system for gasoline. Malaysia's figure reflects the unsubsidized market rate. Chart: Noah Bressner/Axios The Iran war is driving fuel prices higher worldwide, leading to angry protests around the globe and straining the economies of countries that have nothing to do with the war. Why it matters: It's not just driving up prices in the U.S. The war is causing problems around the world — in some cases far worse than anything Americans are experiencing. The surge in prices squeezes consumers, and worsens the finances of governments trying to contain the shock — especially poorer and developing countries with little fiscal running room. It affects many nations that are also facing higher prices for natural gas, diesel and other fuels. Zoom out: The map above, based on World Bank data, shows the upward global trend. Yes, but: Price increases vary greatly from country to country. A number of countries that are heavily reliant on fuel imports, like Pakistan and Myanmar, have seen steep price hikes. But the U.S., the world's largest oil and gasoline producer, also has soaring prices. Crude oil prices, the biggest input into gasoline costs, are set on global markets. The U.S. federal government, unlike some nations, has not set caps or subsidies on retail prices. Context: Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries are also helping to boost motor fuel prices, especially diesel. The big picture: With no resolution to the conflict in sight, many governments face hard choices — strain their budgets with fuel support or face the political consequences of higher fuel costs. State of play: Dozens of nations have taken steps to cap, subsidize or lower taxes on various fuels, per the International Energy Agency. Governments are also taking steps to reduce demand, such as more remote work and limiting government travel. The International Monetary Fund is worried about the fiscal hit from price supports, especially if they outlast the energy shock. "[A] large share of measures described as temporary lack clear expiration dates or fiscal cost estimates," senior IMF officials wrote over the summer. What they're saying: "Many places have failed to reduce demand and are instead artificially constraining prices," said Joseph Webster, an energy scholar with the Atlantic Council. "This approach is misguided: gradual, managed demand reduction is far less politically damaging than sudden, sharp, and chaotic rationing," he said via email. He also said countries should taper withdrawal of subsidies, because allowing prices to soar overnight can bring unrest. Zoom in: Rising fuel costs are compounding existing inflation, public debt and youth unemployment problems in Kenya, Carnegie Endowment for International Peace scholars wrote in late August. It's also among the nations slammed with higher fertilizer costs as a result of the war. The country, which relies heavily on Middle East fuel imports, had major protests in May, and its problems are not unique. "Kenya's case serves as a signal for others in the region caught downstream of the war's economic blow," they write, arguing for greater "resilience" measures that make nations less vulnerable to external shocks.

'Enough is enough': Women protest after string of murders near Johannesburg
Runners gathered in South Africa to pay tribute to Elizabeth Moselakgomo after her body was found east of Johannesburg.
She is one of nine women found in the Kempton Park area, since July.
The jogger, known as "Tsontso", went missing during a routine run.
Runners organised an event in city of Centurion to honour her and defend women's right to run freely.
"This is for her - we just want to live and go running and come back home without having to think that it may be one of us", said Nonhle Mpohlo.
In Cape Town, people gathered in a vigil to honour the victims and called on the government to act.
The police have since set up a task team to investigate the murders and have urged women in the Kempton Park area to avoid walking or running alone "particularly in isolated areas".

A nature reserve will double in size due to a generous gift left in a will, a wildlife trust has said.
The donation has secured more land at Jackson's Coppice and Marsh Nature Reserve near Eccleshall, Staffordshire.
An area of wet woodland and marsh has been acquired alongside pastureland south of the River Sow. Public footpaths and a scheme to slow the flow of the river in heavy rainfall are being planned.
"This is fantastic news for wildlife and a wonderful example of how gifts in wills can create lasting change for nature," Jeff Sim of Staffordshire Wildlife Trust said. The donation was made by trust supporter David Aldred.
Plans for the floodplain land include coppicing mature alder trees and managing willow growth to support a greater diversity of plants and wildlife.
Under the trust's ownership, the floodplain will enable the river to flow slower during heavy rainfall and will alleviate flooding downstream.
The reserve's expansion provides public footpaths over the new land, so visitors will be able to explore different trails, the trust said.
"We can restore habitats on a much bigger scale, making more of a difference to the wildlife that relies on these places to live, feed and breed," Sim added.

d70f85b7c203.text: By — Jocelyn Noveck, Associated Press Jocelyn Noveck, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/ms-now-cnn-and-politico-say-their-journalists-were-denied-access-to-white-house-after-trump-ban Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter MS NOW, CNN and Politico say their journalists were denied access to White House after Trump ban Politics Sep 19, 2026 12:24 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — Reporters from three major news organizations — CNN, MS NOW and Politico — were denied access to the White House on Saturday, a day after President Donald Trump said he was barring them because of reporting he found to be "fake news." The actions were a clear escalation of Trump's long-running efforts — in the courts and through administrative action — to restrict news coverage by journalists he finds objectionable, and the latest test of First Amendment protections in the United States. Trump had said Friday he would ban all three outlets because of coverage he disliked. WATCH: Trump says he's banning 3 outlets from White House in his latest attack on press freedom White House reporters from the two cable networks — Betsy Klein of CNN and Akayla Gardner of MS NOW — both went live to report they'd been turned away when arriving for their jobs at the White House. Soon after, Politico said its White House reporter Cheyenne Haslett was also denied entry and had her badge confiscated. Politico Editor-in-Chief Jonathan Greenberger said in a statement to the Politico newsroom: "We stand by her and all reporters here covering the White House. … We will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights." CNN and MS NOW issued similar statements. "We will not be deflected from our duty to hold the government and other public bodies to account," CNN said. Please check your inbox to confirm. "The White House belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars," MS NOW said in its statement. "MS NOW intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy."' In his second term, Trump and his administration have upped the ante and punished certain media outlets, both in the courtroom and through regulatory action. Trump has also lashed out at individual reporters in person or over social media, sometimes in strikingly personal terms — insulting them in briefings, or in his recent speech at the White House Correspondents' Association dinner. CNN and MS NOW correspondents are turned away Network correspondents are usually present on the weekends when the president is in Washington or at nearby Camp David. Trump is at the presidential retreat in Maryland this weekend. MS NOW's Gardner reported that she had walked through two gates successfully, but once she got to where her badge needed to be scanned, an officer told her it was disabled and asked her to hand it over. He said the decision "was above him," she reported. An MS NOW producer was able to get in, but a photographer's badge was also disabled, Gardner said. Klein, senior White House reporter at CNN, also said her badge had been deactivated. It was confiscated, and she was handed back the clear plastic case. She said she was referred to the White House press office for further information. WATCH: Trump says he's banning 3 outlets from White House in his latest attack on press freedom Amy Kristin Sanders, a professor at Penn State University and an expert in media law, said it has "become pretty clear that this administration is not interested in playing by traditional First Amendment rules and norms. "The second Trump administration's efforts to crack down on press freedom and delegitimize independent journalism far exceed those of any other modern American president," Sanders said. "It is not an exaggeration to say his hostile actions toward news organizations and individual reporters have a chilling effect on freedom of expression around the world." CNN media analyst Brian Stelter called the move "a direct threat to press freedom in the United States." "It's so much bigger than CNN," Stelter said. "This is a free speech test in America." Trump calls these and other outlets 'fake news' The president wrote on his social media site Friday that effective immediately, "I am banning" CNN, MS NOW and Politico "from the White House as a result of their constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!" Minutes later, speaking at an event in the Oval Office, Trump was asked to explain his statement. "Because they're fake news," he said. "You get so tired of reading and seeing fake news. When you look at CNN, it's just fake. That's why their ratings are no good. When you look at MS NOW … , it's fake news." "And when you look at Politico ... the stories they wrote are fake. So there's a lot of news and there may be others to join them, and maybe they can get better," he said. "But our country has to have honest news." The move follows the president's decision last year to bar Associated Press reporters from the Oval Office, Air Force One and other events in retaliation for the news outlet's decision not to follow his lead in changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico, which lies partially in Mexican and other waters. The AP said that it would note when appropriate that Trump had ordered it renamed the "Gulf of America." The AP filed suit and the case is ongoing. Since returning to office, Trump has pursued other legal action against a variety of different outlets, including The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and the BBC. His administration is also involved in a long-simmering confrontation involving ABC over renewal of its broadcast licenses. Associated Press journalist Mike Householder contributed. A free press i

Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts on Friday evening to protest President Donald Trump's plans for the facility, lending their voices to a chorus of organizations and individuals who have been horrified that he might make good on his threat to close and tear down the storied institution. The crowd streamed in from the nearest subway stop, crowding streets in the Foggy Bottom area of Washington and locking down traffic as they walked, many carrying signs, as they joined in "Hands Around the Kennedy Center." At one point some held hands and formed a human chain around the center. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Chris Raleigh, co-founder of Hands Off the Arts, which set up the gathering, said in an interview that he hoped the event would show that people are willing to fight to keep Trump's plans for the building at bay. One of the most iconic buildings on the Potomac River waterfront, the Kennedy Center has been a focus of Trump's remake of Washington since 2025, when he began installing favorites onto its governing board. Late last year, he had his named placed on the center. A judge ruled that Trump's name was illegally added and ordered it removed. WATCH: News Wrap: Judge says Kennedy Center must provide notice before making changes to building The Kennedy Center board, which is aligned with the president, voted Tuesday to close the center indefinitely for repairs hours after U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper blocked their plans to return Trump's name to the building. On Thursday, the judge ordered the Kennedy Center to provide 30 days' notice before making any major physical changes to the building, including demolishing it. Raleigh said he, like others, is concerned that Trump could take the step without notifying the court. "Look at the East Wing," he said. "We got up one morning and there was a giant hole there." Raleigh said the Kennedy Center is more in the public eye than the East Wing was. He added he doesn't believe the president fully understands why people are so upset "but that's our job right? This may be the line that no one expected but this is where the line is going to be." A landmark of the performing arts has gone silent Protesters talked about the importance of the center as the pinnacle of the nation's performing arts world. Bud Wilkinson, a local member of the arts community, set up a chalkboard with Trump's name written on it hundreds of times. Protesters flocked to him to erase the names and replace them with hearts. "The Kennedy Center is vital to the arts in Washington. We need it. We need this," Wilkinson said. "This is not just about putting the president's name on the Kennedy Center. It's about censoring the performances and the programming. That's what started all this. So that's what the nitty-gritty really is about this. So I want to replace all of this with love. That's why there's a heart." Alina Baciu talked about the opportunities and relationships that students at the Duke Ellington School of the Arts have with the center and how those relationships might be impacted by what's going on. People attend at a protest to denounce the Kennedy Center board's vote to close one of the nation's premier performing arts venues, outside the John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 18, 2026. Photo by Leah Millis/Reuters Her daughter had numerous opportunities to take advantage of all the center had to offer as a student at Duke Ellington, she said. "I mean, they borrowed the beautiful costumes and the beautiful dresses from the Washington National Opera for their performances at Duke Ellington," she said. They also performed on the center's Millennium Stage. "All of those things have gone away because of this craziness. And it just hurts my heart," Baciu said. Laura Steinberg, a volunteer for the last 10 years, said the loss of performances has already been heart- wrenching. "This reminds me of that picture from Tiananmen Square, where that young man stood in front of the tank," she said of the throngs present. "This was my visceral response to this. I'll stand in front of the wrecking ball if it's going to come to that. My guess is many of these people would come down because we saw what he did to the East Wing. Nobody thought he would actually do it. So I think the shock has mobilized people." Friday's event followed a tumultuous week in federal courts in Washington where filings and counter-filings flooded the courts as the administration continues pushing for the president's vanity projects. The administration has made substantive steps to begin work on a number of projects, despite the fact they are still being litigated. Such projects include Trump's triumphal arch and the administration's takeover of East Potomac Golf Links and the U.S. Institute of Peace. Speaking from the Oval Office, Trump said he was willing to save the center, which he said was losing money. He did not address a question about demolishing it. "We have a lot of people working very hard on it to save it," he said. "I can save it easily, but why should we be doing that and then raise money for the rest of our lives to keep it afloat?
